nodes.title: Classical Weil cohomology theories
nodes.statement: A classical Weil cohomology theory over an algebraically closed field k with coefficients in a field F of characteristic zero is data (D1), (D2), (D3) satisfying: (A) Poincare duality, namely for X of dimension d, finite dimensionality of each H^i(X), perfectness of the pairing from H^i(X) times H^{2d-i}(X) to F given by cup product followed by the trace, vanishing of H^i(X) outside the interval from 0 to 2d, and bijectivity of the trace map; (B) the Kuenneth formula, namely that the map from the tensor product of H^*(X) and H^*(Y) to H^*(X times Y) sending a tensor b to the cup product of the two pullbacks is an isomorphism; and (C) compatibility of cycle classes with Gysin pullback, with proper pushforward, with the intersection product against the cup product, and the normalisation that the trace of the class of the spectrum of k is one.
hypotheses: k is algebraically closed and F has characteristic zero.
The data (D1), (D2), (D3) is fixed.
Axiom (A) is stated for a variety of dimension d, so the four parts are indexed by that dimension.
proofSteps: State the four parts of Poincaré duality separately; the cohomological pushforward of MC.2/weil-pushforward uses only (A)(a) and (A)(b).
State the Künneth axiom as the requirement that a ⊗ b ↦ pr_1^*a ∪ pr_2^*b be an isomorphism of graded F-vector spaces, not as an equality of dimensions.

State the four parts of (C) separately: (C)(a) for the Gysin pullback f^! of SF.5 along an arbitrary morphism of smooth projective varieties, (C)(b) for proper pushforward, (C)(c) for the intersection product and (C)(d) for the class of Spec k.

Record Remark 0FGU: given (C)(a), axiom (C)(c) is equivalent to γ(α × β) = pr_1^*γ(α) ∪ pr_2^*γ(β); the identity α × β = pr_1^*α · pr_2^*β behind it is stated in the source without proof and is imported from SF.5.
acceptance: All three axioms are required; the data alone do not determine any of them.
Axiom (C)(d) is a normalisation: multiplying every trace map by the same nonzero scalar λ ≠ 1 preserves (A), (B) and (C)(a) to (C)(c), since the pushforward does not change, and violates only (C)(d).
Given (C)(a), axiom (C)(c) is equivalent to compatibility of cycle classes with exterior products, the form used in Kleiman's definition.

nodes.title: Cohomological pushforward and the projection formula
nodes.statement: Assume data (D1) and (D3) satisfying axiom (A). For a morphism f from X to Y of smooth projective varieties with X of dimension d and Y of dimension e, define the pushforward from H^{2d-i}(X) to H^{2e-i}(Y) as the contragredient of the pullback under the two Poincare pairings; explicitly, the pushforward of a is characterised by the identity that the trace over X of the cup product of the pullback of b with a equals the trace over Y of the cup product of b with the pushforward of a, for all b. Then the pushforward of the cup product of a pullback with a class is the cup product of that class with the pushforward, and pushforward is functorial in f.
hypotheses: Data (D1) and (D3) satisfying (A) is given; axioms (B) and (C) are not used.
f is a morphism of smooth projective varieties and g a second one, composable with f.
proofSteps: Use (A)(a) and (A)(b) to identify H^{2d-i}(X) with the F-dual of H^i(X), and likewise for Y.
Define the pushforward as the dual of the pullback under these identifications, and record the characterising identity.
Prove the projection formula by testing both sides against an arbitrary class under the pairing on Y and moving everything to X by the characterising identity.
Prove functoriality by the same test, using functoriality of pullback.
acceptance: The pushforward lowers the cohomological degree by twice the difference of dimensions, as displayed.
The projection formula and functoriality use only (A) and no other axiom.
For f the identity the pushforward is the identity.

For a in H^{2d-i}(X), the element f_*a is characterised by: the integral over X of f^*b cup a equals the integral over Y of b cup f_*a. Assume given (D1) and (D3) satisfying (A). Then f_*(f^*b cup a) = b cup f_*a, and g_* after f_* = (g after f)_*.

nodes.title: The trace of a cycle class is the degree
nodes.statement: Let H be a classical Weil cohomology theory and X a smooth projective variety of dimension d. Then the square formed by the cycle class map from CH^d(X) to H^{2d}(X), the identification of CH^d(X) with CH_0(X), the trace map, and the degree map on zero cycles, commutes.
hypotheses: H is a classical Weil cohomology theory and X is smooth projective of dimension d.
proofSteps: Reduce to the class of a closed point, since CH_0(X) is generated by such classes.
For a closed point, factor the class through the structure morphism of the point and use compatibility of cycle classes with proper pushforward.
Apply the normalisation (C)(d) and functoriality of the trace under pushforward to identify the trace with the degree.
acceptance: The statement identifies two maps into F, the trace of the cycle class and the image of the degree; it is not an inequality or a proportionality.
It uses the normalisation axiom (C)(d): with every trace multiplied by λ the two maps differ by λ.
For X a point both maps send the class of the point to one.

For a divisor D on a smooth projective curve C over k, ∫_C γ(c_1(O_C(D)) ∩ [C]) = deg D, using c_1(O_C(D)) ∩ [C] = [D] from SF.5; this is the stage's required check of degree, trace and first Chern class for a divisor on a curve.

sources.excerpt: Let H^* be a classical Weil cohomology theory. Let X be a smooth projective variety of dimension d. The diagram with CH^d(X) to H^{2d}(X) by gamma, CH^d(X) equal to CH_0(X), the trace from H^{2d}(X) to F and the degree from CH_0(X) to Z commutes, where the degree is the degree of zero cycles.
sources.match: The node is that lemma, with the reduction to the class of a closed point made explicit as the first proof step.

nodes.title: The trace on a product
nodes.statement: Let H be a classical Weil cohomology theory and X and Y smooth projective varieties of dimensions d and e. Then ∫_{X×Y} = ∫_X ⊗ ∫_Y under the Künneth isomorphism: for a in H^{2d}(X) and b in H^{2e}(Y), the trace over X × Y of pr_1^*a ∪ pr_2^*b is (∫_X a)(∫_Y b).
hypotheses: H is a classical Weil cohomology theory and X and Y are smooth projective varieties of dimensions d and e.
Classes on the product are written through the Künneth isomorphism (B).
proofSteps: By (B) and the vanishing range (A)(c), H^{2d+2e}(X × Y) is H^{2d}(X) ⊗ H^{2e}(Y), which is one-dimensional by (A)(d).
For closed points x of X and y of Y, the class γ([x × y]) spans this space and has trace one, by MC.2/cycle-class-degree applied to X × Y.

By (C)(a) and (C)(c), in the exterior-product form of Remark 0FGU with [x × y] = pr_1^*[x] · pr_2^*[y] from SF.5, γ([x × y]) = pr_1^*γ([x]) ∪ pr_2^*γ([y]); the traces of γ([x]) and γ([y]) are one by MC.2/cycle-class-degree, so the two maps agree on a spanning vector.
acceptance: Both sides are F-linear maps on the one-dimensional space H^{2d+2e}(X × Y), and the identity is checked on the class of a closed point.
The proof uses (A)(c) to identify the top degree of the product, so the statement is about classical theories.
For Y a point it says that ∫ over X × Spec k is ∫_X.

sources.excerpt: Let X and Y be smooth projective varieties. Then ∫_{X × Y} = ∫_X ⊗ ∫_Y. ... By Lemma 0FGW this 1-dimensional vector space generated by the class γ([x × y]) of a closed point (x, y) and ∫_{X × Y} γ([x × y]) = 1.

nodes.title: The Kuenneth decomposition of the class of the diagonal
nodes.statement: Let H be a classical Weil cohomology theory and X a smooth projective variety of dimension d. Choose a basis of each H^i(X) over F and write the cycle class of the diagonal through the Kuenneth isomorphism as a sum over i and over the basis of tensors of a basis element in degree i with an element in degree 2d - i. Then the trace over X of the cup product of the i-th basis element with the corresponding element in complementary degree is the sign minus one to the i times the Kronecker delta of the two indices.
hypotheses: H is a classical Weil cohomology theory and X is smooth projective of dimension d.
A basis of each H^i(X) has been chosen; the statement is about the elements produced by the Kuenneth expansion of the diagonal class relative to that basis.
proofSteps: By MC.2/cycle-class-of-fundamental-class γ([X]) = 1, so by (C)(b) γ([Δ]) = Δ_*γ([X]) = Δ_*1.
By the definition of Δ_* and Remark 0FGU (pullback along the diagonal composed with the Künneth map is the cup product), ∫_{X×X} γ([Δ]) ∪ (a ⊗ b) = ∫_X a ∪ b.

Expanding γ([Δ]) in the chosen basis and applying MC.2/trace-of-a-product, ∫_{X×X} (Σ e_{i,j} ⊗ e'_{2d−i,j}) ∪ (a ⊗ b) = Σ (∫_X a ∪ e_{i,j})(∫_X e'_{2d−i,j} ∪ b); the two reorderings give the sign (−1)^{|a|·2d} = 1.

Choosing a with ∫_X a ∪ e_{i,j} = 1 and all other pairings with the basis zero, Poincaré duality (A)(b) gives e'_{2d−i,j} = a, and graded commutativity gives ∫_X e_{i,j'} ∪ e'_{2d−i,j} = (−1)^{i(2d−i)} δ_{jj'} = (−1)^i δ_{jj'}.
acceptance: The sign minus one to the i appears; a statement without it is wrong in odd degrees and breaks the computation of the Euler characteristic.
The elements in complementary degree form the dual basis up to that sign, which is what makes the diagonal the identity correspondence.
For X a point the statement is that the trace of the class of the point is one.

sources.excerpt: Let X be a smooth projective variety of dimension d. Choose a basis e_{i,j} of H^i(X) over F. Using Kuenneth write gamma([Delta]) as the sum over i and j of e_{i,j} tensor e'_{2d-i,j} with e'_{2d-i,j} in H^{2d-i}(X). Then the integral over X of e_{i,j} cup e'_{2d-i,j'} is minus one to the i times the Kronecker delta of j and j'.
sources.match: The node is that lemma verbatim, with the sign retained.

nodes.title: The Euler characteristic as a self-intersection of the diagonal
nodes.statement: Let H be a classical Weil cohomology theory and X a smooth projective variety of dimension d. Then the alternating sum over i from 0 to 2d of the F-dimension of H^i(X) equals the degree of the self-intersection of the class of the diagonal, and also the degree of the top Chern class of the tangent sheaf of X capped with the fundamental class.
hypotheses: H is a classical Weil cohomology theory and X is smooth projective of dimension d.
proofSteps: Right-hand equality, which involves no cohomology: [Δ] · [Δ] = Δ_*(Δ^![Δ]) and Δ^![Δ] is the top Chern class of the normal sheaf of the diagonal capped with [Δ]; the normal sheaf is the tangent sheaf T_X because the conormal sheaf of the diagonal is Ω_{X/k}; these are Chow Homology Lemmas 0FFE and 0FBM and Morphisms Lemma 08S2, imported from SF.5, and Δ_* preserves degrees of zero cycles.
Left-hand equality: by MC.2/cycle-class-degree and (C)(c), deg([Δ] · [Δ]) = ∫_{X×X} γ([Δ]) ∪ γ([Δ]).
By MC.2/cycle-class-of-fundamental-class and (C)(b), γ([Δ]) = Δ_*1, so by the projection formula of MC.2/weil-pushforward this equals ∫_{X×X} Δ_*(Δ^*γ([Δ])) = ∫_X Δ^*γ([Δ]).

Write γ([Δ]) = Σ e_{i,j} ⊗ e'_{2d−i,j} as in MC.2/class-of-the-diagonal; since Δ^* composed with the Künneth map is the cup product, ∫_X Δ^*γ([Δ]) = Σ_{i,j} ∫_X e_{i,j} ∪ e'_{2d−i,j} = Σ_i (−1)^i dim_F H^i(X).
acceptance: The left-hand side is an alternating sum, so the identity is a statement about the Euler characteristic and not about the total dimension.
The middle and right terms are numbers computed from cycles alone, independent of the chosen theory; in particular the Euler characteristic is the same for every classical Weil cohomology theory.
For X the projective line both sides are two.

sources.excerpt: Let X be a smooth projective variety. We have the sum over i from 0 to 2 dim(X) of minus one to the i times dim_F H^i(X) equals deg([Delta] . [Delta]) equals deg(c_d(T_X) cap [X]).

nodes.title: A monoidal functor on motives gives Weil data
nodes.statement: Let k be algebraically closed and F of characteristic zero, and give graded F-vector spaces the symmetric monoidal structure with the Koszul sign of MC.2/graded-vector-spaces-koszul, F[n] denoting F placed in degree −n. Let G be a Q-linear symmetric monoidal functor from Chow motives over k to graded F-vector spaces such that G(1(1)) is nonzero only in degree −2. Then G(1(1)) is one-dimensional; after choosing an isomorphism F[2] → G(1(1)), setting H^*(X) = G(h(X)) with the cup product induced by the diagonal, the cycle class map CH^r(X) → CH^r(X) ⊗ Q = Hom(1(−r), h(X)) → H^{2r}(X), and the trace map induced by [X] : h(X)(d) → 1, gives data (D1), (D2), (D3) satisfying all of (A), (B) and (C) except possibly (A)(c) and (A)(d). The cycle class and trace maps depend on the chosen isomorphism.
hypotheses: G is Q-linear and symmetric monoidal for the Koszul commutativity constraint on graded F-vector spaces; with the unsigned constraint the cup product obtained would not be graded commutative in the sense of (D1).
G(1(1)) is concentrated in degree −2, that is, isomorphic to F[2]; this is what makes the cycle class map double degrees.
An isomorphism F[2] → G(1(1)) is chosen; rescaling it by λ in F^× multiplies the cycle class map on CH^r by λ^{−r} and the trace of a d-dimensional X by λ^d.
proofSteps: (D1): set H^*(X) = G(h(X)); monoidality gives H^*(X × Y) = H^*(X) ⊗ H^*(Y) compatibly with pullbacks, and pullback along the diagonal defines the cup product; since the diagonal commutes with the switch of factors and G respects commutativity constraints, H^*(X) is graded commutative for the Koszul sign.
1(1) is invertible, so G(1(1)) is invertible, hence one-dimensional (MC.2/graded-vector-spaces-koszul); choose F[2] → G(1(1)) and deduce F[2n] → G(1(n)) compatible with tensor products.
(D2): CH^r(X) ⊗ Q = Corr^r(Spec k, X) = Hom(1(−r), h(X)) (MC.0/composition-associative, MC.1/chow-groups-representable); applying G and the chosen isomorphism gives γ : CH^r(X) → H^{2r}(X).
(D3): Hom(h(X)(d), 1) = CH_d(X), so [X] gives h(X)(d) → 1, and G of it is a map H^*(X) ⊗ F[2d] → F whose degree zero part is ∫_X : H^{2d}(X) → F.

(A)(a) and (A)(b): h(X)(d) is a left dual of h(X) with counit the class of the diagonal, which is [X] composed with h(Δ)(d) (MC.1/motive-dual); so G(h(X)(d)) is a left dual of H^*(X), and by MC.2/graded-vector-spaces-koszul H^*(X) has finite total dimension and cup product followed by ∫_X is a perfect pairing.

(B) from monoidality; (C)(a) from MC.0/graph-acts-as-gysin-and-pushforward and functoriality of G; (C)(b) from MC.2/graph-duality-compatibility; (C)(c) through the exterior-product form of Remark 0FGU and monoidality; (C)(d) because [Spec k] is the identity of h(Spec k).
acceptance: Exactly two parts of the axioms are not obtained: the vanishing range (A)(c) and the bijectivity of the trace (A)(d). Stacks Example 0FHZ shows that (A)(c) can fail.
The cycle class map goes through CH^r(X) ⊗ Q = Hom(1(−r), h(X)), so γ is defined on rational Chow groups and restricted to CH^r(X).
The normalisation G(1(1)) ≅ F[2], with F in degree −2, is what makes degrees double.
The data depend on the chosen isomorphism F[2] → G(1(1)); this is why Proposition 0FH3 includes it in the data.

sources.excerpt: Consider a Q-linear functor G : M_k → graded F-vector spaces of symmetric monoidal categories such that G(1(1)) is nonzero only in degree −2. Then we obtain data (D1), (D2), (D3) satisfying all of (A), (B), (C) except for possibly (A)(c) and (A)(d).

nodes.title: A Weil cohomology theory is a monoidal functor on motives
nodes.statement: Let k be algebraically closed, F of characteristic zero and H a classical Weil cohomology theory. Then there is a Q-linear symmetric monoidal functor G from Chow motives over k to graded F-vector spaces with the Koszul commutativity constraint such that G(h(X)) = H^*(X) for every smooth projective variety X; on a correspondence c of degree zero from X to Y it is a ↦ pr_{2,*}(γ(c) ∪ pr_1^*a).
hypotheses: H is a classical Weil cohomology theory over k with coefficients in F.
proofSteps: Extend H additively to smooth projective schemes over k by MC.2/weil-cohomology-of-schemes; the source makes this reduction with details omitted (source issue E18).
For c in Corr^0(X, Y) set G(c)(a) = pr_{2,*}(γ(c) ∪ pr_1^*a); it is additive, hence Q-linear, in c.

G(c' ∘ c) = G(c') ∘ G(c) by the source's six-step computation: MC.2/pushforward-along-projection for pr^{23,*}_2 ∘ pr^{12}_{2,*} = pr^{123}_{23,*} ∘ pr^{123,*}_{12}, the projection formula and functoriality of MC.2/weil-pushforward, (C)(a) with the agreement of the Gysin map and flat pullback for flat morphisms (Chow Homology Lemma 0FF4, from SF.5), (C)(b) and (C)(c).
G([Δ]) is the identity by MC.2/class-of-the-diagonal and MC.2/pushforward-along-projection.
G(Spec k) = F as an F-algebra by (A)(c) and (A)(d); (B) makes G compatible with tensor products, and graded commutativity of the cup product makes it compatible with the commutativity constraints.

H^1(P^1) = 0: by (A)(b) and (A)(d), H^0(P^1) and H^2(P^1) are one-dimensional, and MC.2/euler-characteristic-self-intersection with (A)(c) gives 2 − dim H^1(P^1) = deg([Δ] · [Δ]) = 2, the last equality from [Δ] = c_0 + c_2 (MC.0/projective-line-idempotents) and the proper intersection formula of SF.5.

c_0 = a ∘ b with b ∘ a = 1 (MC.1/lefschetz-motive), so G(c_0) is the projector onto H^0(P^1) and G(c_2) the projector onto H^2(P^1), one-dimensional in degree 2 and hence invertible; MC.1/motives-universal-property extends G to motives.
acceptance: The extension to motives exists because the image of c_2 is invertible; a theory in which that image were zero would not extend.
The value on h(X) is H^*(X) on the nose, and G applied to h(f) = [Γ_f] for f : Y → X is f^*, since γ([Γ_f]) = (f, id)_*1 and the projection formula gives pr_{Y,*}((f, id)_*1 ∪ pr_X^*a) = f^*a.
The functor is symmetric monoidal for the Koszul constraint, so it takes duals to duals and ranks to super-dimensions.

sources.excerpt: Let H^* be a classical Weil cohomology theory. Then we can construct a Q-linear functor G from M_k to graded F-vector spaces of symmetric monoidal categories such that H^*(X) = G(h(X)).
sources.match: The node is that lemma; the construction of the functor on correspondences and the verification that the image of c_2 is invertible are written out as proof steps because the extension to motives is what the universal property needs.

nodes.title: Realisations are exactly monoidal functors on motives
nodes.statement: Let k be algebraically closed and F of characteristic zero. A classical Weil cohomology theory over k with coefficients in F is the same thing as a Q-linear symmetric monoidal functor G from Chow motives over k to graded F-vector spaces with the Koszul commutativity constraint, together with an isomorphism F[2] → G(1(1)), where F[2] is F placed in degree −2, such that for every smooth projective variety X (1) G(h(X)) lives in nonnegative degrees and (2) the degree zero part of G(h(X)) is one-dimensional over F. The constructions are those of MC.2/weil-to-monoidal-functor and MC.2/weil-from-monoidal-functor, and they are mutually inverse by MC.2/realization-round-trip.
hypotheses: k is algebraically closed and F has characteristic zero.
The normalisation is an isomorphism F[2] → G(1(1)), where F[2] has F in degree −2, the degree in which G(1(1)) sits.
The two extra conditions are quantified over all smooth projective varieties X.
proofSteps: From a pair (G, F[2] → G(1(1))) satisfying (1) and (2), MC.2/weil-from-monoidal-functor gives data satisfying all axioms except (A)(c) and (A)(d).
Condition (1) with the perfect pairings of (A)(b) gives (A)(c): H^i(X) = 0 for i < 0, and H^i(X) = 0 for i > 2d because it is dual to H^{2d−i}(X).
Condition (2) with (A)(b) makes H^{2d}(X) one-dimensional, and ∫_X is nonzero on it because the pairing is perfect, which is (A)(d).

From a classical theory H, MC.2/weil-to-monoidal-functor gives G; the isomorphism 1(−1) → (P^1, c_2, 0) of MC.1/lefschetz-motive identifies G(1(−1)) with H^2(P^1) placed in degree 2, and ∫_{P^1}, an isomorphism by (A)(d), gives G(1(−1)) → F[−2] and hence F[2] → G(1(1)); conditions (1) and (2) follow from (A)(c), (A)(b) and (A)(d).
The two constructions are mutually inverse by MC.2/realization-round-trip; the source asserts this without the verification (source issue E13).
acceptance: The two extra conditions are exactly what replaces the two axioms the functorial description does not see; the functor of Stacks Example 0FHZ fails condition (1).
The normalisation is part of the data on both sides; it lives in degree −2, and G(1(−1)) is H^2(P^1) placed in degree 2.
This is the precise sense in which the category of Chow motives is the universal receptacle of classical Weil cohomology theories.

sources.excerpt: A classical Weil cohomology theory is the same thing as a Q-linear functor G from M_k to graded F-vector spaces of symmetric monoidal categories together with an isomorphism F[2] to G(1(1)) of graded F-vector spaces such that in addition (1) G(h(X)) lives in nonnegative degrees, and (2) dim_F G^0(h(X)) = 1 for any smooth projective variety X.
sources.match: The node is that proposition, with the two extra conditions kept in the statement and identified in the proof steps with the two axioms the functorial description does not otherwise give.

nodes.title: Chow groups over an algebraic extension are a colimit
nodes.statement: Let K over k be an algebraic field extension and X a scheme of finite type over k. Then CH_i(X_K) is the colimit of CH_i(X_{k'}) over the subextensions K/k'/k with k'/k finite, the transition maps and the maps to CH_i(X_K) being flat pullback.
hypotheses: K over k is an algebraic extension and X is of finite type over k.
Chow groups here are the integral ones.
proofSteps: Write X_K as the limit of the X_{k'} over the finite subextensions, a cofiltered limit with affine flat transition morphisms.
Apply Chow Homology Lemma 0FVQ, that Chow groups turn such limits into colimits, imported from SF.5; the source's proof is this citation.
acceptance: The colimit is over finite subextensions, which is what lets a statement over K be checked over a finite extension.
Every class on X_K comes from some finite subextension.
For K = k the statement is trivial.

sources.excerpt: Let K/k be an algebraic field extension. Let X be a finite type scheme over k. Then CH_i(X_K) = colim CH_i(X_{k'}) where the colimit is over the subextensions K/k'/k with k'/k finite. Proof. This is a special case of Chow Homology, Lemma 0FVQ.
sources.match: The node is that lemma with its one-line proof.

nodes.title: The trace formula for correspondences modulo homological equivalence
nodes.statement: Let k be a field, X a smooth projective variety over k and H a classical Weil cohomology theory over an algebraic closure of k with coefficient field A, applied to X through MC.2/weil-cohomology-by-base-change. Let F ⊆ A be a subfield, B the F-linear correspondences of degree zero from X to X modulo homological equivalence with respect to H, with Jannsen's composition g ∘ f = p_{13,*}(p_{12}^*f · p_{23}^*g), and f ↦ ᵗf the transposition induced by interchanging the factors of X × X. Then for f and g in B, ⟨f · ᵗg⟩ = Σ_{i=0}^{2 dim X} (−1)^i Tr_i(f ∘ g), where ⟨ ⟩ is the intersection number on X × X and Tr_i(h) is the trace of h acting on H^i(X).
hypotheses: k is any field; the theory is classical over an algebraic closure of k and applied to X after base change, as Jannsen does with etale cohomology of X over a separable closure.
F is a subfield of the coefficient field A of H, so that F-linear cycles modulo homological equivalence are defined; intersection numbers lie in F and traces in A.
The traces are taken on the finite-dimensional A-vector spaces H^i(X), and Tr_i(f ∘ g) = Tr_i(g ∘ f).
proofSteps: Intersection numbers are unchanged by base change to an algebraic closure (degree of zero cycles, SF.5), and correspondences act on H^*(X) through MC.2/weil-cohomology-by-base-change compatibly with composition; so it suffices to treat X over the algebraic closure, a disjoint union of varieties of dimension dim X, and by additivity over the blocks of a correspondence, a single variety.

Chow identity: ⟨f · ᵗg⟩ = deg((g ∘ f) · [Δ]). By the projection formula along p_{13} (SF.5), deg((g ∘ f) · [Δ]) is the degree of p_{12}^*f · p_{23}^*g · p_{13}^*[Δ]; p_{13}^*[Δ] is the class of the image of X × X under (x, y) ↦ (x, y, x), and restricting along that closed immersion turns p_{12}^*f into f and p_{23}^*g into ᵗg (MC.0/transpose-correspondence).

Lefschetz: deg((g ∘ f) · [Δ]) = Σ_i (−1)^i Tr_i(g ∘ f) by MC.2/lefschetz-trace-formula applied to g ∘ f, whose action on H^i(X) is the composite of the actions (MC.2/homological-correspondences-embed).
Tr_i(g ∘ f) = Tr_i(f ∘ g) by symmetry of the trace of a composite (mathlib:LinearMap.trace_comp_comm').

Both sides depend only on the homological classes: homologically trivial correspondences act by zero (MC.2/homological-correspondences-embed) and are numerically trivial (MC.2/homological-equivalence).
acceptance: The alternating sign is present: for f = g = [Δ] on a curve of genus g ≥ 1 the left side is 2 − 2g, while the unsigned sum of traces is 2 + 2g.
Both sides are defined on homological classes; the left side is an intersection number over k, the right side a sum of traces over the coefficient field of H.
For f = g = [Δ] the identity returns the Euler characteristic, the left-hand equality of MC.2/euler-characteristic-self-intersection.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 1. Let f ↦ ᵗf, B^{dim(X)}(X × X) → B^{dim(X)}(X × X), be the transposition, induced by interchanging the factors of X × X. Then for f, g ∈ B^{dim(X)}(X × X) one has ⟨f · ᵗg⟩ = Σ_{i=0}^{2dim(X)} (−1)^i Tr_i(f ∘ g), where Tr_i(f) is the trace of f acting on H^i(X).
sources.match: The node is Jannsen's Lemma 1. He calls it well known and cites Kleiman's 1968 article, which was not obtained; the proof steps derive it from the Lefschetz formula of MC.2/lefschetz-trace-formula and an identity of correspondences.

sources.excerpt: Then ∫_X e_{i,j} ∪ e'_{2d−i,j'} = (−1)^i δ_{jj'}. ... We have Σ_{i = 0, ..., 2 dim(X)} (−1)^i dim_F H^i(X) = deg([Δ] · [Δ]) = deg(c_d(T_X) ∩ [X])
sources.match: Cited for the method: the case f = g = [Δ] is Lemma 0FH0, and the general case goes through MC.2/lefschetz-trace-formula, which uses the basis of Lemma 0FGZ.

nodes.title: A pseudo-abelian category with semisimple endomorphism algebras is semisimple abelian
nodes.statement: Let F be a field and C an F-linear pseudo-abelian category, that is, an F-linear additive category in which idempotents split, such that End(M) is a finite-dimensional semisimple F-algebra for every object M of C. Then C is a semisimple abelian category (MC.3/semisimple-abelian-category).
hypotheses: F is a field.
C is F-linear and pseudo-abelian, that is, idempotents split.
Every object has a finite dimensional semisimple endomorphism algebra; the hypothesis is on all objects and not only on the generators.
proofSteps: By the Artin–Wedderburn theorem End(M) is a finite product of matrix algebras over division rings; since idempotents split, M is indecomposable exactly when End(M) has no idempotents other than 0 and 1, that is, when End(M) is a division ring.
Every object is a finite direct sum of indecomposables, by induction on dim_F End(M), splitting a nontrivial idempotent at each step.

For indecomposable M and N with Hom(M, N) ≠ 0, some composite M → N → M is nonzero: otherwise Hom(M, N), placed in the lower left corner of End(M ⊕ N), is a nonzero left ideal of square zero, which a semisimple algebra does not have since its Jacobson radical is zero. Jannsen calls this corner a two-sided ideal; closure under left multiplication is all the argument needs (source issue E15).
A nonzero composite f ∘ g with g : M → N is invertible in the division ring End(M), so (f ∘ g)^{−1} ∘ f is a left inverse of g; N being indecomposable, g is an isomorphism.

Hence C is equivalent to a direct sum, indexed by the isomorphism classes of indecomposables, of categories of finite-dimensional vector spaces over the division rings End(M); each summand is abelian with every object a finite sum of copies of one simple object, so C is semisimple abelian.
acceptance: The hypothesis of semisimplicity of the endomorphism algebras cannot be replaced by the existence of a faithful functor to vector spaces together with 'indecomposable implies simple': MC.3/dual-numbers-non-example.
The conclusion is that the category is abelian, which is more than the splitting of idempotents.
Finite dimensionality is used, for the Artin–Wedderburn theorem and for the finite decomposition into indecomposables.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 2. Let C be an F-linear, pseudo-abelian category such that End(M) is a finite-dimensional, semi-simple F-algebra for every object M of C. Then C is a semi-simple abelian category. Proof. By Wedderburn's theorem, End(M) is a product of full matrix algebras over skewfields.
sources.match: The node is Jannsen's Lemma 2 with his proof, kept in its steps; the last step is the equivalence with a sum of categories of vector spaces over division rings.

nodes.title: Indecomposable and simple is not enough
nodes.statement: Let Q of epsilon be the Q-algebra of dual numbers, with epsilon squared zero. The category of finitely generated free modules over it is a Q-linear pseudo-abelian category carrying a faithful Q-linear functor to Q-vector spaces, every indecomposable object of it is simple, and it is not an abelian category: the endomorphism given by multiplication by epsilon on the ring itself has no kernel in the category.
hypotheses: The base is the Q-algebra of dual numbers.
Objects are the finitely generated free modules over it and morphisms are module maps.
proofSteps: The category is Q-linear and additive, and idempotents split: a direct summand of a finitely generated free module over the local ring Q[ε] is free.
The forgetful functor to Q-vector spaces is Q-linear and faithful.
Every finitely generated free module is Q[ε]^n, indecomposable exactly when n = 1.

Monomorphisms of the category are injective maps: if f : P → Q[ε] kills a nonzero v, the map Q[ε] → P with 1 ↦ v is a nonzero morphism with zero composite. An injective map Q[ε]^n → Q[ε] has n ≤ 1 by comparing Q-dimensions and is bijective for n = 1; so every nonzero monomorphism into Q[ε] is an isomorphism, and Q[ε] is simple in the sense of mathlib:CategoryTheory.Simple.

Multiplication by ε has no kernel: a kernel K → Q[ε] would be a monomorphism, hence injective, with image in the one-dimensional εQ[ε], so K = 0; but the nonzero map Q[ε] → Q[ε], 1 ↦ ε, has zero composite with ε and would have to factor through K.
acceptance: The example shows that the hypothesis of the previous lemma cannot be replaced by the weaker one used in the literature; the endomorphism algebra of the ring is the ring itself, which is not semisimple.
The functor to vector spaces is faithful, so faithfulness of a fibre functor does not repair the argument.
The failure is the absence of a kernel and not the absence of a splitting of idempotents.

sources.excerpt: Then the category C of finitely generated free Q[ε]-modules is a Q-linear pseudo-abelian category with a faithful Q-linear functor into Vec_Q (the forgetful functor), and every indecomposable object of C is simple, but C is not an abelian category. In fact, the endomorphism ε of Q[ε] has no kernel.
sources.match: The node is that remark; Jannsen adds that the endomorphism ε of Q[ε] has no kernel, that Lemma 2 should replace Lemma 6.6 of Deligne and Milne, which is false, and that the same wrong argument seems to appear in Saavedra Rivano's book.

nodes.title: Jannsen's theorem: semisimplicity characterises numerical equivalence
nodes.statement: Let k be a field and F a field of characteristic zero, and form the category M_k of motives from F-linear cycles modulo an adequate equivalence relation ∼ (MC.1/motives-mod-adequate-relation). The following are equivalent: (a) M_k is a semisimple abelian category; (b) A^{dim X}(X × X) is a finite-dimensional semisimple F-algebra for every variety X; (c) ∼ is numerical equivalence.
hypotheses: k is any field, F has characteristic zero and ∼ is adequate on F-linear cycles.
Varieties are smooth projective over k, possibly disconnected, with A^{dim X + r}(X × Y) defined componentwise as in the source.
No standard conjecture is assumed; the theorem is unconditional.
proofSteps: (a) implies (c): MC.3/semisimple-category-implies-numerical.

(c) implies (b): MC.3/numerical-implies-semisimple-algebras, applied with l-adic etale cohomology over an algebraic closure of k for a prime l invertible in k (MC.2/etale-cohomology-is-weil); this is the only place a Weil cohomology theory enters, and its existence over every field is why the theorem is unconditional.
(b) implies (a): MC.3/semisimple-algebras-imply-semisimple-category.
acceptance: The theorem is an equivalence of three conditions and is unconditional: no standard conjecture is used, as the source stresses against what it calls general belief.
The middle condition concerns the algebra of correspondences of a single variety, so it is a finiteness and semisimplicity statement in linear algebra once a relation is fixed.
Semisimplicity fails for Chow motives whenever rational and numerical equivalence differ on some variety over k, by (a) implies (c).

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1. The following properties are equivalent. a) M_k is a semi-simple abelian category. b) A^{dim(X)}(X × X) is a finite-dimensional, semi-simple F-algebra for every variety X. c) The relation ∼ is numerical equivalence.
sources.match: The node is that theorem; its three implications are MC.3/semisimple-category-implies-numerical, MC.3/numerical-implies-semisimple-algebras and MC.3/semisimple-algebras-imply-semisimple-category.

sources.excerpt: is a semi-simple abelian category if - and in fact, only if - the relation is numerical equivalence. Contrary to general belief Grothendieck's standard conjectures are not needed for this.
sources.match: Cited for the unconditionality: an implementation that assumes a standard conjecture has not proved this theorem.

nodes.title: The radical of the algebra of homological correspondences
nodes.statement: Let k be a field, H a classical Weil cohomology theory over an algebraic closure of k with coefficient field A, F ⊆ A a subfield, and X a smooth projective variety over k whose Künneth components (MC.2/kunneth-components) are algebraic. Let S be the surjective ring homomorphism from B = A_hom^{dim X}(X × X, F) to A_num^{dim X}(X × X, F). Then every numerically trivial f in B has Tr_i(f) = 0 for all i and is nilpotent, and the kernel of S is the Jacobson radical of B and is a nilpotent ideal.
hypotheses: k is any field and H a classical Weil cohomology theory over an algebraic closure of k with coefficient field A; X is a smooth projective variety over k whose Künneth components are algebraic.
The coefficient field A of the theory is an F-algebra, which is what makes both quotients defined.
For F different from A the conclusion is obtained by comparison with F = A, since finite dimensionality of B over F is not known in positive characteristic.
proofSteps: The radical of B lies in the kernel of S: S maps the radical of B into the radical of A_num^{dim X}(X × X, F), which is zero by MC.3/numerical-implies-semisimple-algebras.

By MC.2/kunneth-components, Tr_i(f ∘ π^j) = δ_{ij} Tr_j(f) for f in B. If f is numerically trivial and the π^j are algebraic, MC.3/trace-formula-for-correspondences gives (−1)^j Tr_j(f) = ⟨f · ᵗπ^j⟩ = 0 for every j.

The powers of f are numerically trivial too, so each induced endomorphism of H^i(X) has vanishing power traces and is nilpotent (MC.3/nilpotent-of-vanishing-power-traces); since B embeds in ⊕_i End_A(H^i(X)) as a ring (MC.2/homological-correspondences-embed), f is nilpotent.
For F = A, B is finite-dimensional over A, so the nil ideal ker S is nilpotent (mathlib:IsArtinianRing.isNilpotent_jacobson_bot) and lies in the radical.
For general F, the injective map A_hom(X × X, F) → A_hom(X × X, A) carries ker S_F into ker S_A, so ker S_F is nilpotent and lies in the radical of B.
acceptance: The hypothesis is algebraicity of the Kuenneth components for this X, and the conclusion is about this X.
The kernel is nilpotent, not merely nil; the passage from nil to nilpotent is the step that needs the finiteness or the base change argument.
The source is explicit that finite dimensionality of the algebra of homological correspondences over F is conjectural in positive characteristic, which is why the base change argument is needed.

sources.locator: page 449, Corollary 1, with its proof on pages 449 to 450
sources.excerpt: If, for a variety X, the Künneth components π^j ∈ H^{2dim(X)−j}(X) ⊗ H^j(X) of the diagonal are algebraic (cf. [K1] Sect. 2), then the kernel of the surjective ring homomorphism S : B = A_hom^{dim(X)}(X × X) → A_num^{dim(X)}(X × X) = A is the Jacobson radical of B, and is a nilpotent ideal.
sources.match: The node is that corollary with its proof, including the comparison of coefficient fields and the source's statement that finite dimensionality over F is open in positive characteristic.

nodes.title: The rank of a motive and the obstruction to a fibre functor
nodes.statement: Let k be a field and F of characteristic zero. In the category of motives modulo numerical equivalence with the commutativity constraint induced by the switch of factors, the rank (MC.3/categorical-rank) of the motive h(X) of a smooth projective variety X is the self-intersection number ⟨Δ · Δ⟩ of its diagonal. For a smooth projective geometrically connected curve C of genus g it is 2 − 2g. Consequently, if k admits such a curve with g ≥ 2, the numerical motives with this constraint have no fibre functor with values in an extension field of F and are not Tannakian (MC.3/tannakian-category).
hypotheses: The category is the numerical one, which is rigid (MC.1/motives-mod-adequate-relation).
The rank is the categorical trace of the identity (MC.3/categorical-rank), an element of End(1) = F.
The commutativity constraint is the unmodified one induced by the switch of factors; after the sign change of MC.3/numerical-motives-tannakian the rank becomes a sum of Betti numbers.
proofSteps: The dual of h(X) is h(X)(d) for X of dimension d, with coevaluation and evaluation both the class of the diagonal (MC.1/motive-dual, valid modulo any adequate relation).

The composite of coevaluation, switch of factors and evaluation that defines rk(h(X)) is, by the composition law, the degree of the intersection of the diagonal with its image under the switch, which is the diagonal: rk(h(X)) = ⟨Δ · Δ⟩.

For a curve C of genus g, ⟨Δ · Δ⟩ = deg c_1(T_C) = −deg K_C = 2 − 2g, by the right-hand equality of MC.2/euler-characteristic-self-intersection (an identity of cycles, SF.5) and the degree 2g − 2 of the canonical divisor (SF.3).
A fibre functor would send h(C) to a vector space of dimension rk(h(C)) (MC.3/categorical-rank), which cannot be negative; so for g ≥ 2 none exists.
acceptance: The obstruction is a sign and not a size: the rank is an integer of either sign.
The computation of the rank uses only rigidity and the duality, which hold for every adequate relation.
For a curve of genus g the rank of h(C) is 2 − 2g: positive for g = 0, zero for g = 1, negative for g ≥ 2.

sources.locator: page 450, inside the proof of Corollary 2
sources.excerpt: under the above normalizations the rank (in the sense of [DM] p. 113) of a motive h(X) = (X, id, 0) can be negative, while in the presence of a fibre functor it should be non-negative, as the dimension of a vector space ... one easily computes rk(h(X)) = ⟨Δ · Δ⟩ for the diagonal
sources.match: The node is that step of the proof, made a lemma because it is what forces the sign change.

sources.excerpt: For example, if X is a curve of genus g, then Tr(u|hX) = dim H^0 − dim H^1 + dim H^2 = 2 − 2g, which may be negative. This proves that there does not exist an exact faithful tensor functor ω: M_num(k) → Vec_F for any field F.
sources.match: Milne's version, with the genus formula the node uses.

nodes.title: Numerical motives are Tannakian after a sign change
nodes.statement: Let k be a field, F of characteristic zero and H a classical Weil cohomology theory over an algebraic closure of k with coefficient field A ⊇ F. Suppose that for every variety X over k the Künneth components of the diagonal (MC.2/kunneth-components) are algebraic. Then their images π^j in A_num^{dim X}(X × X) are central idempotents, pairwise orthogonal, and every numerical motive acquires a Z-grading (X, p, m)^r = (X, p π^{r+2m}, m) respected by all morphisms. Modifying the commutativity constraint on M^r ⊗ N^s by the sign (−1)^{rs} gives a symmetric monoidal structure for which rk((X, p, m)) = Σ_{i≥0} dim_A pH^i(X) ≥ 0, and with this structure the motives modulo numerical equivalence form a semisimple F-linear Tannakian category (MC.3/tannakian-category).
hypotheses: The Künneth components of the diagonal are algebraic for every variety over k.
The relation is numerical equivalence and F has characteristic zero.
The commutativity constraint is modified by the displayed sign; without the modification the conclusion is false (MC.3/rank-of-a-motive).
The conclusion is Tannakian, not neutral: the fibre functor supplied by Deligne's criterion takes values in an extension of F.
proofSteps: The images π^j in A_num are orthogonal idempotents summing to the diagonal; more generally f ∘ π^i_X = π^{i+2(n−m)}_Y ∘ f for f of degree n − m from X to Y, because both sides act in the same way on cohomology and the action is faithful modulo homological equivalence (MC.2/kunneth-components, MC.2/homological-correspondences-embed). In particular the π^j are central.
Define (X, p, m)^r = (X, p π^{r+2m}, m); the graded pieces are direct summands of (X, p, m), and morphisms respect the grading by the first step.

Decompose the commutativity constraint as the sum of its restrictions ψ^{r,s} : M^r ⊗ N^s → N^s ⊗ M^r and replace it by the sum of (−1)^{rs} ψ^{r,s}; this is again symmetric and compatible with associativity because the grading is additive under tensor product.

Compute the rank of (X, p, m) for the modified constraint as in MC.3/trace-formula-for-correspondences: the sign (−1)^i of the Lefschetz formula is cancelled by the modification, and rk((X, p, m)) = Σ_i Tr_i(p) = Σ_i dim_A pH^i(X), the traces being defined on numerical classes and equal to dimensions for an idempotent lift (MC.3/cohomology-of-numerical-motives); so every rank is a nonnegative integer.

By MC.3/jannsen-semisimplicity the category is semisimple abelian, and it is rigid with End(1) = F (MC.1/motives-mod-adequate-relation). Deligne's criterion, that such a category whose objects all have nonnegative integer rank is Tannakian, gives the conclusion; the criterion was not obtained and is a recorded gap.
acceptance: The sign change is indispensable: without it the rank of a motive can be negative and no fibre functor exists.
The hypothesis is the algebraicity of the Künneth components for every variety, which is open in general; the conclusion is therefore conditional.

Jannsen's Remark 2 gives the same conclusion for the subcategory generated as an abelian tensor category by 1(1) and a family of varieties whose Künneth components are algebraic, consisting of the motives (X, p, m) with X a product of members of the family; the abelian-variety case rests on Lieberman's theorem, recorded in MC.7 and not proved from a source read here.
The conclusion is not neutrality: a fibre functor with values in F itself is a separate obligation.

sources.excerpt: Corollary 2. If the Künneth components of the diagonal (w.r.t. some fixed Weil cohomology X ↦ H(X)) are algebraic for every variety X over k, then the category M_k of motives with respect to numerical equivalence is a semi-simple F-linear Tannakian category
sources.match: The node is that corollary.

sources.excerpt: If we modify the constraints by defining ψ_new = ⊕_{r,s} (−1)^{rs} ψ^{r,s}, then the computation leading to Lemma 1 easily shows rk((X, p, m)) = Σ_{i≥0} dim_A pH^i(X) ≥ 0 for every motive (X, p, m) in M_k. By Deligne's theorem 7.1 in [D], M_k is Tannakian.
sources.match: The sign change and the rank formula, with the grading printed just before as (X, p, m)^r = (X, pπ^{r+2m}, r), a misprint for twist m (source issue E16).

sources.excerpt: Moreover, the result of Corollary 2 holds for every subcategory C of M_k generated (as an abelian tensor category) by 1(1) and a family of varieties (X_i | i ∈ I) such that the Künneth components of the diagonal are algebraic for the X_i.
sources.match: Recorded as an acceptance point; the abelian-variety case of the remark rests on Lieberman's theorem, cited by Jannsen and not read.

nodes.title: The category of effective geometric motives
nodes.statement: Let k be a field and R a commutative ring. Inside the triangulated category DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R) of effective motives (the A^1-localisation of the derived category of bounded above complexes of Nisnevich sheaves of R-modules with transfers, imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a), the category DM^eff_gm(k,R) of effective geometric motives is the thick subcategory generated by the motives M(X) of smooth schemes X over k: the smallest full triangulated subcategory that contains every M(X), is closed under isomorphisms and is closed under direct summands. In Mathlib's vocabulary it is the triangulated envelope closed under retracts (triangEnvelope) of the object property 'isomorphic to M(X) for some smooth X'. It is stable under the tensor product and the Tate twist, and every effective geometric motive is compact.
hypotheses: k is a field and R a commutative ring; the definition needs no further hypothesis on k.
The ambient category DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R), its tensor structure, the motive M(X) of a smooth scheme and the Tate object R(1) are imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a.
Thick is meant in the sense of MVW Definition 9.1: if two vertices of a distinguished triangle lie in the subcategory so does the third, and both summands of an object of the subcategory lie in it.
proofSteps: Define the object property P of the ambient category: an object has P when it is isomorphic to M(X) for some smooth X over k.

Define DM^eff_gm as the full subcategory on P.triangEnvelope; by triangEnvelope_le_iff it is the smallest triangulated object property closed under retracts containing P, which is MVW's thick subcategory generated by the M(X); the full subcategory is pretriangulated by Mathlib's IsTriangulated API.

Stability under the tensor product: for fixed smooth Y the class of A with A tensor M(Y) in the envelope is triangulated, closed under retracts and contains every M(X), because M(X) tensor M(Y) is M(X x Y) (MVW 14.2 with 8.10, supplied by M.5a); hence it contains the envelope; repeat in the second variable.

Stability under the Tate twist: R(1)[1] is a direct summand of M(G_m), because R_tr(G_m) = R plus R_tr(G_m, 1) (MVW Lemma 2.13) and R(1) = C_*R_tr(G_m^{wedge 1})[-1] (MVW Definition 3.1); so R(1) lies in the envelope and so does M tensor R(1) for every effective geometric motive M.

Compactness: Hom(M(X)[n], -) commutes with direct sums (MVW 13.5, as used in the proof of Theorem 16.25), and the class of compact objects is triangulated and closed under retracts, so it contains the envelope.
acceptance: The subcategory is thick, so it is closed under direct summands; without that the image of an idempotent correspondence, in particular of a Chow projector, would not be a geometric motive.

The assertions that DM^eff_gm contains the motive of every scheme of finite type and is generated by the motives of smooth projective schemes need resolution of singularities and are the separate node MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.4/geometric-motives-generated-by-smooth-projective.
The ambient category and the motives of smooth schemes are imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a; nothing about finite correspondences or A^1-localisation is proved here.

sources.excerpt: We define DM^eff_gm(k,R) to be the thick subcategory of DM^{eff,-}_Nis(k,R) generated by the motives M(X), where X is smooth over k. Objects in DM^eff_gm(k,R) will be called effective geometric motives.
sources.match: The definition, literally; the rest of the paragraph (the resolution-dependent consequences) is the node MC.4/geometric-motives-generated-by-smooth-projective.

sources.excerpt: A full additive subcategory E of D^- is thick if: (1) Let A -> B -> C -> A[1] be a distinguished triangle. Then if two out of A,B,C are in E then so is the third. (2) if A+B is in E then both A and B are in E.
sources.match: Fixes the meaning of 'thick' used in Definition 14.1: a triangulated subcategory closed under summands, which is Mathlib's triangulated envelope closed under retracts.

nodes.title: Geometric motives by inverting the Tate twist
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field and R a commutative ring. The category DM_gm(k,R) of geometric motives is DM^eff_gm(k,R)[R(1)^{-1}], the category obtained by inverting the object T = R(1) as in MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.4/inverting-a-tensor-object: its objects are pairs (M, m) with M an effective geometric motive and m an integer, standing for M(m), and Hom((M,m),(N,n)) is the colimit over i of Hom(M(m+i), N(n+i)). It is a tensor triangulated category, because the cyclic permutation of R(1)^{tensor 3} is the identity (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.4/symmetric-group-acts-trivially-on-tate-twists); every object is isomorphic to M(-n) for some n >= 0 and some effective M; tensoring with R(1) is an autoequivalence; and, by the cancellation theorem over a perfect field imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a, the functor DM^eff_gm(k,R) -> DM_gm(k,R) is fully faithful. The same construction applied to DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R) gives DM^-(k,R), in which DM_gm(k,R) is a full tensor triangulated subcategory.
hypotheses: k is a perfect field. Full faithfulness uses the cancellation theorem in Voevodsky's form over a perfect field (arXiv:math/0202012, Corollary 4.10), imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a; the tensor structure uses MVW Corollary 15.8, which rests on Theorem 15.2 and so on k perfect.
R is a commutative ring of coefficients, fixed throughout.
R(1) is the motivic complex C_*R_tr(G_m^{wedge 1})[-1] of MVW Definition 3.1, imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a.
proofSteps: Apply MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.4/inverting-a-tensor-object to the tensor triangulated category DM^eff_gm(k,R), which is stable under tensoring with R(1) (API of MC.4/effective-geometric-motives), and T = R(1).

Verify the hypothesis of MVW Proposition 8A.10 and Corollary 8A.11: by MC.4/symmetric-group-acts-trivially-on-tate-twists the cyclic permutation of R(1)^{tensor 3}, isomorphic to R(3), is the identity in DM^eff,-_Nis, hence in the localised category; conclude that DM_gm is tensor triangulated.
Every object (M, -n) with n >= 0 is M(-n) by construction, and (M, m) with m >= 0 is isomorphic to M tensor R(1)^{tensor m}, which is effective.

Full faithfulness: by the imported cancellation theorem Hom(M, N) -> Hom(M(1), N(1)) is bijective for effective M and N, so every transition map in the colimit defining Hom((M,0),(N,0)) is bijective and the colimit is Hom(M, N).

Apply the same construction to DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R) to obtain DM^-(k,R), and check that the functor DM_gm -> DM^- induced by the inclusion is fully faithful, both Hom groups being colimits of the same groups.
acceptance: Full faithfulness of DM^eff_gm -> DM_gm is the cancellation theorem and is not formal; it carries the hypothesis that k is perfect.
Every object is a twist M(-n), n >= 0, of an effective object.

The symmetric monoidal structure needs the cyclic permutation of R(1)^{tensor 3} to be the identity; for an arbitrary object T of a symmetric monoidal category C[T^{-1}] need not be symmetric monoidal (MVW Exercise 8A.9).

nodes.title: Homotopy invariance and the Mayer-Vietoris triangle
nodes.statement: Let k be a field. For X smooth over k the projection X x A^1 -> X induces an isomorphism M(X x A^1) -> M(X) in DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R). For a Zariski open cover X = U union V of a smooth scheme there is a distinguished Mayer-Vietoris triangle M(U intersect V) -> M(U) + M(V) -> M(X) -> M(U intersect V)[1], natural in the cover.
hypotheses: k is any field; X is smooth; U and V are Zariski opens covering X.

The ambient category and the exactness of the Cech complex of sheaves with transfers attached to a Zariski cover (MVW 6.12, valid for the Nisnevich topology) are imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a.
proofSteps: Homotopy invariance: R_tr(X x A^1) -> R_tr(X) lies in the class W_A inverted by the A^1-localisation (MVW Definition 9.2 with 14.1), so its image in DM^eff,-_Nis is an isomorphism.

Mayer-Vietoris: 0 -> R_tr(U intersect V) -> R_tr(U) + R_tr(V) -> R_tr(X) -> 0 is exact as a sequence of Nisnevich sheaves with transfers (MVW 6.12), so it gives a distinguished triangle in D^-(Sh_Nis(Cor_k, R)) and hence in its localisation.
Record the triangle in the form (14.5.1), with the intersection first and the first map the difference of the two restrictions.

Record that MVW derive (14.5.1) from Proposition 13.15, a stronger statement about Zariski quasi-isomorphisms of Suslin complexes that uses Theorem 13.12 and so a perfect base field; the triangle in DM needs only the Nisnevich exactness.
acceptance: Homotopy invariance is an isomorphism in DM^eff,-_Nis, by construction of the localisation.
The Mayer-Vietoris triangle is distinguished, so any cohomological functor turns it into a long exact sequence; for H^{*,i}(-, R) this is the Mayer-Vietoris sequence of motivic cohomology.
For P^1 covered by two affine lines the triangle and homotopy invariance give M(P^1)/R isomorphic to (M(G_m)/R)[1].

sources.excerpt: By 14.4, we have M(X) = Z_tr(X) = C_*Z_tr(X). By 8.10, we see that M(X) tensor M(Y) = M(X x Y), and 2.24 yields M(X) = M(X x A^1).
sources.match: Homotopy invariance, literally (with isomorphism signs written as =).

sources.excerpt: (Mayer-Vietoris) For each open cover {U,V} of a smooth scheme X, proposition 13.15 yields the Mayer-Vietoris triangle in DM^{eff,-}_Nis(k,R): (14.5.1) M(U intersect V) -> M(V)+M(U) -> M(X) -> M(U intersect V)[1].
sources.match: The triangle, literally.

sources.excerpt: If U = {U1,...,Un} is a Zariski covering of X, we saw in 6.12 that the Cech complex Z_tr(U^): 0 -> Z_tr(U1 intersect ... intersect Un) -> ... -> +_i Z_tr(Ui) -> 0 is a resolution of Z_tr(X) in the etale topology (and the Nisnevich topology).

nodes.title: The motives of the affine line, the multiplicative group and projective space
nodes.statement: Let k be a field and R a commutative ring. In DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R): M(A^1) is isomorphic to R; M(G_m) to R + R(1)[1]; and M(P^1) to R + R(1)[2]. If k is perfect then for every n >= 0, M(P^n) is isomorphic to R + R(1)[2] + ... + R(n)[2n], the summand R(i)[2i] being split off by the extension to P^n (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.4/projective-space-inclusion-split) of the map M(P^i) -> R(i)[2i] of MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.4/projective-space-quotient.
hypotheses: The computations of M(A^1), M(G_m) and M(P^1) hold over any field; the computation of M(P^n) for n >= 2 uses Theorem 15.2 and so k perfect (MVW flag that perfectness is needed only for Theorem 13.8).
R is a commutative ring of coefficients.
proofSteps: M(A^1) is isomorphic to M(Spec k) = R by homotopy invariance.

M(G_m): R_tr(G_m) = R + R_tr(G_m, 1) by MVW Lemma 2.13 (the idempotent 1 - [1] splits off the base point) and R(1) = C_*R_tr(G_m^{wedge 1})[-1] by MVW Definition 3.1 (both supplied by M.5a), so M(G_m) is isomorphic to R + R(1)[1].

M(P^1): the Mayer-Vietoris triangle for P^1 = (P^1 - 0) union (P^1 - infinity) with homotopy invariance gives M(P^1)/R isomorphic to (M(G_m)/R)[1] = R(1)[2] (MVW Example 13.17, whose display is corrected in MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E20); the triangle R -> M(P^1) -> R(1)[2] -> splits because the structure map P^1 -> Spec k retracts a rational point (exists_iso_binaryBiproduct_of_distTriang).

M(P^n) by induction (MVW Corollary 15.5): MC.4/projective-space-quotient gives the triangle M(P^{n-1}) -> M(P^n) -> R(n)[2n] ->, and the maps of MC.4/projective-space-inclusion-split assemble to M(P^n) -> sum over i < n of R(i)[2i], whose composite with M(P^{n-1}) -> M(P^n) is the inductive isomorphism; so the first map is split injective and the triangle splits. MVW's proof prints R(i)[i] and R(n)[n] for R(i)[2i] and R(n)[2n] (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E22, corrected in the authors' errata).
acceptance: The summands are twists R(i)[2i] and not untwisted copies of the unit; this is the first computation any implementation should reproduce.
The motive of the multiplicative group has two summands, one of which is R(1)[1]: twist one, shift one.
For n equal to one the decomposition matches that of the Chow motive of the projective line under the comparison of MC.4/chow-motives-into-geometric-motives.

sources.excerpt: Applying 13.15 to the usual cover of P1 (by P1 - {0} and P1 - {infinity}) allows us to deduce that C_*(Z_tr(P1)/Z) = C_*Z_tr(G_m)[1] = Z(1)[2] for the Zariski topology, because C_*Z_tr(A1)/Z = 0 by 2.24.

nodes.title: The Gysin triangle and the boundary map at a closed point of a curve
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities, X a smooth scheme over k and Z a smooth closed subscheme of pure codimension c. The Gysin map gamma: M(X) -> M(Z)(c)[2c] of MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.4/blow-up-smooth-centre-and-gysin-map vanishes on M(X - Z) and fits into a distinguished triangle M(X - Z) -> M(X) -> M(Z)(c)[2c] -> M(X - Z)[1] in DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R). In particular, for X a smooth curve and x a closed point, whose residue field k(x) is finite and separable over k so that Spec k(x) is smooth, the triangle reads M(X - x) -> M(X) -> M(Spec k(x))(1)[2] -> M(X - x)[1]; for a rational point the third term is R(1)[2]. Applying Hom(-, R(i)[n]) and cancellation gives the localisation sequence ... -> H^{n-2,i-1}(Spec k(x), R) -> H^{n,i}(X, R) -> H^{n,i}(X - x, R) -> H^{n-1,i-1}(Spec k(x), R) -> ..., whose last map is the boundary map at x.
hypotheses: k is perfect (MVW Theorem 15.15) and, for the proof in the source read, admits resolution of singularities: the Gysin map comes from MVW Corollary 15.13, whose proof uses Theorem 13.26. A proof over an arbitrary perfect field is not in any source read here (gap).
Z is a smooth closed subscheme of pure codimension c of the smooth scheme X.
For the special case X is a smooth curve and x a closed point, so c = 1; the localisation sequence uses the cancellation theorem imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a.
proofSteps: Take gamma from MC.4/blow-up-smooth-centre-and-gysin-map; since it vanishes on M(X - Z) it induces gamma-bar: C_*(R_tr(X)/R_tr(X - Z)) -> M(Z)(c)[2c].

Show gamma-bar is a quasi-isomorphism: by Nisnevich excision (MVW 12.20, supplied by M.5a) the quotient R_tr(X)/R_tr(X - Z) depends only on an etale neighbourhood of Z, so one may assume X = Y x A^c and Z = Y x 0.

In that case gamma-bar is the map of MVW Exercise 15.14 for (A^c, 0) tensored with C_*R_tr(Y); Exercise 15.14 (stated without proof) identifies it, through (A^c, A^c - 0) and (P^c, P^c - 0), with the quasi-isomorphism of MC.4/projective-space-quotient; its verification is part of this step.
The triangle is the cone triangle of R_tr(X - Z) -> R_tr(X) with the cone identified through gamma-bar.

Specialise to a closed point of a smooth curve: c = 1 and Spec k(x) is smooth because k is perfect; apply Hom(-, R(i)[n]) and identify Hom(M(Spec k(x))(1)[2], R(i)[n]) with H^{n-2,i-1}(Spec k(x), R) by cancellation.
acceptance: The third term carries both the twist by c and the shift by 2c.
For X = P^1 and a rational point the triangle M(A^1) -> M(P^1) -> R(1)[2] recovers M(A^1) = R from M(P^1) = R + R(1)[2].
For a closed point x with k(x) different from k the third term is M(Spec k(x))(1)[2], not R(1)[2]: for X = A^1 over Q and x = V(t^2 + 1) it is M(Spec Q(i))(1)[2].
In weight i = 1 and degree n = 2 the sequence is Z = H^{0,0}(Spec k(x), Z) -> Pic(X) -> Pic(X - x) -> 0, the first map sending 1 to the class of x.

sources.excerpt: Let X be a smooth scheme over a perfect field and Z a smooth closed subscheme of X of codimension c. Then there is a "Gysin" triangle: C_*Z_tr(X - Z) -> C_*Z_tr(X) -> C_*Z_tr(Z)(c)[2c] -> C_*Z_tr(X - Z)[1].

sources.excerpt: We have to show that the Gysin map gamma-bar : C_*(Z_tr(X)/Z_tr(X - Z)) -> C_*Z_tr(Z)(c)[2c] of 15.13 is a quasi-isomorphism. By 12.20 we may assume that X = Y x A^c and Z = Y x 0. But then gamma-bar is the isomorphism of 15.14, tensored with C_*Z_tr(Y).
sources.match: The proof the node's steps follow.

nodes.title: Geometric motives are rigid
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities. For L, M, N in DM_gm(k, Z) there is a natural isomorphism Hom_gm(L tensor M, N) -> Hom_gm(L, M^* tensor N), so the internal Hom of M and N is M^* tensor N, again a geometric motive; it is bi-distributive for the tensor product and M -> M^** is an isomorphism, so DM_gm is rigid in the sense of Deligne-Milne (MVW Theorem 20.17). Equivalently, in Mathlib's sense every object M has the dual M^* with evaluation epsilon_M and coevaluation the image of the identity of M under Hom(M, M) = Hom(Z, M^* tensor M) followed by the symmetry, so DM_gm is a rigid symmetric monoidal category.
hypotheses: k is a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities, the standing hypothesis of MVW Lecture 20.
Coefficients are the integers, as in the source.
Deligne-Milne rigidity (internal Hom, bi-distributive, reflexive) is what MVW prove; for a symmetric monoidal category it is equivalent to Mathlib's RigidCategory, which the last step checks.
proofSteps: Proposition 20.14: Hom(L tensor M, N) = Hom(L tensor M tensor N^*, Z) = Hom(L tensor (M^* tensor N)^*, Z) = Hom(L, M^* tensor N), using MC.4/double-dual-isomorphism for N and M^* tensor N, MC.4/dual-of-tensor-product and the representability of MC.4/geometric-motive-dual.
Define the internal Hom as M^* tensor N (Definition 20.15); it is a geometric motive.
Bi-distributivity: (M_1 tensor M_2)^* tensor (N_1 tensor N_2) = (M_1^* tensor N_1) tensor (M_2^* tensor N_2) by MC.4/dual-of-tensor-product and the symmetry.
With the double dual isomorphism this is Deligne-Milne rigidity (Theorem 20.17).

Mathlib form: coevaluation Z -> M tensor M^* is the image of the identity of M under Hom(M, M) = Hom(Z, M^* tensor M), followed by the symmetry; evaluation is epsilon_M; the zig-zag identities follow from naturality of 20.14; this gives ExactPairing M M^*, hence right duals and, with the symmetry, left duals, i.e. RigidCategory.
acceptance: Rigidity is stated for the Tate-stabilised category and not for the effective one; the dual of M(X) for X smooth of dimension d is M^c(X)(-d)[-2d], which involves a negative twist.
The double dual map is an isomorphism, proved and not assumed.
For X smooth projective of dimension d, M(X) is isomorphic to M(X)^*(d)[2d], which matches the duality of Chow motives under MC.4/chow-motives-into-geometric-motives.

sources.excerpt: Let L, M, and N be three objects of DM_gm. Then there is a natural isomorphism Hom_gm(L tensor M,N) = Hom_gm(L,M^* tensor N). ... DEFINITION 20.15. If M and N are two objects of DM_gm, we define their internal Hom to be: Hom(M,N) = M^* tensor N.
sources.match: The adjunction and the internal Hom.

sources.locator: Lecture 20, before Theorem 20.17 and the theorem (pp. 170-171)
sources.excerpt: Recall from [DMOS82, p. 111] that a tensor category A is said to be rigid if it has an internal Hom, bi-distributive for the tensor, and if A -> (A^*)^* is an isomorphism for every A. THEOREM 20.17. The tensor category DM_gm is rigid.
sources.match: The notion of rigidity and the theorem.

nodes.title: Chow motives embed into geometric motives
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities. For smooth projective X and Y over k, with d = dim Y, there is an isomorphism CH^d(X x Y) = CH_{dim X}(X x Y) -> Hom_{DM^eff_gm(k,Z)}(M(X), M(Y)), sending the class of the graph of f: X -> Y to M(f). In MVW's convention Grothendieck's category Chow^eff of effective integral Chow motives is the idempotent completion of the category of smooth projective varieties with Hom_Chow(Y, X) = CH_{dim X}(X x Y), so these are bijections Hom_Chow(Y, X) -> Hom(M(X), M(Y)); the source asserts (Remark 20.2) that they come from a fully faithful contravariant tensor functor (Chow^eff)^op -> DM^eff_gm(k,Z) sending the Lefschetz motive to Z(1)[2] and extending to Chow^op -> DM_gm(k,Z). This roadmap's Chow motives (MC.1) are Q-linear, with Hom(h(Y), h(X)) = Corr^0(Y, X) = CH^{dim Y}(Y x X) tensor Q and Lefschetz motive 1(-1); tensoring the bijections with Q identifies Hom(h(Y), h(X)) with Hom(M(X), M(Y)) tensor Q, and the functor, once constructed, sends h(X) to M(X), 1(m) to Q(-m)[-2m] and (X, p, m) to the summand of M(X)(-m)[-2m] cut out by the image of p.
hypotheses: k is perfect and admits resolution of singularities (the standing hypothesis of MVW Lecture 20); integral coefficients.
X and Y are smooth projective over k and d = dim Y. MVW's proof prints d = dim X; the authors' errata correct it to d = dim Y (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E23).

The Hom-group bijections are proved in the source; that they come from a functor compatible with composition and with the tensor product is asserted in Remark 20.2 without proof (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E24; gap).
proofSteps: CH^d(X x Y) is isomorphic to H^{2d,d}(X x Y, Z) by MC.4/motivic-cohomology-higher-chow (MVW Corollary 19.2).
H^{2d,d}(X x Y, Z) = Hom(M(X x Y), Z(d)[2d]) by representability (MVW 14.16, M.5a).

Hom(M(X x Y), Z(d)[2d]) = Hom(M(X x Y), M^c(A^d)) is isomorphic to Hom(M(X)(d)[2d], M^c(Y x A^d)) = Hom(M(X)(d)[2d], M(Y)(d)[2d]) by MC.4/friedlander-voevodsky-duality with T = Y, MC.4/compact-support-kunneth and M^c(Y) = M(Y) for Y proper.
Hom(M(X)(d)[2d], M(Y)(d)[2d]) = Hom(M(X), M(Y)) by the cancellation theorem (imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a) applied d times.
The Lefschetz summand of M(P^1) = Z + Z(1)[2] (MC.4/motive-of-projective-space) is Z(1)[2] (MVW Remark 20.2).
Compatibility with composition and with tensor products, needed for a functor, is not proved in the source (gap); record the bijections and do not build on the functor until it is supplied.
Q-linear form for MC.1: tensor the bijections with Q, compare Corr^0(Y, X) = CH^{dim Y}(Y x X) tensor Q with CH^{dim Y}(X x Y) tensor Q through the transpose, and pass to idempotent completions.
acceptance: The embedding is contravariant: the graph of f: X -> Y lies in CH^{dim Y}(X x Y) = Hom_Chow(Y, X) and goes to M(f).
For X = Y = P^1, CH^1(P^1 x P^1) = Z^2 matches End(Z + Z(1)[2]) = Z + Z, the off-diagonal groups being H^{2,1}(Spec k, Z) = 0 and Hom(Z(1)[2], Z) = 0.
The hypotheses on k are used through duality and cancellation.

nodes.title: Motivic cohomology is higher Chow groups
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth separated scheme over a perfect field k. For all n and all i >= 0 there is an isomorphism H^{n,i}(X, Z) -> CH^i(X, 2i - n), natural in X for the pullbacks of motivic cohomology and the Bloch-Levine pullbacks of higher Chow groups. In particular H^{2i,i}(X, Z) is isomorphic to CH^i(X), and H^{n,i}(X, Z) = 0 for n > 2i.
hypotheses: X is smooth and separated over a perfect field k.
Motivic cohomology is H^{n,i}(X, Z) = Hom(M(X), Z(i)[n]) in DM^eff,-_Nis (MVW 14.16), imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a.

Bloch's higher Chow groups, their homotopy invariance, their Zariski descent (MVW 19.12, from Bloch's localisation theorem and the Brown-Gersten theorem) and the Bloch-Levine pullbacks (MVW 19.13-19.16) are imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.4.
proofSteps: By MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.4/suslin-friedlander-into-cycle-complex, H^{n,i}(X, Z) is isomorphic to H^{n-2i}(X, z^i(- x A^i, *)) (MVW Corollary 19.9).
By Zariski descent for Bloch's complexes (imported from M.4), H^{-m}(X, z^i(- x A^i, *)) is CH^i(X x A^i, m), which is CH^i(X, m) by homotopy invariance of higher Chow groups.
Define the comparison as the composite, with m = 2i - n (MVW, proof of Theorem 19.1).

Naturality: the pullbacks on higher Chow groups are the Bloch-Levine maps defined through Zariski descent, which compose correctly and agree with pullback by graphs of finite correspondences (MVW 19.13-19.16, imported from M.4).
Consequences: CH^i(X, 0) = CH^i(X) gives H^{2i,i}(X, Z) = CH^i(X) (Corollary 19.2), and CH^i(X, m) = 0 for m < 0 gives the vanishing (Theorem 19.3).
acceptance: The bidegree conversion is that the simplicial degree is 2i - n; a comparison with a different conversion fails the specialisation to the classical Chow group.
The isomorphism is natural in X, which is what makes it a comparison of theories rather than a family of isomorphisms.
The vanishing statement is a consequence and is worth recording separately, since it is the first sanity check on any implementation.

nodes.title: The blow-up triangle for an abstract blow-up
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities. Let p: X' -> X be an abstract blow-up with centre Z (a proper morphism of schemes of finite type over k that is an isomorphism over X - Z, with Z closed) and Z' = Z x_X X'. Then there is a distinguished triangle C_*R_tr(Z') -> C_*R_tr(Z) + C_*R_tr(X') -> C_*R_tr(X) -> C_*R_tr(Z')[1] in D^-(Sh_Nis(Cor_k, R)), hence M(Z') -> M(Z) + M(X') -> M(X) -> M(Z')[1] in DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R), where for Y of finite type M(Y) denotes the class of R_tr(Y).
hypotheses: k is perfect and admits resolution of singularities in MVW's sense (every integral scheme of finite type has a proper birational map from a smooth scheme, and every proper birational cdh cover of a smooth scheme is refined by a composite of blow-ups with smooth centres, MVW p. 97). MVW 13.26 states only resolution; its proof uses Theorem 13.25, which assumes k perfect.
X, X' and Z are of finite type over k; smoothness is not assumed.
The cdh topology with Lemma 12.30 and Theorem 13.25 are requested from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a; resolution of singularities and platification from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.4.
proofSteps: Let Q be the cokernel of R_tr(X') + R_tr(Z) -> R_tr(X); the sequence R_tr(Z') -> R_tr(Z) + R_tr(X') -> R_tr(X) is quasi-isomorphic to Q (MVW Exercise 12.22), so it suffices that C_*(Q) is acyclic.
By MVW Theorem 13.25 (imported: over a perfect field with resolution, C_*(F) is acyclic when F_cdh = 0) it suffices that Q_cdh = 0.

Represent generators of Q(U) by elementary correspondences W_i in U x X not contained in U x Z; take proper transforms in U x X', flatten them over a blow-up U' -> U by platification (Raynaud-Gruson), refine U' to a smooth U'' by resolution so that U'' -> U is a cdh cover, and conclude that each generator dies in Q_cdh(U'') (MVW Lemma 12.30).
Pass to DM^eff,-_Nis.
acceptance: For Z empty and X' = X the triangle is trivial.
For X a nodal curve, X' its normalisation and Z the node, Z' is two points and the triangle is R + R -> R + M(X') -> M(X) ->.
Without resolution of singularities the triangle is not available by this argument; every node that uses it carries the hypothesis.

nodes.title: Motives with compact support
nodes.statement: For a scheme X of finite type over k, the motive with compact support M^c(X) is the Nisnevich sheaf with transfers z_equi(X, 0) of MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.4/equidimensional-cycle-sheaves, regarded as an object of DM^eff,-_Nis(k); it is isomorphic there to C_*z_equi(X, 0). It is contravariant in X for etale maps and covariant for proper maps; the inclusion Z_tr(X) in z_equi(X, 0) induces a canonical map M(X) -> M^c(X), which is an isomorphism (indeed an equality of sheaves) when X is proper. If k is perfect, M^c(A^i) is isomorphic to Z(i)[2i]. The localisation triangle, the Kuenneth isomorphism and geometricity are the nodes MC.4/compact-support-localisation-triangle, MC.4/compact-support-kunneth and MC.4/compact-support-geometric.
hypotheses: X is a scheme of finite type over k; smoothness is not assumed.
The computation of M^c(A^i) uses MC.4/suslin-friedlander-comparison and hence k perfect; MVW Example 16.14 states it without that hypothesis (part of MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E25).
Integral coefficients as in the source; the definition works verbatim with R-coefficients.
proofSteps: Take z_equi(X, 0) from MC.4/equidimensional-cycle-sheaves, regard it as an object of D^-(Sh_Nis(Cor_k)) and pass to DM^eff,-_Nis; it is isomorphic to C_*z_equi(X, 0) by MVW Lemma 14.4 (M.5a).
Functoriality: etale maps are flat of relative dimension 0 and proper maps push forward, both preserving relative dimension 0 (API of MC.4/equidimensional-cycle-sheaves).

Canonical map and proper case: Z_tr(X) in z_equi(X, 0) is a morphism of sheaves with transfers, with equality for X proper because a closed subvariety of U x X that is quasi-finite over U and proper over U is finite (MVW Example 16.2).
M^c(A^i): C_*z_equi(A^i, 0) = Z_SF(i)[2i] by definition, and Z_SF(i) is quasi-isomorphic to Z(i) by MC.4/suslin-friedlander-comparison.
acceptance: For X proper M^c(X) = M(X), so the construction extends the motive of a smooth scheme invisibly on proper schemes.
M^c(A^1) is Z(1)[2], not Z: the construction differs from the motive, which is homotopy invariant.
For X the spectrum of a finite etale k-algebra, M^c(X) = M(X).

sources.excerpt: For any scheme X of finite type over k, let M^c(X) denote z_equi(X,0), regarded as an object in DM^{eff,-}_Nis(k). By 14.4, M^c(X) = C_*z_equi(X,0) in DM^{eff,-}_Nis(k).
sources.match: The definition, literally.

sources.excerpt: As pointed out in 16.1, M^c(X) is contravariant in X for etale maps and covariant in X for proper maps. As observed in 16.2, there is a canonical map M(X) -> M^c(X), induced by Z_tr(X) in z_equi(X,0). Moreover, M(X) = M^c(X) if X is proper over k.
sources.match: The elementary functoriality, literally.

sources.excerpt: We have an isomorphism M^c(A^i) = Z(i)[2i] in DM^{eff,-}_Nis(k). To see this, recall from 16.7 that the Suslin-Friedlander motivic complex Z_SF(i) = C_*z_equi(A^i,0)[-2i] is quasi-isomorphic to Z(i).

nodes.title: Motivic cohomology with compact supports and Borel-Moore motivic homology
nodes.statement: For X of finite type over k and i >= 0, motivic cohomology with compact supports is H^{n,i}_c(X, R) = Hom(M^c(X), R(i)[n]) and Borel-Moore motivic homology is H^BM_{n,i}(X, R) = Hom(R(i)[n], M^c(X)), both in DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R). If k is perfect and admits resolution of singularities, a closed subscheme Z with open complement U gives long exact sequences ... -> H^{n,i}_c(U) -> H^{n,i}_c(X) -> H^{n,i}_c(Z) -> H^{n+1,i}_c(U) -> ... and ... -> H^BM_{n,i}(Z) -> H^BM_{n,i}(X) -> H^BM_{n,i}(U) -> H^BM_{n-1,i}(Z) -> ....
hypotheses: The definitions need no hypothesis on k.
The long exact sequences use MC.4/compact-support-localisation-triangle and so k perfect with resolution of singularities.
The Borel-Moore groups are indexed so that the localisation sequence runs in the direction opposite to that of the cohomology with compact supports, as the source displays.
proofSteps: Define the two groups as the displayed Hom groups.
Functoriality: H_c is contravariant for proper maps and covariant for etale maps, H^BM the reverse, from the functoriality of M^c.
Apply the cohomological functor Hom(-, R(i)[n]) and the homological functor Hom(R(i)[n], -) to the triangle of MC.4/compact-support-localisation-triangle.
acceptance: For X proper H^{n,i}_c(X, R) = Hom(M(X), R(i)[n]), the motivic cohomology of MVW Definition 14.17.
Over a perfect field H^BM_{2,1}(A^1, Z) = Hom(Z(1)[2], Z(1)[2]) = Z by cancellation.
The identification of Borel-Moore motivic homology with higher Chow groups (MVW Proposition 19.18) uses the shifting theorem; no target of this layer uses it and it is not planned.

nodes.title: Diagrams and their representations
nodes.statement: A small diagram D is a directed graph on a set of vertices with, for every vertex v, a distinguished edge id_v: v -> v. It is finite if it has finitely many vertices, and a finite subdiagram is the diagram on a finite set of vertices with all edges of D between them. A representation T of D in a category C is a map of directed graphs from D to the underlying graph of C that sends every identity edge to the identity morphism; in the case of interest C is the category R-Mod of finitely generated modules over a noetherian commutative ring R (R = Q for Nori motives). In Mathlib's vocabulary a diagram is a quiver with a chosen loop at each vertex, and a representation is a prefunctor to C sending those loops to identities.
hypotheses: R is a noetherian commutative ring (HMS Appendix B); for Nori motives R = Q.
Identity edges are part of the data (HMS Remark B.2) and a representation maps them to identities (HMS Definition B.4).
No compatibility with composites of edges is imposed: a diagram has no composition.
proofSteps: Define a small diagram as a quiver with a chosen loop id_v at each vertex.
Define finite diagrams and the finite subdiagram on a finite set of vertices (the full subquiver).
Define a representation in C as a prefunctor to C that sends each id_v to the identity of T(v).

Record that a small category gives a diagram (vertices its objects, edges its morphisms, id its identities: HMS Example B.3) and a functor gives a representation, and that the finite subdiagrams, ordered by inclusion, form a directed set.
acceptance: A representation need not respect composites of edges: for the diagram of a category it is a prefunctor, not a functor.
Identity edges go to identities.
Every functor gives a representation of the diagram of its source category, but not conversely.
