nodes.title: The endomorphism coalgebra of a representation
nodes.statement: Let T be a representation of a diagram in finitely generated R-modules. For each finite subdiagram F let the endomorphism ring of the restriction of T to F be the subring of the product over the vertices of F of the endomorphism rings of the assigned modules, cut out by the condition that the components commute with the maps assigned to the edges of F. Taking R-duals and passing to the filtered colimit over finite subdiagrams produces an R-coalgebra attached to T.
hypotheses: T is a representation of a small diagram in finitely generated R-modules, R noetherian, so that each End(T|F) is finitely generated (HMS Proposition B.8, proof).
For the coalgebra structure R is a field or a Dedekind domain and T takes values in R-Proj (HMS Proposition B.7).
The colimit is over the directed system of finite subdiagrams.
proofSteps: Define the endomorphism ring of a restriction as the displayed subring of a finite product.
Take the R-dual of each such ring, which is again finitely generated under the hypotheses, and check that the dual of a ring is a coalgebra.
Check that an inclusion of finite subdiagrams gives a map of duals in the right direction, so the system is filtered and its colimit exists.
Define the coalgebra as that colimit.
acceptance: The construction takes duals, so the colimit is over a filtered system and not a limit; this is what makes the coalgebra a union of finite pieces.
The endomorphism ring is cut out by commuting with the edge maps, so it depends on the edges and not only on the vertices.
Over a field the dual of a finite dimensional algebra is a coalgebra, which is the case the construction is used in.

sources.excerpt: Let T be a representation of D in R-Mod. For each finite subdiagram F in D let End(T|F) be the ring of endomorphisms of the functor T|F, more precisely, as End(T|F) := {(e_p) in prod_{p in F} End_R(T(p)) | e_q o T(m) = T(m) o e_p for all p, q in F, m in Mor(p, q)}.
sources.match: The endomorphism ring, literally.

sources.excerpt: Suppose R is a Dedekind domain or a field and T takes values in R-Proj. Let A(F, T) := Hom_R(End(T|F), R). We set A(T) := colim_F A(F, T). Then C(T) is the category of finitely generated R-modules with an R-linear A(T)-comodule structure.
sources.match: The coalgebra and its role; the proof is referred to von Wangenheim's thesis.

nodes.title: The diagram category of a representation
nodes.statement: Let R be a field (the case used; HMS also allow a Dedekind domain with T in R-Proj) and T a representation of a small diagram D in finitely generated R-modules. The diagram category C(D, T) is the category of right A(T)-comodules that are finitely generated over R, that is Tau Ceti's FGComoduleCat over the endomorphism coalgebra A(T). Each T(v) is an A(T)-comodule and each T(e) a comodule map, which gives a representation T~: D -> C(D, T) whose composite with the forgetful functor f_T: C(D, T) -> R-Mod is T. C(D, T) is an R-linear abelian category and f_T is exact and faithful. HMS define C(T) as the colimit over finite subdiagrams F of the categories of finitely generated End(T|F)-modules and identify it with A(T)-comodules (Proposition B.7, whose proof the source refers to von Wangenheim's thesis); this node takes the comodule description as the definition.
hypotheses: R is a field in the case used here.

Comodules are right comodules, as in Tau Ceti's FGComoduleCat; End(T|F) acts on T(v) on the left, and the dual coalgebra structure on A(F, T) is dual to the multiplication, which makes T(v) a right comodule.
proofSteps: Define C(D, T) as FGComoduleCat over A(T).

Give each T(v) its A(T)-comodule structure: for a finite F containing v, dualising the action End(T|F) x T(v) -> T(v) gives T(v) -> T(v) tensor A(F, T) -> T(v) tensor A(T), compatibly with the transition maps.
Each T(e) is a comodule map, since the components of an element of End(T|F) commute with T(e); this gives T~ with f_T o T~ = T, identity edges going to identities.
The abelian structure and the exactness and faithfulness of f_T come from MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.5/finite-comodules-abelian.
Record the module-theoretic description of HMS Definition B.6 and its identification with comodules (B.7) as a compatibility; the source sketches it and refers to von Wangenheim's thesis.
acceptance: f_T is faithful and exact, and T factors as f_T o T~ on the nose.
For the empty diagram A(T) = 0 and C(D, T) consists of the zero comodule.
For one vertex with T(v) = V, C(D, T) is equivalent to finitely generated modules over the matrix algebra End(V), hence to R-Mod.

nodes.title: Graded multiplicative diagrams and the tensor structure
nodes.statement: A graded diagram is a small diagram D with a map |.| from its vertices to Z/2Z; for an edge g: e -> e', |g| = |e| - |e'|. A commutative product structure is a map of graded diagrams x: D x D -> D (D x D having vertices (f, g), edges (a, id) and (id, b), and grading |f| + |g|), or in the weak form of HMS Remark B.17 a map into the path category P(D), together with chosen edges a_{f,g}: f x g -> g x f, b_{f,g,h}: f x (g x h) -> (f x g) x h and b'_{f,g,h} in the other direction; a unit is a vertex 1 of degree 0 with edges u_f: f -> 1 x f. A graded multiplicative representation in R-Proj is a representation T with isomorphisms tau_{f,g}: T(f x g) -> T(f) tensor T(g) such that (1) tau o T(a_{f,g}) o tau^{-1} is (-1)^{|f||g|} times the swap; (2) for an edge g: f -> f', tau o T(g x id_h) = (-1)^{|g||h|} (T(g) tensor id) o tau; (3) tau o T(id_h x g) = (id tensor T(g)) o tau; (4) tau is compatible with T(b) and the associativity of the tensor product; (5) T(b) and T(b') are inverse; it is unital if every T(u_f) is an isomorphism. For such D and T, C(D, T) is a commutative, associative, unital tensor category and f_T is a tensor functor; if R is a field or a Dedekind domain, A(T) is a commutative bialgebra with unit and counit (HMS Proposition B.16).
hypotheses: The grading takes values in Z/2Z: only parities enter the signs.

The sign sits in the first variable (condition (2)) and not in the second (condition (3)), as HMS Remark B.19(2) explains; the proof of HMS Theorem 1.6 describes the opposite placement (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E29).
T takes values in R-Proj; for the bialgebra, R is a field or a Dedekind domain.
proofSteps: For finite subdiagrams F, F' with all f x g (f, g in F) in F', define mu*_F: End(T|F') -> End(T|F) tensor End(T|F) by sending a to the family of tau o a_{f x g} o tau^{-1}, using End(T(f) tensor T(g)) = End(T(f)) tensor End(T(g)).

Check that mu*(a) commutes with the images of edges (a, id) and (id, b): condition (2) contributes the same sign (-1)^{|g||a|} on both sides and condition (3) none (the source cites property (3) where (2) is meant: MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E32).

Cocommutativity of mu* from condition (1) and the edges a_{f,g}; coassociativity from condition (4) (the source says (3): E32); the counit is the projection End(T|F) -> End(T(1)) = R, using unitality and that T(1) is free of rank one (Remark B.15).
Define X tensor Y for X, Y in C(T|F) as X tensor_R Y with End(T|F')-action through mu*_F; it is independent of F and F', defines the tensor structure and makes f_T a tensor functor.

Over a field or a Dedekind domain, dualise mu*_F to mu_F: A(F, T) tensor A(F, T) -> A(F', T) and pass to the colimit to get the commutative bialgebra A(T); then C(D, T) = FGComoduleCat over A(T) carries Tau Ceti's monoidal and symmetric structures, which agree with the above.
acceptance: The tensor structure exists on the diagram category and not merely on the values of the representation.

The signs are those of Definition B.14 (2)-(3), in the first variable; with the usual conventions for the cross product and the coboundary of relative cohomology, relative singular cohomology satisfies them with tau^{-1}(a tensor b) = (-1)^{|a||b|} a x b.
Over a field the coalgebra becomes a commutative bialgebra, which is what makes the Tannakian theory available.

nodes.title: Localisation of a diagram at an invertible vertex
nodes.statement: Let D^eff be a graded diagram with commutative product structure and unit, and f_0 a vertex. The localised diagram D has vertices f(n) for f in D^eff and n an integer, edges a(n): f(n) -> g(n) for every edge a: f -> g of D^eff, and edges c_{f,n}: (f x f_0)(n) -> f(n + 1); |f(n)| = |f|; it carries the weak product structure f(n) x g(m) = (f x g)(n + m) into its path category, with a, b, b' and the unit induced from D^eff (HMS Definition B.18, Remark B.19). Let R be a field or a Dedekind domain and T a graded multiplicative unital representation of D^eff in R-Proj with T(f_0) locally free of rank one (Assumption B.20). Then T extends uniquely to a graded multiplicative unital representation of D with T(f(n)) = T(f) tensor T(f_0)^{tensor n} and T(a(n)) = T(a) tensor id (Lemma B.21); C(D, T) is the localisation of C(D^eff, T) at the object T~(f_0), namely the colimit over n of copies of C(D^eff, T) along tensoring with T~(f_0); and A(D, T) is the localisation A^eff_chi of the algebra A^eff = A(D^eff, T) at the element chi of A({f_0}, T) = End(T(f_0))^dual dual to the identity (Proposition B.22).
hypotheses: T is graded multiplicative and unital with values in R-Proj, R a field or a Dedekind domain.
T(f_0) is locally free of rank one (HMS Assumption B.20); negative powers T(f_0)^{tensor n} are powers of the dual.
Only the vertex product of D^eff enters the definition of D; the weak product structure on edges is induced as in Remark B.19.
proofSteps: Define D as in Definition B.18 with its weak product structure (Remark B.19).

Lemma B.21: define T on vertices and edges by the formula, with T(c_{f,n}) given by tau_{f,f_0} tensor id; check the conditions of a graded multiplicative unital representation (the source calls this tedious but straightforward); uniqueness because the formula and the values on the c_{f,n} are forced.

Write D as the union of the subdiagrams D^{>=n}; the shift f(m) -> f(m + 1) is an isomorphism D^{>=n} -> D^{>=n+1}, and with the fibre functor f_T tensor T(f_0)^dual the universal property (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.5/diagram-category-universal-property) gives C(D^{>=n}, T) equivalent to C(D^{>=n+1}, T).
D^eff -> D^{>=0} induces an equivalence of tensor categories: represent D^{>=0} in C(D^eff, T) by f(m) -> T~(f) tensor T~(f_0)^{tensor m} and apply the universal property.

On coalgebras A is the colimit of the A^{>=n}, each isomorphic to A^eff, with transition maps x -> x chi computed from End(T(f)) -> End(T(f x f_0)) = End(T(f)) tensor End(T(f_0)), a -> a tensor id; this colimit is A^eff_chi.
acceptance: The assumption of rank one is essential: the localisation is at an invertible object and there is nothing to invert otherwise.
The extension is unique, so the localised theory is determined by the effective one together with the choice of vertex.
Localising the coalgebra at a group-like element is the algebraic counterpart of inverting the corresponding object.

nodes.title: The diagrams of effective pairs, good pairs and very good pairs
nodes.statement: Work over Q, with variety meaning a reduced separated scheme of finite type over Q. The diagram D^eff of effective pairs has as vertices the triples (X, Y, i) of a variety X, a closed subvariety Y and an integer i, and two kinds of edges: for every morphism f: X -> X' with f(Y) in Y', a functoriality edge f^*: (X', Y', i) -> (X, Y, i); and for every chain of closed subschemes X contains Y contains Z, a coboundary edge (Y, Z, i) -> (X, Y, i + 1). It is graded, in the sense of HMS Definition B.14, by the parity of i. The diagram D^eff_Nori of effective good pairs is the full subdiagram of triples with H^j(X(C), Y(C); Q) = 0 for j different from i, and the diagram of effective very good pairs is the full subdiagram of good pairs with X affine, X - Y smooth and either dim X = i and dim Y = i - 1, or X = Y of dimension less than i. The diagrams D, D_Nori and D~ of pairs, good pairs and very good pairs are their localisations (Definition B.18) at (G_m, {1}, 1); only the product of vertices (X, Y, i) x (X', Y', i') = (X x X', X x Y' union Y x X', i + i') enters that definition.
hypotheses: The base field is Q and coefficients are rational; the source notes that Nori's machine also works with integral coefficients, where Definition D.1 adds that H^i(X(C), Y(C); R) be free.
Variety means a reduced separated scheme of finite type over Q; Y is a closed subvariety of X, and for the coboundary edges Z is a closed subscheme of Y.

Relative singular cohomology of the complex points, used in the definition of a good pair, is the dual of Tau Ceti's relative singular homology of the pair (X(C), Y(C)); the complex points with the analytic topology are requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2.
proofSteps: Define the vertices and the two kinds of edges, with the directions displayed.
Define the grading by the parity of i; a coboundary edge has odd degree and a functoriality edge even degree.
Define good pairs by the vanishing of relative singular cohomology outside degree i (with rational coefficients the freeness condition of Definition D.1 is automatic).
Define very good pairs by the four geometric conditions.

Localise all three diagrams at (G_m, {1}, 1) by Definition B.18, using the vertex product; check that products of good, respectively very good, pairs are good, respectively very good (Kuenneth in degree i + i', affineness and smoothness of (X - Y) x (X' - Y')).
acceptance: Functoriality edges go against the morphisms, since singular cohomology is contravariant, and coboundary edges go from degree i to degree i + 1.
A good pair is a condition on the pair and the degree together; (G_m, {1}, 0) is not good while (G_m, {1}, 1) is.
The very good condition includes affineness and smoothness of the complement, which the Basic Lemma provides.

sources.excerpt: The diagram Deff of effective pairs consists of triples (X, Y, i) with X a Q-variety, Y in X a closed subvariety and an integer i. There are two types of edges between effective good pairs: (a) (functoriality) For every morphism f : X -> X' with f(Y) in Y' an edge f^* : (X', Y', i) -> (X, Y, i)

sources.excerpt: (b) (coboundary) For every chain X contains Y contains Z of closed Q-subschemes of X an edge d : (Y, Z, i) -> (X, Y, i + 1). The diagram is graded (see Definition B.14) by |(X, Y, i)| = i. (2) The diagram Deff_Nori of effective good pairs is the full subdiagram of Deff

nodes.title: Nori motives
nodes.statement: The category MM^eff_Nori of effective mixed Nori motives is the diagram category C(D^eff_Nori, H^*) of the diagram of effective good pairs with respect to the representation H^* by relative singular cohomology (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.5/singular-cohomology-representation), and the category MM_Nori of mixed Nori motives is C(D_Nori, H^*), the diagram category of its localisation at (G_m, {1}, 1), H^* being extended by Lemma B.21. For a good pair (X, Y, i), H^i_Nori(X, Y) denotes the corresponding object, and the twisted unit is 1(-1) = H^1_Nori(G_m, {1}), with 1(-n) = 1(-1)^{tensor n}. HMS Definition 1.11 later writes 1(-1) = H^1_Nori(G_m); the two agree canonically (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E35).
hypotheses: The base field is Q and the coefficients are rational.
The representation is relative singular cohomology of the complex points, extended to the localised diagram by Lemma B.21, which applies because H^1(G_m(C), {1}; Q) = Q has rank one.
The categories are the diagram categories of the corresponding diagrams.
proofSteps: Take the diagram of effective good pairs and the representation H^*.
Form the diagram category, the finitely generated comodules over the endomorphism coalgebra.
Extend H^* to the localised diagram (MC.5/diagram-localisation) and form its diagram category.

Define 1(-1) = H^1_Nori(G_m, {1}) and 1(-n) as its tensor powers (the tensor structure is MC.5/nori-tensor-category); record the canonical isomorphism with H^1_Nori(G_m) of Definition 1.11, from the long exact sequence of the triple (G_m, {1}, empty).
acceptance: The twist is defined as a cohomology object of an explicit pair and not axiomatically.

The canonical functor MM^eff_Nori -> MM_Nori is exact and faithful, compatible with the fibre functors; the source writes it as an inclusion but does not prove it full, and fullness is not claimed here.
The definition is unconditional: no conjecture is used to produce the category.

sources.excerpt: The category of (effective) mixed Nori motives MM_Nori (resp. MM^eff_Nori) is defined as the diagram category C(D_Nori, H^*) (resp. C(D^eff_Nori, H^*)). For a good pair (X, Y, i) we write H^i_Nori(X, Y) for the corresponding object in MM_Nori. We put 1(-1) = H^1_Nori(G_m, {1}) in MM^eff_Nori.
sources.match: The definition, literally.

nodes.title: Nori motives form a tensor category and the localisation statement
nodes.statement: MM^eff_Nori and MM_Nori are commutative tensor categories with faithful exact tensor fibre functor H^*, the product of good pairs being (X, Y, i) x (X', Y', i') = (X x X', X x Y' union Y x X', i + i') with unit (Spec Q, empty, 0); MM_Nori is the localisation of MM^eff_Nori at 1(-1); and the construction agrees with Nori's original definition as comodules over A^eff localised at chi. The sign convention is that of HMS Definition B.14: with the usual conventions for the cross product and the coboundary, tau^{-1}(a tensor b) = (-1)^{|a||b|} a x b makes coboundaries in the second variable commute on the nose and those in the first commute up to (-1)^{|g|}; the proof of HMS Theorem 1.6 describes the opposite placement (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E29). The source does not define the product of a coboundary edge with a pair, and for general pairs no edge or path of D^eff_Nori has the required ends (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E30); the node records this as a gap together with the repair it needs.
hypotheses: The diagram of effective good pairs with its grading and vertex product, and the representation by singular cohomology, are as above.
The relative Kuenneth isomorphism for good pairs and the compatibility of the cross product with coboundaries are requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2.

The product on coboundary edges must be supplied (gap), for instance by adding to the diagram the excision edges between (Y x X', Y x Y' union Z x X') and (X x Y' union Y x X', X x Y' union Z x X'), which singular cohomology sends to isomorphisms.
proofSteps: Check that D^eff_Nori with the vertex product, the swap a, the associativity b, b' and the unit is a graded diagram with commutative product structure: on functoriality edges f^* x id = (f x id)^*; on coboundary edges the product must be supplied (gap), for example through excision edges, which do not change the diagram category because singular cohomology sends them to isomorphisms (MC.5/diagram-category-generation (3) with the universal property).

Check that H^* is graded multiplicative and unital with tau^{-1}(a tensor b) = (-1)^{|a||b|} a x b: the relative Kuenneth isomorphism for good pairs, graded commutativity of the cross product for condition (1), the coboundary formulas for (2) and (3), associativity for (4).
Apply MC.5/graded-multiplicative-diagram: MM^eff_Nori is a commutative tensor category and H^* a tensor functor.
(G_m, {1}, 1) satisfies Assumption B.20, since H^1 = Q; MC.5/diagram-localisation gives MM_Nori as the localisation at 1(-1) with A = A^eff_chi.
Compare with the definition in Levine's survey, comodules of finite type over A^eff_chi, which is B.22(2).
acceptance: The sign convention is part of the theorem and is that of Definition B.14 (2)-(3).
The localisation statement identifies MM_Nori with the localisation of MM^eff_Nori at 1(-1), which makes the twist invertible.
H^1_Nori(G_m, {1}) tensor H^1_Nori(G_m, {1}) has fibre H^2(C^* x C^*, C^* x {1} union {1} x C^*; Q) = Q.

sources.excerpt: (1) This definition is equivalent to Nori's original definition. (2) MM^eff_Nori in MM_Nori are commutative tensor categories with a faithful fiber functor H^*. (3) MM_Nori is the localization of MM^eff_Nori with respect to the Lefschetz object 1(-1).
sources.match: The theorem, literally.

nodes.title: Pairs, good pairs and very good pairs give the same category
nodes.statement: The diagram categories of the diagram D^eff of all effective pairs and of the diagram of effective very good pairs, with respect to singular cohomology, are equivalent to MM^eff_Nori as abelian categories, compatibly with the fibre functors; the diagram categories of D and D~ are equivalent to MM_Nori.
hypotheses: The three diagrams are as defined in MC.5/effective-pairs-diagram and the representation is singular cohomology.

The proof uses the realisation functor of HMS Proposition D.3 (MC.5/cellular-realisation-functor) and the universal property (MC.5/diagram-category-universal-property), neither proved in full in the source read.
proofSteps: It suffices to treat the effective case; the localised case follows by MC.5/diagram-localisation.
The inclusions of very good pairs into good pairs into all pairs induce faithful exact functors i: C(D~eff) -> MM^eff_Nori -> C(D^eff) by the universal property.

Represent D^eff in C(D~eff): by MC.5/cellular-realisation-functor for A = C(D~eff) and T = H^*, send (X, Y, i) to H^i(R(Cone(Y -> X))), functoriality edges to R of the morphisms of pairs and coboundary edges to the connecting morphisms of the natural triangle R(X, Y) -> R(X, Z) -> R(Y, Z); restricted to very good pairs this returns H^* up to natural isomorphism.
The universal property gives j: C(D^eff) -> C(D~eff) with j o i isomorphic to the identity; so j is essentially surjective and full, hence, being faithful, an equivalence, and so is i.
acceptance: The three diagrams give equivalent categories, so nothing depends on which one is used.
The comparison is an equivalence of abelian categories compatible with the fibre functors, and after localisation of tensor categories.
H^i_Nori(X, Y) is defined for every effective pair, not only for good ones, through C(D^eff).

sources.excerpt: The diagram categories of Deff and D~eff with respect to singular cohomology are equivalent to MM^eff_Nori as abelian categories. The diagram categories of D and D~ are equivalent to MM_Nori.

sources.match: The structure of the proof.

nodes.title: Cohomology with supports and its long exact sequence in Nori motives
nodes.statement: Let Z be a closed subvariety of a variety X over Q with complement U. Then H^i_Z(X) := H^i(R(Cone(U -> X))), for the realisation functor R of MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles:MC.5/cellular-realisation-functor with values in MM_Nori, is an object of MM_Nori whose image under the fibre functor is singular cohomology with supports H^i_{Z(C)}(X(C); Q), and there is a natural long exact sequence ... -> H^i_Z(X) -> H^i_Nori(X) -> H^i_Nori(X - Z) -> H^{i+1}_Z(X) -> ... in MM_Nori.
hypotheses: X is a variety over Q and Z a closed subvariety with complement U.
The realisation functor of HMS Proposition D.3 is used, with A = MM_Nori and H^i_Nori(X) = H^i(R(X)).
proofSteps: Apply R to Cone(U -> X) and take cohomology in degree i.
The distinguished triangle R(Cone(U -> X)) -> R(X) -> R(U) -> (R is a contravariant triangulated functor) gives the long exact sequence.
Naturality in morphisms of pairs (X', Z') -> (X, Z) with Z' containing the preimage of Z, from the functoriality of R.
Under the fibre functor R computes singular cohomology (Proposition D.3), so H^i_Z(X) realises to cohomology with supports.
acceptance: For Z = X, H^i_Z(X) = H^i_Nori(X); for Z empty, H^i_Z(X) = 0.
The long exact sequence is obtained from a triangle and is natural, not assembled by hand.
For the origin in A^1 the sequence gives H^2_{0}(A^1), isomorphic to H^1_Nori(G_m), which is the case the Gysin computation reduces to.

sources.excerpt: Let Z in X be a closed immersion. Then there is a natural object H^i_Z(X) in MM_Nori representing cohomology with supports. There is a natural long exact sequence ... -> H^i_Z(X) -> H^i_Nori(X) -> H^i_Nori(X - Z) -> H^{i+1}_Z(X) -> ...

sources.excerpt: Let U = X - Z. Put R_Z(X) = R(Cone(U -> X)), H^i_Z(X) = H^i(R_Z(X)).

nodes.title: Rigidity of Nori motives
nodes.statement: The category MM_Nori of mixed Nori motives is rigid: every object V has a dual V^dual with Hom(V tensor A, B) = Hom(A, V^dual tensor B) and Hom(V^dual tensor A, B) = Hom(A, V tensor B); equivalently the bialgebra A(D_Nori, H^*) is a Hopf algebra, so MM_Nori is a neutral Tannakian category over Q with fibre functor H^*, whose Tannaka dual is the motivic Galois group G_mot = Spec A(D_Nori, H^*) (HMS Theorem 1.14 with Theorem B.10).
hypotheses: The generators are H^i_Nori(X, Y)(j) for good pairs of the form of Lemma 1.13; the reduction to that form uses resolution of singularities in characteristic zero.
The fibre functor is singular cohomology, which is faithful and exact.
Theorem B.10 identifies A(T) with the Hopf algebra of the Tannakian dual by the construction of Deligne-Milne, Theorem 2.11 (not read).
proofSteps: By MC.5/nori-generators every object is a subquotient of a direct sum of H^i_Nori(X, Y)(j) for good pairs of the form of Lemma 1.13; by HMS Remark 1.9, enlarging Y one may assume the relevant pair very good (the source's argument is brief).
By MC.5/nori-duality-morphism each such generator V admits q: 1 -> V tensor W with H^*(q)^dual a perfect pairing.
Apply MC.5/rigidity-criterion (Proposition C.4 in the dual form of Remark C.5): A(D_Nori, H^*) is a Hopf algebra.
Rigidity in Mathlib's sense follows from Tau Ceti's instRigidCategory for finitely generated comodules over a commutative Hopf algebra over a field, applied to A(D_Nori, H^*).
Theorem B.10 identifies G_mot.
acceptance: Rigidity is proved and not assumed; it is what makes the Tannakian formalism applicable.
The dual of 1(-1) is 1(1) = 1(-1)^dual, whose fibre is the dual of H^1(C^*, {1}; Q).
The criterion needs the fibre functor to be faithful, which it is.

sources.excerpt: (Nori). MM_Nori is rigid, hence a neutral Tannakian category. Its Tannaka dual is given by G_mot = Spec(A(D_Nori, H^*)). Proof. By Corollary 1.8 every object of MM_Nori is subquotient of M = H^i_Nori(X, Y)(j) for a good pair (X, Y, i) of the particular form occurring in Lemma 1.13.
sources.match: The theorem and the start of its proof.

sources.excerpt: By this Lemma they all admit a perfect pairing. By Proposition C.4, the category MM_Nori is neutral Tannakian. The Hopf algebra of its Tannaka dual agrees with Nori's algebra by Theorem B.10.
sources.match: The criterion used is Proposition C.4.

nodes.title: Torsors in the sense of a ternary operation (heaps)
nodes.statement: A torsor in the sense of Baer and Kontsevich, called a heap below to keep it apart from Mathlib's torsor under a given group, is a set X with a map (x, y, z) ↦ (x, y, z) from X × X × X to X such that (1) (x, y, y) = x and (y, y, x) = x for all x, y in X, and (2) ((x, y, z), u, v) = (x, (u, z, y), v) = (x, y, (z, u, v)) for all x, y, z, u, v in X, where the middle term reverses the order of u, z, y. A morphism of heaps is a map commuting with the ternary operations. For a group G the operation (g, h, k) = g h⁻¹ k makes G a heap (Lemma A.2). For a heap X and an element e of X, the operations g·h = (g, e, h) and g⁻¹ = (e, g, e) make X a group G_e with neutral element e, and the heap operation is recovered as (g, h, k) = g h⁻¹ k in G_e (Lemma A.3). The empty set is a heap; a heap becomes a group only after a point is chosen.
hypotheses: The ternary operation is defined on the whole set, with no basepoint chosen; the set may be empty.
The group structure G_e of Lemma A.3 requires a chosen element e of X.
proofSteps: State the two axioms of Definition A.1, with the reversal of the arguments in the middle term of axiom (2).
Lemma A.2: for a group G check (x, y, y) = x y⁻¹ y = x = y y⁻¹ x = (y, y, x), and that the three nestings in axiom (2) all equal x y⁻¹ z u⁻¹ v, by direct computation.

Lemma A.3: for e in X prove associativity of g·h = (g, e, h) from axiom (2), that e is neutral from axiom (1), that (e, g, e) is a two-sided inverse, and that (g, h, k) = g·h⁻¹·k, each by the chain of equalities the source writes out.
Record the compatibility with Mathlib: a Mathlib torsor P under a group G is a heap by (p, q, r) = (p /ₛ q) • r, which for G acting on itself is the heap of Lemma A.2.
acceptance: The definition is basepoint free: the empty set is a heap, and a nonempty heap has no distinguished element.
Pointing the heap of a group G at its neutral element returns G with its own multiplication; pointing at another element e gives a group isomorphic to G by translation, not equal to it.
The middle nesting in axiom (2) reverses the order of its three arguments; the identity without the reversal fails already for the additive group Z/3.

sources.locator: Appendix A, Definition A.1, Lemma A.2 and Lemma A.3 (pages 14 to 15), arXiv:1105.0865v5
sources.excerpt: A torsor is a set X together with a map (·, ·, ·) : X × X × X → X satisfying: (1) (x, y, y) = (y, y, x) = x for all x, y ∈ X (2) ((x, y, z), u, v) = (x, (u, z, y), v) = (x, y, (z, u, v)) for all x, y, z, u, v ∈ X.
sources.match: The node is Definition A.1 with Lemmas A.2 and A.3. Proposition A.4, Definition A.5 and Proposition A.6 are the separate nodes MC.6/torsor-groups, MC.6/affine-torsor and MC.6/affine-torsor-groups. The source traces the notion to Baer (1929).

nodes.title: The tensor automorphism group of a diagram category, and the motivic Galois group
nodes.statement: Let T be a unital graded multiplicative representation, in finite dimensional vector spaces over a field k, of a graded diagram with commutative product structure and unit, and suppose the diagram category C(T) is rigid. Identify C(T) with the finite dimensional comodules over A(T), with f_T the forgetful functor. Then A(T) is a commutative Hopf algebra, the functor sending a commutative k-algebra R to the group of tensor automorphisms of f_T ⊗ R is represented by the affine group scheme G(T) = Spec A(T), and C(T) is equivalent, compatibly with f_T, to the finite dimensional representations of G(T). For Nori motives, MM_Nori = C(D_Nori, H*) with H* relative singular cohomology is rigid (Theorem 1.14), and G_mot = G(H*) = Spec A(D_Nori, H*) is the motivic Galois group; it is attached to the singular cohomology fibre functor.
hypotheses: T is a unital graded multiplicative representation (Definition B.14) over a field, so that A(T) is a commutative bialgebra (Proposition B.16).
C(T) is rigid; for Nori motives this is Theorem 1.14, the node MC.5/nori-rigidity.
The fibre functor is f_T; another fibre functor gives another group, related to this one by the torsor of MC.6/tensor-iso-torsor.
proofSteps: Identify C(T) with the finite dimensional comodules over A(T) and f_T with the forgetful functor (MC.5/diagram-category), so that the pinned category of finite comodules applies.
Apply MC.6/rigid-bialgebra-is-hopf to obtain the antipode of A(T) from the rigidity of C(T).

Apply the pinned Tannakian reconstruction for commutative Hopf algebras over a field, the natural isomorphism between the functor of points of A(T) and the tensor automorphism group functor of the forgetful functor on finite comodules; this is the representability statement, and it contains both directions of reconstruction.
Apply the pinned equivalence between finitely generated point representations of A(T) and finite comodules to identify C(T) with the finite dimensional representations of G(T).
For Nori motives take T = H* on D_Nori: rigidity is Theorem 1.14 and G_mot = Spec A(D_Nori, H*) as there; Theorem B.10 records that A(T) is the Hopf algebra of the Tannaka dual.
acceptance: G_mot is defined with singular cohomology; the de Rham fibre functor gives a different group, related to G_mot by the torsor of periods and not by a canonical isomorphism over the rational numbers.
Rigidity is used only to produce the antipode; without it the same argument gives an affine monoid scheme.
The twisted unit 1(−1) is one dimensional under H*, so it is a character of G_mot.

nodes.title: The comparison algebra of two representations
nodes.statement: Let D be a graded diagram with commutative product structure and unit, and T_1, T_2 two unital graded multiplicative representations of D in finite dimensional vector spaces over Q (the source works over Q; the construction uses only that Q is a field). The comparison algebra is A_{1,2} = colim_F Hom(T_1|F, T_2|F)^∨, the filtered colimit over finite subdiagrams F of the duals of the spaces of families of linear maps T_1(p) → T_2(p), p in F, commuting with the edges of F. It is a commutative Q-algebra, with multiplication induced as for the tensor structure of the diagram category (Proposition B.16) with Hom(T_1|F, T_2|F) in place of End(T|F); the composition End(T_1|F) × Hom(T_1|F, T_2|F) → Hom(T_1|F, T_2|F) induces a coaction A_{1,2} → A_1 ⊗ A_{1,2} of the bialgebra A_1 = A(D, T_1), compatible with the multiplication, and composition with End(T_2|F) induces a coaction of A_2 on the other side. For T_1 = T_2 = T it is A(D, T).
hypotheses: T_1 and T_2 are unital graded multiplicative representations (Definition B.14) of the same graded diagram with commutative product structure and unit, in finite dimensional Q-vector spaces; the source says only 'two representations', and the multiplicativity is needed for the ring structure (finding E36).
The colimit is over the filtered system of finite subdiagrams, ordered by inclusion.
proofSteps: Define Hom(T_1|F, T_2|F) as the subspace of the product of the Hom(T_1(p), T_2(p)), p in F, cut out by the edges of F, its dual, and the filtered colimit.

Construct the multiplication by repeating the construction of the tensor structure in Proposition B.16 with homomorphisms in place of endomorphisms, using the isomorphisms T_i(f × g) ≅ T_i(f) ⊗ T_i(g) of both representations; the source calls this the hard part.
Construct the two coactions from composition with endomorphisms of T_1|F and of T_2|F, and check compatibility with the multiplication.
Record that for T_1 = T_2 = T the construction is A(D, T) with its multiplication.
acceptance: The object is a commutative Q-algebra with two coactions; it has no counit in general, since an algebra map A_{1,2} → Q is a tensor isomorphism T_1 → T_2 over Q, which need not exist.
The multiplication is the substantial part of the construction and uses the multiplicative structures of both representations.
For de Rham and singular cohomology on the diagram of pairs this is the algebra whose spectrum is the torsor of periods.

nodes.title: The space of periods of a diagram
nodes.statement: Let T_1 and T_2 be two representations of a diagram in finite dimensional vector spaces. The space of periods of the pair is the vector space generated by symbols consisting of a vertex, an element of the first representation at that vertex and an element of the dual of the second representation at that vertex, modulo linearity in the two elements and the change of variables relation attached to each edge. It is a commutative algebra, with multiplication given on generators by the product of vertices and the tensor products of the two entries, and there is a natural map from it to the comparison algebra.
hypotheses: T_1 and T_2 are representations of the same diagram in finite dimensional Q-vector spaces; for the multiplication they are unital graded multiplicative representations of a graded diagram with commutative product structure and unit (finding E36).
The change of variables relation is attached to each edge f : p → p′ and equates (p′, T_1(f)(ω), γ) with (p, ω, T_2(f)^∨(γ)) for ω in T_1(p) and γ in T_2(p′)^∨.
proofSteps: Define the generators and the two families of relations.
Check that the displayed multiplication respects the relations, which is immediate from their shape.
Construct the natural map to the comparison algebra by sending a generator to the functional on homomorphisms that evaluates a homomorphism at the first entry and pairs the result with the second.
Record that the map is a homomorphism of algebras.
acceptance: The relations are linearity and change of variables only; no further relation is imposed.
The multiplication is defined on generators and is well defined precisely because the relations are stable under it.
The map to the comparison algebra is natural in the diagram and in the two representations.

nodes.title: The space of periods is the comparison algebra
nodes.statement: The natural map from the space of periods of a pair of representations of a diagram to their comparison algebra is an isomorphism of algebras. The same statement holds with coefficients in a Dedekind ring as long as the representations take values in projective modules of finite type.
hypotheses: T_1 and T_2 are representations of the same diagram in finite dimensional vector spaces over a field, or in projective modules of finite type over a Dedekind ring; for the statement about algebras they are unital graded multiplicative representations (finding E36).
The natural map is Ψ, sending (p, ω, γ) to the functional φ ↦ γ(φ(p)(ω)).
proofSteps: Reduce to a finite subdiagram F: both sides are filtered colimits over F and Ψ is compatible with the transition maps.

For finite F, write both P_{1,2}(F) and Hom(T_1|F, T_2|F)^∨ as quotients of the direct sum of the T_1(p) ⊗ T_2(p)^∨, p in F, by the span of the elements T_1(f)ω ⊗ γ − ω ⊗ T_2(f)^∨γ, one per edge; for the second this is the duality between the subspace Hom(T_1|F, T_2|F), cut out by the edge conditions, and the quotient of the dual by their span. The source writes 'subspace' for both, which is wrong as written (finding E38).
Conclude that Ψ is an isomorphism of vector spaces, and that it is multiplicative on generators.
Record that the argument uses only duality for finite dimensional (or finitely generated projective) values, which gives the Dedekind version of Remark 2.7.
acceptance: The statement is an isomorphism of algebras and not only of vector spaces.
The proof is by reduction to finite subdiagrams, which is why the colimit in the definition of the comparison algebra is filtered.
The extension to Dedekind coefficients is stated in the source and is recorded here because it is what makes the integral version of the theory possible.

nodes.title: Formal periods
nodes.statement: The space of effective formal periods is the vector space over the rational numbers generated by symbols consisting of a variety over the rational numbers, a subvariety, a class in relative algebraic de Rham cohomology in degree d and a class in relative singular homology in degree d, modulo three families of relations: linearity in the last two entries; for every morphism of pairs, the equality of the symbol formed with the pullback of a de Rham class and the symbol formed with the pushforward of the homology class; and for every triple of nested subvarieties, the equality of the symbol formed with the connecting map in homology and the symbol formed with the connecting map in de Rham cohomology. It becomes an algebra by the product of pairs with the exterior product of the two entries. The space of formal periods is the localisation of the effective one at the period of the pair given by the multiplicative group, the point one, the logarithmic differential form and the unit circle.
hypotheses: The base field is the rational numbers.
The relative de Rham and singular homology groups are those of the pair, in the same degree d.
The localisation is at the single displayed element.
proofSteps: List the generators and the three families of relations, in the order the source gives them.
Define the algebra structure by the product of pairs, with the union of the two mixed products as the subvariety and the exterior products of the two entries.
Define the localisation at the displayed period.

Record that the definition is a variant of Kontsevich's, which restricts to smooth varieties with a normal crossings divisor, uses top degree differential forms rather than cohomology classes, and imposes the third relation only in a special case.
acceptance: All three relations are part of the definition; Kontsevich imposes the third only in a special case, and the source does not know whether his generators give all relations (Remark 2.9).
The localisation is at one explicit element, the formal period of (G_m, {1}, dX/X, S^1), whose evaluation (constructed in PeriodsAndSpecialValues:PS.2) is 2πi.
The definition does not presuppose any category of mixed motives; it is a presentation by generators and relations.

sources.excerpt: P^+ is generated by symbols (X, D, omega, gamma), omega in H^d_dR(X, D), gamma in H_d(X(C), D(C), Q), with relations (1) linearity; (2) for f from X to X' with f(D) inside D', (X, D, f^* omega', gamma) = (X', D', omega', f_* gamma); (3) for Z inside Y inside X, (Y, Z, omega, boundary gamma) = (X, Y, delta omega, gamma). P is the localization of P^+ at the period of (G_m, {1}, dX/X, S^1).
sources.match: The node is that definition together with the remark recording the three ways in which it differs from Kontsevich's.

nodes.title: Formal periods are the comparison algebra of de Rham and singular cohomology
nodes.statement: Let D be the diagram of pairs over Q, T_1 = H*_dR algebraic de Rham cohomology and T_2 = H* singular cohomology with rational coefficients. Then the algebra of formal periods P agrees with the space of periods P_{1,2} of these two representations and with their comparison algebra A_{1,2}: the three are canonically isomorphic Q-algebras, P = P_{1,2} = A_{1,2}, the ring structure on the comparison algebra of the diagram of all pairs being that of the diagram of good pairs, to which it is canonically identified.
hypotheses: The base field is Q and D is the diagram of pairs of Definition 1.1, localised at (G_m, {1}, 1).
The two representations are algebraic de Rham cohomology and singular cohomology of pairs, in the degree of the vertex; the comparison isomorphism plays no part in the identification.
On the diagram of all pairs the two cohomologies are not graded multiplicative representations, so the algebra structures are taken through the diagram of good pairs (finding E37).
proofSteps: Effective case: identify the generators and the three families of relations of P^+ with those of P^eff_{1,2}, using that H_d(X(C), D(C), Q) is the dual of H^d(X(C), D(C), Q); relation (2) is change of variables along the functoriality edges and relation (3) along the coboundary edges.

Route the algebra structure through good pairs: the comparison algebras of all pairs and of good pairs are identified (the analogue for two representations of Corollary 1.7, MC.5/diagram-comparison), and on good pairs both cohomologies are graded multiplicative, so Theorem 2.6 applies as a statement about algebras (finding E37).

Apply Theorem 2.6 (MC.6/periods-equal-comparison-algebra) to obtain P^eff_{1,2} = A^eff_{1,2} and check that the resulting identification with P^+ is multiplicative on generators, where it is the Künneth product.
Localise: both sides are localised at the class of (G_m, {1}, 1), by the analogue of Proposition B.22 for comparison algebras (MC.5/diagram-localisation).
acceptance: The theorem identifies three algebras and turns a presentation by generators and relations into a Tannakian object.
The identification is of algebras, not only of vector spaces; the multiplicative structure is carried by good pairs.
The evaluation to the complex numbers plays no part in the theorem; its injectivity is the period conjecture, which the source does not address.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 2.10. Let D be the diagram of pairs (see Deﬁnition 1.1). Let T1 = H∗dR : D → Q-Mod (de Rham cohomology) T2 = H∗: D → Q-Mod (singular cohomology) then the space of formal periods P (Deﬁnition 2.4) agrees with the comparison algebra A1,2 (Deﬁnition 2.8). P = P1,2 = A1,2 .
sources.match: The node is Theorem 2.10. Its two parenthetical cross references are misprinted (finding E1), and its proof applies Theorem 2.6 as a statement about algebras on the diagram of all pairs (finding E37).

nodes.title: A second representation extends to a fibre functor
nodes.statement: Let T_1 and T_2 be two representations of the same diagram in finite dimensional Q-vector spaces, and φ : T_1 ⊗ K → T_2 ⊗ K an isomorphism of representations after extension of scalars to a field K containing Q. Then T_2 extends to a fibre functor, a faithful exact Q-linear functor to finite dimensional Q-vector spaces, on the diagram category C(T_1). If T_1 and T_2 are unital graded multiplicative representations and φ is compatible with the multiplicative structures, the extension is a tensor functor (finding E36).
hypotheses: T_1 and T_2 are representations of the same diagram in finite dimensional Q-vector spaces.
φ is an isomorphism of representations after extension of scalars to a field K containing Q; it is part of the data.
For the tensor statement, T_1 and T_2 are unital graded multiplicative representations and φ is compatible with the multiplicative structures; the source does not say this (finding E36).
The universal property of C(T_1) is used as stated in Proposition B.8; its proof is in von Wangenheim's work, not obtained (gap).
proofSteps: Form the abelian category A of pairs (V_1, V_2) of finite dimensional Q-vector spaces with an isomorphism V_1 ⊗ K → V_2 ⊗ K, and observe that T_1, T_2 and φ define a representation T of the diagram in A.
The projection p_1 : A → Q-Mod is faithful and exact and p_1 ∘ T = T_1, so the universal property of the diagram category gives a faithful exact functor C(T_1) → A over p_1.

Compose with the projection p_2 to obtain the extension of T_2; it is exact since p_2 is, and faithful since a morphism whose second component vanishes has, after conjugating by the isomorphisms over K, vanishing first component, and f_{T_1} is faithful.

Under the multiplicative hypotheses, A is a tensor category with the componentwise tensor product, T is a graded multiplicative representation in it, and the multiplicative universal property (Proposition B.16) makes the functor, and so the extension of T_2, a tensor functor.
acceptance: The extension is through the universal property and not by hand; this is where the universality of the diagram category is used.
The resulting functor is a fibre functor, so both representations give fibre functors on the same category.
The comparison isomorphism over the extension field is part of the data, and the construction depends on it.

sources.locator: Section 3, the setting paragraph and Lemma 3.1 with its proof (page 12), arXiv:1105.0865v5
sources.excerpt: Let D be a graded diagram with commutative product structure, T1, T2 → Q-Mod two representations which become isomorphic after some ﬁeld extension K/Q. The isomorphism is denoted by ϕ : T1 ⊗ K → T2 ⊗ K. ... Lemma 3.1. T2 extends to a ﬁber functor

nodes.title: The scheme of tensor isomorphisms is a torsor
nodes.statement: In the setting of MC.6/tensor-iso-scheme, inversion f ↦ f⁻¹ is an isomorphism of affine schemes X_{1,2} → X_{2,1}, and the composite X_{1,2} × X_{1,2} × X_{1,2} → X_{1,2} × X_{2,1} × X_{1,2} → X_{1,2}, (f, g, h) ↦ f ∘ g⁻¹ ∘ h, makes X_{1,2} an affine heap in the sense of MC.6/affine-torsor; likewise X_{2,1}. The composition actions of G_1 and G_2 are compatible with the heap operation, and on points they are the left and right groups of the heap.
hypotheses: The diagram category of the first representation is neutral Tannakian, and the second representation is extended to it as a tensor fibre functor (MC.6/fibre-functor-extension under the multiplicative hypothesis of finding E36).
The schemes are the spectra of the comparison algebras, as in MC.6/tensor-iso-scheme.
proofSteps: Construct the inversion map X_{1,2} → X_{2,1} on points and check that it is an isomorphism of affine schemes with inverse the inversion X_{2,1} → X_{1,2}.
Construct the ternary operation as the composite in the source's diagram: inversion in the middle factor followed by the composition maps of MC.6/tensor-iso-scheme.
Check the two heap axioms on R-points for every R, where they are identities of composition of tensor isomorphisms: f f⁻¹ h = h, f g⁻¹ g = f, and (f g⁻¹ h) u⁻¹ v = f (u h⁻¹ g)⁻¹ v = f g⁻¹ (h u⁻¹ v).

Check that composition with G_1 and G_2 commutes with the operation, (f g⁻¹ h)·a = f g⁻¹ (h·a) and b·(f g⁻¹ h) = (b·f) g⁻¹ h, so that on points the two groups are the left and right groups of the heap (MC.6/torsor-groups); Proposition A.6 is not needed.
acceptance: The torsor structure is basepoint free, which is essential because there is no canonical isomorphism between de Rham and singular cohomology over the rationals.
The inversion identifies the two schemes of isomorphisms, so the choice of order of the two fibre functors is immaterial.
The identities are checked at the level of affine schemes and not only on rational points.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 3.3. There is a natural isomorphism of aﬃne schemes ι : X1,2 → X2,1 given by f ↦ f −1. Furthermore, X1,2 and X2,1 carry the structure of aﬃne torsors in the sense of appendix A.

nodes.title: The spectrum of the formal periods is a torsor under the motivic Galois group
nodes.statement: Let T_1 = H*_dR and T_2 = H* on the diagram of pairs over Q, with the comparison isomorphism over C. The algebra of formal periods P carries a natural map P → P ⊗ P ⊗ P making Spec P an affine heap: through P = A_{1,2} it is the heap X_{1,2} = Iso⊗(H*_dR, H*) of MC.6/iso-torsor. The motivic Galois group G_mot = Aut⊗(H*) of MC.6/tensor-automorphism-group acts on Spec P by composition, compatibly with the heap map, and Spec P is a G_mot-torsor, faithfully flat over Q; the tensor automorphism group of de Rham cohomology acts on the other side. On period matrices the heap map is P_{ij} ↦ Σ_{k,l} P_{ik} ⊗ P⁻¹_{kl} ⊗ P_{lj}.
hypotheses: The base field is Q; the diagram is the diagram of pairs; T_1 is de Rham and T_2 singular cohomology, with the comparison isomorphism over C compatible with pullbacks, connecting maps and products (request SF.6).

The Tannakian input is taken on MM_Nori = C(D_Nori, H*), which Theorem 1.14 proves neutral Tannakian; de Rham cohomology is extended to it by MC.6/fibre-functor-extension with the roles of the two representations exchanged, and X_{2,1} is identified with X_{1,2} by inversion (finding E39).
G_mot is the tensor automorphism group of singular cohomology, as in Theorem 1.14.
proofSteps: Identify P with A_{1,2} (MC.6/formal-periods-equal-comparison-algebra).

Apply MC.6/tensor-iso-scheme and MC.6/iso-torsor with base category MM_Nori: X_{2,1} = Iso⊗(H*, H*_dR) = Spec A_{2,1} is an affine heap, and inversion identifies it with X_{1,2} = Spec A_{1,2}; this gives the map P → P ⊗ P ⊗ P.
Let G_mot = Aut⊗(H*) act by composition; the action commutes with the heap map, and MC.6/tensor-iso-torsor gives faithful flatness over Q and the torsor property.
Record the formula on period matrices (Remark 3.5) and the source's remark that these torsors are torsors in the pro-fppf topology.
acceptance: The statement is about a heap structure and a torsor structure on an explicitly presented algebra, so it is a theorem about generators and relations and not only an abstract Tannakian statement.
The group under which Spec P is a torsor is G_mot, defined through singular cohomology; the source's proof writes G_1, the de Rham group (finding E39); both groups act, on the two sides.
The period conjecture, the injectivity of the evaluation map to the complex numbers, plays no part.
The result is due to Nori and stated without proof by Kontsevich; the source supplies the proof.

sources.excerpt: Corollary 3.4. The algebra of formal periods P (see Deﬁnition 2.8) has a natural torsor structure under Gmot. Proof. By Theorems 2.6 and 2.9 we have A1,2 = P = P1,2 ... Finally note that G1 = Gmot is the motivic fundamental group by deﬁnition.

nodes.title: Conjecture C: algebraicity of the Kuenneth projectors
nodes.statement: Fix a classical Weil cohomology theory H over an algebraically closed field k with coefficients in a field F of characteristic zero. For a smooth projective variety X of dimension d, the Künneth isomorphism writes the class of the diagonal in H^{2d}(X × X) as a sum of components π^j_X in H^{2d−j}(X) ⊗ H^j(X), j = 0, ..., 2d. Conjecture C for X relative to H asserts that every π^j_X is algebraic, that is, lies in the image of the cycle class map from F-linear cycles of codimension d on X × X. Under it, the classes modulo numerical equivalence of cycles representing the π^j_X are well defined, central, idempotent, pairwise orthogonal and sum to the diagonal in the ring of degree zero numerical correspondences of X; this is the decomposition Δ_X = π_0 + ... + π_{2 dim X} of End(hX) = C^{dim X}_num(X × X) that Milne states as Conjecture C. The general conjecture is the assertion for every X. No source read claims the converse, from Milne's numerical form to algebraicity for a given H, and the node does not.
hypotheses: H is a classical Weil cohomology theory over an algebraically closed field k in the sense of MC.2; the predicate takes H as an argument.
X is smooth projective over k, of dimension d.
The unqualified name refers to the assertion for all X.
proofSteps: Define the components π^j_X of the class of the diagonal through the Künneth isomorphism of H for X × X (MC.2/class-of-the-diagonal).
Define Conjecture C for X as the membership of each π^j_X in the image of the cycle class map on X × X.

Under the predicate, show that the numerical classes of cycles representing the π^j are central orthogonal idempotents summing to the diagonal: they are so modulo homological equivalence, since the cycle map embeds those correspondences into the graded endomorphisms of H(X), and the properties pass to the quotient by numerical equivalence.
Record Milne's statement of Conjecture C as the resulting decomposition modulo numerical equivalence, and his remark that it is a weak form of the Lefschetz standard conjecture.
acceptance: The predicate takes the Weil cohomology theory and the variety as arguments.
For a point, the projective line and a pointed curve the predicate holds, with the explicit projectors of MC.0.
Only the implication from the cohomological predicate to the numerical decomposition is asserted; nothing in the roadmap takes the conjecture as an unstated hypothesis.

nodes.title: Conjecture D: numerical equivalence implies homological equivalence
nodes.statement: Fix a classical Weil cohomology theory H over an algebraically closed field k. Conjecture D asserts that an algebraic cycle numerically equivalent to zero has cohomology class zero, that is, that homological and numerical equivalence agree. By Poincaré duality it says: if there is a cohomology class whose cup product with the class of a given cycle is nonzero, then there is an algebraic cycle whose intersection number with the given cycle is nonzero. It is what a Weil cohomology theory needs in order to factor through the numerical motives. Milne records that in characteristic zero it is known for abelian varieties, in all codimensions and with the coefficients of H, and that it is implied by the Hodge conjecture.
hypotheses: A Weil cohomology theory over k is fixed.
The conjecture is stated for all varieties and all codimensions unless restricted explicitly.
proofSteps: State the conjecture as the implication from numerical to homological triviality.
State the equivalent form obtained by Poincare duality, and record that in that form it is an existence statement about algebraic cycles.

Record the reason the conjecture is wanted: a correspondence numerically equivalent to zero defines the zero map on motives, and a Weil cohomology theory factors through numerical motives exactly when such a correspondence also acts as zero on cohomology.
Record the known cases: in characteristic zero the conjecture holds for abelian varieties and follows from the Hodge conjecture.
acceptance: The converse implication, that homological triviality implies numerical triviality, is a theorem and is recorded separately; only this direction is open.
The conjecture is what makes the category of numerical motives a receptacle for cohomology theories; without it the quotient by numerical equivalence loses information a theory may see.
The equivalent form is an existence statement for algebraic cycles, which is why no general method attacks it.

nodes.title: The register of known cases of Conjecture C
nodes.statement: Relative to a fixed classical Weil cohomology theory H over an algebraically closed field k, with coefficients a field F of characteristic zero (Jannsen works over an arbitrary field with, for example, the étale cohomology of the base change to a separable closure; the theories of MC.2 are over algebraically closed fields, and the register is recorded for them), Jannsen records that Conjecture C holds, the π^j being cycles of codimension dim X on X × X with F coefficients: (i) for every X of dimension at most two, in any characteristic (attributed to Murre); (ii) for every abelian variety X, in any characteristic (attributed to Lieberman, as reported in Kleiman's survey); (iii) for every X when k is the algebraic closure of a finite field (attributed to Katz and Messing); (iv) for X × Y whenever it holds for X and for Y, since π^j_{X×Y} is the sum over r + s = j of π^r_X × π^s_Y by the Künneth formula. Consequently (Jannsen, Remark 2) the Tannakian conclusion for numerical motives holds unconditionally when k is algebraic over a finite field, and for the subcategory generated by 1(1) and any family of varieties covered by (i) to (iv), in particular for the category generated by abelian varieties, over any base field.
hypotheses: A classical Weil cohomology theory over an algebraically closed field is fixed, as in the statement of the conjecture.

Cases (i) to (iii) are attributed by the source to primary references that were not obtained: Murre (1990), Lieberman as reported by Kleiman (1968), and Katz and Messing (1974). Katz and Messing argue through the Riemann hypothesis for varieties over finite fields; before case (iii) is used for an arbitrary Weil cohomology theory in the sense of MC.2, the continuation that obtains the paper must check which theories it covers.
Case (iv) is proved in the source from the Künneth formula.
proofSteps: Record each case with its attribution.
Prove the product case: the Kuenneth components of the diagonal of a product are the sums of the products of the components of the two factors, by the Kuenneth formula.
Deduce the two unconditional Tannakian conclusions from the corresponding corollary of the semisimplicity layer.
Record that the three individual cases rest on primary sources that were not obtained for this packet, and that this node therefore stands on the source's own report of them.
acceptance: The four cases are as listed, each with its field, characteristic and coefficients; no case beyond dimension two is claimed in general.
The product case is the only one proved in a source read here.
The two Tannakian consequences are unconditional, unlike the general corollary, and rest in addition on Deligne's Tannakian criterion (a recorded gap of MC.3).
Milne records case (ii) in characteristic zero and case (iii) over finite fields; Jannsen's statements are the stronger ones and are the ones recorded.

If it holds for X and Y, it holds for X times Y. Corollary 2 holds for every subcategory generated by 1(1) and varieties for which the components are algebraic; in particular the category generated by abelian varieties is Tannakian over any k.

nodes.title: Smash nilpotence of a difference of rational points
nodes.statement: Let X be a geometrically irreducible smooth projective scheme over a field k and let x and x' be k-rational points of X. Then for n large enough the class of the zero cycle given by the n-fold exterior product of the difference of the two points, on the n-fold product of X, is torsion in the Chow group of zero cycles.
hypotheses: X is geometrically irreducible, smooth and projective over k.
x and x' are k-rational points.
The conclusion is that the class is torsion, over the base field, for n large enough.
proofSteps: Reduce to k algebraically closed: the kernel of pullback of Chow groups along an algebraic extension is torsion (Lemma 0FH8, part of MC.2/chow-groups-under-field-extension).
Reduce to X a curve: by Bertini there is a smooth curve C in X through x and x′ (as in the proof of Lemma 0FH7), and the class on C^n pushes forward to the class on X^n.

For a curve of genus g, write α_n = c_1(L_1) ∩ ... ∩ c_1(L_n) ∩ [X^n] with L = O_X(x − x′) and L_i its pullbacks; let π : X^n → S^n(X) be the finite flat map of degree n! to the symmetric power, N = Norm_π(L_1), and β_n = c_1(N)^n ∩ [S^n(X)].

Show π^*N = (L_1 ⊗ ... ⊗ L_n)^{⊗ (n−1)!} (the source omits the computation: finding E46), and, using c_1(L_i)² = 0 since L_i comes from a curve, π^*β_n = (n!)^n α_n; so it suffices that β_n is torsion.

For n ≥ 2g − 1 the map f : S^n(X) → Pic^n_{X/k} is a projective space bundle (details omitted in the source: finding E47); N is trivial on its fibres, shown by an Euler characteristic argument in a family over T = X, so N = f^*M, and c_1(N)^n = f^*(c_1(M)^n) = 0 because n > g = dim Pic^n.
acceptance: The conclusion is torsion, not zero, and it holds only for n large enough.
The two points are rational; the statement does not apply verbatim to closed points of higher degree.
The source attributes the lemma to Voevodsky; the general smash nilpotence conjecture is stated in no source read and is not planned.

nodes.title: The Hodge conjecture
nodes.statement: Let X be a projective non-singular algebraic variety over C and p ≥ 0. The Hodge conjecture for X in degree 2p asserts that every Hodge class in H^{2p}(X, Q) (MC.7/hodge-class) is a rational linear combination of classes cl(Z) of algebraic cycles of codimension p; since every cycle class is a Hodge class (MC.7/cycle-classes-are-hodge), it asserts that the Q-span of the cycle classes equals the space of Hodge classes. The Hodge conjecture for X is the assertion for every p. The source records, and this node does not plan: (ii) integral combinations of cycle classes are the integral combinations of products of Chern classes of algebraic vector bundles; (iii) the case p = 1 holds, even integrally, by the exponential sequence (an entry of MC.7/tate-and-hodge-known-cases); (iv) the integral form fails (Atiyah and Hirzebruch); (v) algebraicity of X cannot be weakened to Kähler (complex tori); (vi) Hodge formulated it integrally.
hypotheses: X is projective and non-singular over C; the conjecture is false for a general compact Kähler manifold (a complex torus, as the source records).
The coefficients are rational; the integral form is false.
The Hodge classes are those of MC.7/hodge-class.
proofSteps: Take the Hodge classes of MC.7/hodge-class and the cycle class map of Betti cohomology.
Define the predicate for (X, p) as the inclusion of the Hodge classes in the Q-span of the cycle classes, and the Hodge conjecture for X as the predicate for all p.
Record remarks (ii) to (vi) of the source as statements not planned here: their proofs are in primary sources not obtained, and the degree-two case is the register entry.

Record from Deligne, Section 4, Examples 1 and 2, that the Künneth components of the diagonal and the class inverting hard Lefschetz are Hodge classes, so the Hodge conjecture for X × X implies Conjecture C for X over C (Betti cohomology) and the typed Lefschetz predicate of MC.7/lefschetz-and-hodge-standard-conjectures.
acceptance: The predicate is rational; no node states an integral form as the Hodge conjecture.
For connected X the predicate holds in degree 0 and in degree 2 dim X, through the classes of X and of a point.
The conjecture implies Conjecture D in characteristic zero for Betti cohomology (Milne), and Conjecture C over C (Deligne, Example 1).

On a projective non-singular algebraic variety over C, any Hodge class is a rational linear combination of classes cl(Z) of algebraic cycles.

nodes.title: The Tate conjecture
nodes.statement: Let k be a field finitely generated over its prime field, X a smooth projective variety over k, and l a prime invertible in k. A closed subvariety of codimension a determines a class in the l-adic cohomology in degree 2a with a-fold Tate twist, and that class is fixed by the Galois group of k because the subvariety is defined over k. A TATE CLASS is an element of that cohomology fixed by the Galois group. The Tate conjecture asserts the converse: the subspace of the degree 2a cohomology with a-fold twist fixed by the Galois group is spanned, over the l-adic numbers, by the classes of codimension a subvarieties of X. The hypothesis that k be finitely generated over the prime field is essential: the statement fails over an algebraically closed field, where the Galois action is trivial, and over some other fields such as the p-adic fields.
hypotheses: k is finitely generated over its prime field, that is over Q or a finite field; X is smooth and projective over k; l is a prime invertible in k.
The coefficients are Q_l; the integral form is a separate statement, mostly false, recorded in the variants node.
The cohomology is geometric étale cohomology H^{2a}(X_{k_s}, Q_l(a)) of the base change to a separable closure, with its Galois action (request SF.2).
proofSteps: Define the Tate twist Z_l(1) as the inverse limit of the l-power roots of unity with its Galois action, and its integral powers.
Take the cycle class of a codimension-a subvariety in H^{2a}(X_{k_s}, Q_l(a)) and its Galois invariance for subvarieties defined over k, from the Galois-equivariant cycle class map (request SF.2).
Define a Tate class as a Galois-fixed element of that group.
State the conjecture as the assertion that the Tate classes are spanned over Q_l by cycle classes.

Record the source's remarks on the base field: the analogue fails over an algebraically closed field, where every class is fixed, and for some other fields such as p-adic fields; for p-adic cohomology of varieties with totally degenerate reduction over a p-adic field Raskind conjectured an analogue.
Record the reduction the source gives: the conjecture for X over k follows from the conjecture for X_E, E/k finite Galois, since for a fixed u algebraic over E, the class of π_*(α) is [E : k] u.
acceptance: Over a finite field the Galois group is topologically generated by the Frobenius, so a Tate class is an eigenvector of the Frobenius with eigenvalue one after the twist; this is the computable shape of the conjecture.
Over an algebraically closed field the statement is false as stated, since every class is fixed.
The conjecture for divisors, that is codimension one, is the case Tate originally stated and is the case in which almost all known results lie.

A cohomology class fixed by the Galois group is sometimes called a Tate class. Thus the conjecture says ...

nodes.title: The variants of the Tate conjecture, and what each implies
nodes.statement: The variants of the Tate conjecture in Totaro's survey, with what is known. The strong Tate conjecture (MC.7/strong-tate-conjecture) and the Tate-Beilinson conjecture (MC.7/tate-beilinson-conjecture) are typed as their own predicates. Jannsen's variant, for an arbitrary variety X over a finitely generated field, not necessarily smooth or proper, asks that every Galois-invariant element of l-adic Borel-Moore homology H_{2a}(X, Q_l(a)) be the class of an algebraic cycle with Q_l coefficients; it follows from the usual conjecture whenever X has a resolution of singularities with a smooth compactification. The variant over the separable closure asks that every class in H^{2a}(X_{k_s}, Q_l(a)) fixed by some open subgroup of the Galois group be algebraic over some finite extension of k; it is equivalent to the usual conjecture over every finite extension of k. The integral Tate conjecture, with Z_l coefficients, is false in most versions; over a finite field the usual conjecture for divisors would imply the integral one for divisors, and over the algebraic closure of a finite field the usual conjecture for divisors on surfaces would imply the integral conjecture for one-cycles on varieties of any dimension (Schoen). The source's diagram of implications: the Tate-Beilinson conjecture implies the Tate conjecture; the Tate conjecture implies the Tate conjecture for divisors and Grothendieck's standard conjectures; the Hodge conjecture implies the standard conjectures; the Tate and Hodge conjectures are joined only by an analogy; and, for a smooth projective surface over a finite field with a morphism with connected fibres onto a smooth projective curve and smooth generic fibre with Jacobian J, the Tate conjecture for divisors on the surface is equivalent to the finiteness of its Brauer group, to the finiteness of the Tate-Shafarevich group of J and to the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture for J.
hypotheses: Every variant is for a variety over a finitely generated field unless it says otherwise; the Borel-Moore variant drops smoothness and properness; the Tate-Beilinson conjecture is for finite fields.

The implications are recorded from the source, which warns that they relate conjectures over different fields; the proofs cited there (Jannsen's book, Schoen, Tate's and Milne's work on the Brauer group) were not obtained.
The integral variant is recorded as mostly false; no node asserts it.
proofSteps: Refer to the strong and Tate-Beilinson predicates of their nodes, and state the Borel-Moore, separable-closure and integral variants with the field and the coefficients named.
Prove the equivalence of the separable-closure variant with the usual conjecture over all finite extensions, from the finite-extension reduction of MC.7/tate-conjecture.
Record the Borel-Moore deduction with its resolution hypothesis, and the two integral implications with their fields.
Record the diagram of implications in words, with the fibred-surface hypotheses for the Brauer, Tate-Shafarevich and Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer equivalence.
acceptance: The equivalence of the Tate conjecture for divisors on a fibred surface over a finite field with the finiteness of its Brauer group and of the Tate-Shafarevich group of the Jacobian of the generic fibre is the source's central example of the link with arithmetic finiteness; its hypotheses are part of the statement.
The integral variant is false in general; recording it as a variant and not as a conjecture is part of the point of the node.
The injectivity in the Tate-Beilinson conjecture is false over the complex numbers, where the degree-zero part of the Chow group of an elliptic curve is uncountable and maps to zero in cohomology.

nodes.title: Grothendieck's standard conjectures: the Lefschetz predicate typed, the Hodge standard conjecture recorded
nodes.statement: Let X be smooth projective of dimension N over an algebraically closed field k, l a prime invertible in k, H the l-adic cohomology of X (or, for k = C, Betti cohomology) and η the class of a hyperplane section. By hard Lefschetz (DeligneWeightsAndPurity:DWP.9 for l-adic cohomology; over C, proved by Hodge, as Deligne recalls), η^p : H^{N−p}(X) → H^{N+p}(X)(p) is an isomorphism for 0 ≤ p ≤ N. Let z_p in H^{N−p}(X) ⊗ H^{N−p}(X) ⊂ H^{2N−2p}(X × X) be the class such that the inverse isomorphism is c ↦ pr_{1!}(z_p ∪ pr_2^* c) (Deligne, Section 4, Example 2, who shows z_p is a Hodge class over C). The Lefschetz standard conjecture for X, as typed in this packet, asserts that every z_p is algebraic. Milne states that Conjecture C is a weak form of the Lefschetz standard conjecture, and Deligne (Section 5) that if the classes of his Examples 1 and 2 were algebraic, Grothendieck's motives over C would form a semisimple abelian tensor category, the representations of a pro-reductive group scheme. The Hodge standard conjecture is recorded only as Milne describes it: a positivity statement implying that the endomorphism algebra of every motive admits a positive definite involution; in characteristic zero it can be proved by analytic methods, in positive characteristic it is known for very few varieties, and it is implied by the Hodge and Tate conjectures. With Conjecture C and Conjecture D it would give, by Weil's argument, the Weil conjectures in arbitrary dimension: C and D give the integrality of the characteristic polynomials of Frobenius, the Hodge standard conjecture the bounds on their roots. Its precise statement, and the identification of the typed Lefschetz predicate with Grothendieck's formulation for an arbitrary Weil cohomology theory, are in no source read (gap); no predicate is typed for the Hodge standard conjecture.
hypotheses: X is smooth and projective over an algebraically closed field, with a chosen hyperplane class η; the cohomology is l-adic, or Betti over C.
Hard Lefschetz is an input, from DeligneWeightsAndPurity:DWP.9 for l-adic cohomology; it is not an axiom of the Weil cohomology theories of MC.2, so the predicate is not defined for an arbitrary one.
The Hodge standard conjecture is not typed: no source read states it precisely (gap).
proofSteps: Take hard Lefschetz for l-adic cohomology from DWP.9, and over C for Betti cohomology through the comparison with l-adic cohomology (request SF.6).
Define z_p through the Künneth formula and Poincaré duality as the class inducing the inverse of η^p, as in Deligne's Example 2.
Define the typed Lefschetz predicate as the algebraicity of every z_p.
Record Milne's statement that Conjecture C is a weak form of the Lefschetz standard conjecture, without a proof: no source read gives the argument.
Record the Hodge standard conjecture's description, status and consequences from Milne, Section 7, and that no predicate is typed for it.
Record that Deligne proved the Weil conjectures without the standard conjectures, and Grothendieck's remark on their urgency.
acceptance: The Lefschetz predicate takes the cohomology theory and the hyperplane class as arguments and needs hard Lefschetz.
In characteristic zero the Hodge standard conjecture is a theorem by the source's account; no node may treat it as open there, and none types it.
Over C the classes z_p are Hodge classes, so the Hodge conjecture for X × X implies the typed Lefschetz predicate for X.

nodes.title: Murre's conjecture and the Bloch-Beilinson filtration
nodes.statement: Murre conjectured that the decomposition of the diagonal into orthogonal idempotents that Conjecture C provides modulo numerical equivalence exists already modulo RATIONAL equivalence, with additional properties relating the components to the Chow groups. It has been shown that his conjecture is equivalent to the existence of a filtration on the Chow groups with prescribed properties, conjectured by Bloch and Beilinson. This node records both as conjectures, with the equivalence, and records that the source read here states neither in full: it gives the existence of the Chow-level decomposition and the equivalence in one sentence, and the precise list of Murre's conditions and of the properties of the filtration is not in any source read for this packet. A continuation job with a source that states them must add the conditions before anything is built on them.
hypotheses: X is smooth and projective over a field; the decomposition is in the ring of correspondences modulo rational equivalence.
The equivalence recorded is the one the source asserts, between Murre's conjecture and the existence of the Bloch-Beilinson filtration; the precise form of both is not available here.
Nothing in this packet assumes either statement.
proofSteps: Record the statement of the source: a decomposition of the diagonal into orthogonal idempotents exists modulo rational equivalence, with certain properties, and this is equivalent to the existence of the conjectured filtration on the Chow groups.
State the part that is precise: the existence of a Chow-level orthogonal idempotent decomposition lifting the numerical one, which is a well-formed predicate with the tools this packet already has.

Record that the additional properties of Murre's conjecture, and the properties required of the filtration, are not stated by any source read here, and that they are what gives the equivalence its content.
Record the gap and the next source action, so that a continuation adds the conditions rather than inventing them.
acceptance: The Chow-level decomposition is strictly stronger as a statement than Conjecture C, whose numerical decomposition is its image.
No property of the filtration is stated here: the source gives none, and properties written from memory are not admissible.
No node of this packet takes either statement as a hypothesis.

nodes.title: A motivic t-structure, and why no statement is planned
nodes.statement: The category of mixed motives over a field is expected to be an abelian category whose derived category is one of the triangulated categories of motives, and the way to produce it would be a t-structure on such a triangulated category whose heart is that abelian category. No source read for this packet defines one, and the sources say why: there is at present no definition of a category of mixed motives, several triangulated candidates for its derived category have been constructed, and it remains to define a t-structure on one of them whose heart is the category of mixed motives itself. This node records the situation, the two boundaries that follow from it, and what the layer may and may not state.
hypotheses: The triangulated categories in question are those of MC.4, over a field.
The statement recorded is negative: what is missing, not what holds.
A conjectural t-structure may not be installed as a theorem, which is what the layer's stage text also demands.
proofSteps: Record the source's statement: there is at present no definition of a category of mixed motives; several triangulated categories have been constructed as candidates for its derived category; and it remains to define a t-structure whose heart is the category of mixed motives.
Record the boundary the roadmap draws: a triangulated category is not an abelian category of mixed motives, and no node may treat one as the other.

Record what a future statement would need: a t-structure on the triangulated category of geometric motives, a proof that its heart is abelian with the expected weight filtration, and a comparison of the realisations; none of it is available.
Record that the conjectural t-structure cannot be installed as a hypothesis-free theorem anywhere in this roadmap.
acceptance: The layer states no motivic t-structure, and this node is the record of why.
The triangulated category of geometric motives exists unconditionally, and its existence is not evidence for the t-structure.
A continuation that wants the statement must obtain a source that formulates it.
