nodes.title: The symmetric group acts trivially on Z(n)
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field. The action of the symmetric group Sigma_n on the motivic complex Z(n), induced by permuting the coordinates of G_m^{wedge n}, is A^1-homotopic to the trivial action; hence it is trivial in DM^eff,-_Nis(k) and on motivic cohomology, and the same holds with coefficients in any ring R. In particular the cyclic permutation of R(1)^{tensor 3}, isomorphic to R(3), is the identity in DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R).
hypotheses: k is perfect: the proof uses MVW Corollary 15.3, which rests on Theorem 15.2.
R(1)^{tensor n} is isomorphic to R(n) compatibly with the Sigma_n-actions (from Z_tr(G_m^{wedge 1})^{tensor n} = Z_tr(G_m^{wedge n}); supplied by MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a).
proofSteps: Example 15.6: the reflection tau(x_0 : ... : x_n) = (-x_0 : x_1 : ... : x_n) of P^n is A^1-homotopic to the identity through the elementary correspondence Z in P^n x A^1 x P^n cut out by y_i(x_0 y_i + t x_i y_0) = (t^2 - 1) x_i y_0^2 (and x_i y_j = x_j y_i for n >= 2), whose restrictions at t = 1 and t = -1 differ by id - tau; the check that Z is an elementary correspondence is left to the reader in the source and is part of this step. Through Theorem 15.2 it induces an A^1-homotopy between tau and the identity on Z(n)[2n].

Proposition 15.7: Sigma_n acts on A^n - 0 through GL_n(k); each transposition is tau times an element of SL_n(k), and elementary matrices e_ij(a) are A^1-homotopic to the identity by (x, t) -> e_ij(at)x, so the action of Sigma_n on C_*Z_tr(A^n - 0) is A^1-homotopic to the trivial one.
Corollary 15.3: C_*(Z_tr(A^n - 0)/Z) is quasi-isomorphic to Z(n)[2n - 1] (from 13.15, 15.1 and 15.2 for the cover of P^n by A^n and P^n - 0), equivariantly for Sigma_n.
Corollary 15.8: combine, and use that A^1-homotopic maps agree in DM (MVW 14.14 and 9.10); tensoring with R does not affect the action.
Specialise to the 3-cycle in Sigma_3 acting on R(1)^{tensor 3}.
acceptance: For n = 2 the swap of R(1) tensor R(1) is the identity in DM, which makes the product in motivic cohomology graded-commutative (MVW Theorem 15.9).
The case n = 3 is exactly the hypothesis of MVW Proposition 8A.10 for T = R(1).
For n = 1 there is nothing to prove.

sources.excerpt: The action of the symmetric group Sigma_n on Z(n) is A1-homotopic to the trivial action. Hence it is trivial in DM^{eff,-}_Nis, and on the motivic cohomology groups H^p(X,Z(n)).
sources.match: The statement, literally.

sources.excerpt: Consider the reflection automorphism tau of Pn, n >= 1, sending (x0 : x1 : ... : xn) to (-x0 : x1 : ... : xn). We claim that the induced automorphism of C_*Z_tr(Pn) is A1-homotopic to the identity map
sources.match: The geometric input of the proof.

nodes.title: Geometric motives contain all schemes and are generated by smooth projective ones
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities. Then DM^eff_gm(k,R) contains M(Y), the class of R_tr(Y), for every scheme Y of finite type over k, and DM^eff_gm(k,R) is the thick subcategory generated by the motives M(X) of smooth projective schemes X over k.
hypotheses: k is perfect with resolution of singularities, including, for every smooth X, a smooth projective compactification whose boundary is a divisor with simple normal crossings (requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.4).
Y is of finite type over k.
proofSteps: Generation: let G be the thick subcategory generated by the M(W), W smooth projective. For X smooth choose X in W smooth projective with boundary D = D_1 union ... union D_r a simple normal crossings divisor; by induction on dim X and on r, the Gysin triangles (MC.4/gysin-triangle) removing the smooth closed strata of D, whose motives lie in G by induction, show M(X) in G; the reverse inclusion is clear.

All schemes of finite type: induct on dim Y; R_tr(Y) = R_tr(Y_red); resolution gives a proper birational Y' -> Y with Y' smooth, an isomorphism outside a closed Z of smaller dimension; the blow-up triangle (MC.4/blow-up-triangle-and-formula) M(Z') -> M(Z) + M(Y') -> M(Y) -> with M(Z), M(Z') geometric by induction and M(Y') geometric by smoothness gives M(Y) in DM^eff_gm.
Record that MVW state both assertions after Definition 14.1 as following from (14.5.3) and (14.5.5) without writing the inductions out.
acceptance: For Y a nodal cubic curve, M(Y) lies in DM^eff_gm through the triangle with its normalisation P^1 and the node.
Without resolution of singularities neither assertion is proved here, and over a field of positive characteristic the node claims nothing.
M(G_m) is obtained from M(P^1) and two points by cones only.

sources.excerpt: If k admits resolution of singularities, it follows from (14.5.3) and (14.5.5) that DM^eff_gm contains M(Y) for every Y in Sch/k, and is generated by M(X), where X is smooth and projective.
sources.match: The two assertions, literally; the inductions are written out in the steps.

nodes.title: The motive of a vector bundle
nodes.statement: Let k be a field, X smooth over k and E -> X a vector bundle. The projection induces an isomorphism M(E) -> M(X) in DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R).
hypotheses: k is any field: the argument uses the Mayer-Vietoris triangle in DM (MVW's route through 13.15 needs k perfect).
E is a vector bundle, trivial on the members of a finite Zariski cover of X.
proofSteps: Choose a finite Zariski cover X = U_1 union ... union U_r on which E is trivial.
On each U_j and on each finite intersection E is isomorphic to U x A^n, and the projection is an isomorphism on motives by homotopy invariance applied n times.

Induct on r: for X = U union V with V = U_r the Mayer-Vietoris triangles of X and of E for the covers by U, V and by E|U, E|V are compatible with the projections; two of the three maps are isomorphisms by induction, so the third is (isIso3_of_isIso12).
acceptance: For E = X x A^n this is homotopy invariance iterated.
The statement is about the total space of E; the projective bundle P(E) has n Tate summands (MC.4/projective-bundle-theorem).
For a line bundle L on P^1 of any degree M(L) is isomorphic to M(P^1) = R + R(1)[2].

sources.excerpt: If E is a vector bundle over X, C_*Z_tr(E) -> C_*Z_tr(X) is a quasi-isomorphism. PROOF. Choose a Zariski cover U of X on which E is a trivial bundle.
sources.match: The statement and the start of the proof.

sources.excerpt: (Vector bundle) If E -> X is a vector bundle, by 13.16 we have an isomorphism M(E) -> M(X).
sources.match: The statement in DM.

nodes.title: The quotient of P^n by P^(n-1) is R(n)[2n]
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field and n >= 1. The linear projection from 0 = (1 : 0 : ... : 0) induces a chain homotopy equivalence C_*R_tr(P^n - 0) -> C_*R_tr(P^{n-1}) (MVW Lemma 15.1), and there is a quasi-isomorphism of complexes of Zariski sheaves C_*(R_tr(P^n)/R_tr(P^{n-1})) -> C_*R_tr(G_m^{wedge n})[n] = R(n)[2n] (Theorem 15.2). Consequently there is a distinguished triangle M(P^{n-1}) -> M(P^n) -> R(n)[2n] -> M(P^{n-1})[1] in DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R), the first map induced by a linear embedding.
hypotheses: k is perfect: MVW state that perfectness is needed only for Theorem 13.8, used through Corollary 13.14, which is imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a.
P^{n-1} is a linear hyperplane of P^n not containing 0.
proofSteps: Lemma 15.1: the projection P^n - 0 -> P^{n-1} has the section (x_1 : ... : x_n) -> (0 : x_1 : ... : x_n), and lambda -> (lambda x_0 : x_1 : ... : x_n) is an A^1-homotopy from the composite to the identity; A^1-homotopy equivalences induce chain homotopy equivalences of Suslin complexes (MVW 2.26, M.5a).
The Cech complexes of the cover of P^n by n + 1 affine spaces and of P^n - 0 by n of them resolve R_tr(P^n) and R_tr(P^n - 0) (MVW 6.14), so the quotient Q_* resolves R_tr(P^n)/R_tr(P^n - 0).

Compare Q_* termwise with the split exact complex R_* of MVW Lemma 2.13 for T = A^1 - 0, whose kernel is R_tr(G_m^{wedge n}); the comparison maps are projections A^{n-i} x T^i -> T^i, which are A^1-homotopy equivalences.
Apply C_* and MVW Corollary 13.14 (imported; this is where k perfect is used) to obtain C_*(R_tr(P^n)/R_tr(P^{n-1})), quasi-isomorphic to Tot C_*Q_*, quasi-isomorphic to C_*R_tr(G_m^{wedge n})[n].
Identify C_*R_tr(G_m^{wedge n})[n] with R(n)[2n] (MVW Definition 3.1) and pass to DM^eff,-_Nis.
acceptance: For n = 1 the quasi-isomorphism agrees with that of MVW Example 13.17 (remark after Theorem 15.2).
The quotient is R(n)[2n]: twist n and shift 2n.
The triangles for n = 1, ..., N are the steps of the filtration P^0 in P^1 in ... in P^N.

sources.excerpt: LEMMA 15.1. There is a chain homotopy equivalence: C_*Z_tr(Pn - 0) = C_*Z_tr(Pn-1). THEOREM 15.2. If k is a perfect field, there is a quasi-isomorphism of Zariski sheaves for each n: C_*(Z_tr(Pn)/Z_tr(Pn-1)) = C_*Z_tr(G_m^{wedge n})[n] = Z(n)[2n].
sources.match: The two statements, literally.

sources.excerpt: Our proof will use theorem 13.12, whose proof depended upon theorem 13.8, a result whose proof we have postponed until lecture 24. The requirement that k be perfect is only needed for 13.8 (and hence 13.12).
sources.match: Where the hypothesis on k enters.

nodes.title: The maps from P^i to R(i)[2i] extend to P^n
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field and 0 <= i < n. The map C_*R_tr(P^i) -> R(i)[2i], obtained from MC.4/projective-space-quotient by composing with C_*R_tr(P^i) -> C_*(R_tr(P^i)/R_tr(P^{i-1})), factors through the map C_*R_tr(P^i) -> C_*R_tr(P^n) induced by a linear embedding.
hypotheses: k perfect, as in MC.4/projective-space-quotient.
The embeddings P^i in P^n are linear and compatible with each other.
The statement is MVW Exercise 15.4, given with a hint and no proof; the proof below follows the hint.
proofSteps: Case i = 1: fix a member U_0 of the standard affine cover U of P^n and construct a map of complexes R_tr(Cech(U)) -> R(1)[2] vanishing on R_tr(U_0) whose restriction to P^1 is the map of MVW Example 13.17.

General i: compose the diagonal R_tr(Cech(U)) -> R_tr(Cech(U))^{tensor i} with the i-th tensor power of that map and the multiplication R(1)[2]^{tensor i} -> R(i)[2i] of motivic complexes (supplied by MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a).
Check that the restriction to P^i is the map of Theorem 15.2.
acceptance: For i = 0 the map is the structure map and the factorisation is trivial.
Assembled for all i < n the extensions give M(P^n) -> sum over i < n of R(i)[2i], which is what splits the triangle of MC.4/projective-space-quotient.
The extension is not unique; only its restriction to P^i is prescribed.

sources.excerpt: Show that the map C_*Z_tr(Pi) -> Z(i)[2i] of theorem 15.2 factors through the natural inclusion C_*Z_tr(Pi) -> C_*Z_tr(Pn) for all n > i. Hint: Fix U0 in U and construct Z_tr(U^) -> Z(1)[2] vanishing on Z_tr(U0).
sources.match: The statement and the hint the proof follows.

nodes.title: The projective bundle theorem for geometric motives
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field, X a smooth scheme over k and E a vector bundle of rank n + 1 on X, with p: P(E) -> X. Let tau: M(P(E)) -> R(1)[2] correspond to the class of the canonical line bundle under Pic(P(E)) = H^{2,1}(P(E), Z) = Hom(Z_tr(P(E)), Z(1)[2]) (MVW 4.2, 13.11, 13.5), tau_i its i-th power through the diagonal and the multiplication R(1)[2]^{tensor i} -> R(i)[2i], and sigma_i = (sigma_0 tensor tau_i) composed with the diagonal, with sigma_0 = M(p). Then sigma = (sigma_0, ..., sigma_n): M(P(E)) -> sum over i from 0 to n of M(X)(i)[2i] is an isomorphism in DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R).
hypotheses: k perfect, through MC.4/motive-of-projective-space for n >= 2.
X smooth; E locally free of rank n + 1, trivial on a finite Zariski cover.
The identification of Pic with H^{2,1} is imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.4 (weight one), its representability from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a.
The map goes from M(P(E)) to the sum, as MVW Construction 15.10 builds it; the displays of Theorem 15.12 and (14.5.2) print the arrow the other way (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E26).
proofSteps: Construct tau, tau_i and sigma_i as in MVW Construction 15.10.

For X = Spec k and E trivial, show that sigma is the isomorphism of MC.4/motive-of-projective-space; this is MVW Exercise 15.11, stated with the hint to use Exercise 15.4, and follows from MC.4/projective-space-inclusion-split.
For E trivial, R_tr(X x P^n) = R_tr(X) tensor R_tr(P^n) and naturality of sigma reduce to X = Spec k.
For general E, induct on the number of opens of a trivialising cover, using the Mayer-Vietoris triangles of X and of P(E), which sigma maps compatibly, and isIso3_of_isIso12.
sigma_0 = M(p) is the projection onto the summand M(X).
acceptance: For X = Spec k this is MC.4/motive-of-projective-space.
The twists run from 0 to n for a bundle of rank n + 1.
For the exceptional divisor of the blow-up of a smooth centre of codimension c the theorem gives c summands M(Z)(i)[2i], i = 0, ..., c - 1.

sources.excerpt: (Projective Bundle Theorem). Let p : P(E) -> X be a projective bundle associated to a vector bundle E of rank n + 1. Then the canonical map +_{i=0}^n Z_tr(X)(i)[2i] -> Z_tr(P(E)) is an isomorphism in DM, and p is the projection onto the factor Z_tr(X).
sources.match: The theorem; the arrow of the display is reversed relative to the construction (E26).

sources.excerpt: From 4.2, 13.11, and 13.5 we have an isomorphism Pic(P) = H2_Nis(P,Z(1)) = Hom_{D-}(Z_tr(P),Z(1)[2]). Therefore the canonical line bundle yields a canonical map tau : Z_tr(P) -> Z(1)[2] in D-.
sources.match: The construction of the canonical map.

nodes.title: The motive of a blow-up along a smooth centre, and the Gysin map
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities, X a smooth scheme over k, Z a smooth closed subscheme of pure codimension c and p: X' -> X the blow-up along Z. Then M(X') is isomorphic to M(X) + sum over i from 1 to c - 1 of M(Z)(i)[2i] in DM^eff,-_Nis(k,R), the first summand being M(p). Moreover there is a natural Gysin map gamma: M(X) -> M(Z)(c)[2c] whose restriction to M(X - Z) is zero.
hypotheses: k perfect with resolution of singularities: the proof uses MC.4/blow-up-triangle-and-formula (MVW Theorem 13.26). MVW state Corollary 15.13 with no hypothesis on k (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E21).
Z is smooth of pure codimension c >= 1 in the smooth X; for c = 1 the blow-up is an isomorphism and the sum is empty.
proofSteps: The exceptional divisor Z' = Z x_X X' is the projective bundle P(N) of the normal bundle N of Z, of rank c, so MC.4/projective-bundle-theorem gives M(Z') = sum over i from 0 to c - 1 of M(Z)(i)[2i].

Let X'' be the blow-up of X x A^1 along Z x 0 and Z'' its exceptional divisor; MC.4/blow-up-triangle-and-formula gives distinguished triangles for X' -> X and for X'' -> X x A^1, with maps f, g, h between them, h = 1_X x 0.
h is an isomorphism by homotopy invariance and is A^1-homotopic to 1_X x 1, so it lifts to M(X) -> M(X''); this splits the map d of the second triangle and hence c.

Z' -> Z'' is P(N) in P(N + O), so f is a split monomorphism by MC.4/projective-bundle-theorem; composing g with the splittings of c and f splits a, hence b, so M(X') -> M(X) is a split epimorphism and the first triangle splits (exists_iso_binaryBiproduct_of_distTriang).
Substitute the decomposition of M(Z') to obtain M(X') = M(X) + sum over i from 1 to c - 1 of M(Z)(i)[2i].
The cokernel of f is M(Z)(c)[2c]; gamma is the composite of the splitting of b, g, the splitting of c and the projection to that cokernel; a diagram chase shows that gamma vanishes on M(X - Z).
acceptance: For the blow-up of a smooth surface at a rational point (c = 2), M(X') = M(X) + R(1)[2], matching CH^1(X') = CH^1(X) + Z.
For c = 1 the sum is empty and p is an isomorphism.
gamma vanishes on M(X - Z), which is what lets it induce the map on the quotient used in MC.4/gysin-triangle.

sources.excerpt: Let X be a smooth scheme and Z a smooth subscheme of pure codimension c. Let p : X' -> X be the blow-up along Z. Then C_*Z_tr(X') = C_*Z_tr(X)+(+_{i=1}^{c-1} C_*Z_tr(Z)(i)[2i]). Moreover, there is a natural "Gysin" map gamma : C_*Z_tr(X) -> C_*Z_tr(Z)(c)[2c], which is zero on C_*Z_tr(X - Z).
sources.match: The statement, literally; MVW's (14.5.4) is its first half.

sources.excerpt: Since Z is smooth, Z' is the projective bundle associated to the normal bundle of Z in X. We claim that the morphism C_*Z_tr(X') -> C_*Z_tr(X) is a split surjection. By 13.26 and 15.12, this will prove the first assertion.
sources.match: Shows that the proof uses Theorem 13.26 and hence resolution (E21).

nodes.title: The sheaves of equidimensional cycles z_equi(T, r)
nodes.statement: Let T be a scheme of finite type over k and r >= 0. For S smooth over k, z_equi(T, r)(S) is the free abelian group on the closed irreducible subvarieties Z of S x T that are dominant and equidimensional of relative dimension r over a component of S; pullback of relative cycles along S' -> S makes z_equi(T, r) a presheaf on Sm/k, which is an etale, hence Nisnevich, sheaf. For an elementary correspondence V from X to Y and Z in z_equi(T, r)(Y), the transfer phi_V(Z) is the pushforward along the finite map V x T -> X x T of the pullback Z_V; with these transfers z_equi(T, r) is a presheaf with transfers. For r = 0, Z_tr(T) is a sub-presheaf with transfers of z_equi(T, 0), equal to it when T is proper. z_equi(T, r) is contravariant for flat maps T' -> T of relative dimension d, landing in z_equi(T', r + d), and covariant for proper maps T -> T'', landing in z_equi(T'', r).
hypotheses: T of finite type over k and r >= 0 (MVW Definition 16.1 names the integer m in its first line and uses r thereafter; r is meant: MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E27).
Pullback of relative cycles and pushforward along finite maps are imported from the theory of relative cycles underlying finite correspondences (MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a; MVW Appendix 1A).

That phi makes z_equi(T, r) a presheaf with transfers is MVW Exercise 16.3 (hint only), and the flat and proper functoriality is cited from Suslin-Voevodsky, Relative cycles and Chow sheaves, 3.6.2 and 3.6.4; neither is proved in the source read (gap).
proofSteps: Define the groups and the pullback maps by pullback of relative cycles (MVW 1A.6, 1A.8).
Record that z_equi(T, r) is an etale sheaf (asserted after MVW Definition 16.1).
Define phi_V and extend it linearly to finite correspondences; verify the presheaf-with-transfers identities using Fulton's identity 2.2(4), as the hint to MVW Exercise 16.3 suggests.

For r = 0 check that the transfers restrict to those of Z_tr(T) (MVW 16.2 with 1A.11 and 1A.13), and that Z_tr(T) = z_equi(T, 0) for T proper, since a closed subvariety of U x T proper over U is quasi-finite over U exactly when it is finite.
Flat pullback and proper pushforward in T with the shift of relative dimension (Relative cycles and Chow sheaves 3.6.2 and 3.6.4, not read; gap).
acceptance: z_equi(Spec k, 0)(S) is the free abelian group on the components of S, and z_equi(Spec k, r) = 0 for r > 0.
The inclusion Z_tr(A^1) in z_equi(A^1, 0) is strict.
Closed immersions T' in T give inclusions z_equi(T', r) in z_equi(T, r).

sources.excerpt: The presheaf z_equi(T,r) on Sm/k is defined as follows. For each smooth S, z_equi(T,r)(S) is the free abelian group generated by the closed and irreducible subvarieties Z of S x T which are dominant and equidimensional of relative dimension r over a component of S.
sources.match: The definition, literally.

sources.excerpt: One can also check that each z_equi(T,r) is contravariant for flat maps in T, and covariant for proper maps in T, both with the appropriate change in the dimension index r
sources.match: The functoriality, cited in the source from Relative cycles and Chow sheaves.

sources.excerpt: If T is projective, or proper, then Z_tr(T) = z_equi(T,0).
sources.match: The proper case.

nodes.title: The Suslin-Friedlander complexes compute motivic cohomology
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field and i >= 0. The Suslin-Friedlander complex Z_SF(i) = C_*z_equi(A^i, 0)[-2i] is quasi-isomorphic to the motivic complex Z(i) as complexes of Zariski sheaves; hence H^{n,i}(X, Z) is isomorphic to H^n(X, Z_SF(i)) for every smooth X and every n. The comparison comes from the map Z_tr(P^i) = z_equi(P^i, 0) -> z_equi(A^i, 0) restricting cycles to A^i = P^i - P^{i-1}, whose kernel is Z_tr(P^{i-1}), together with MC.4/projective-space-quotient.
hypotheses: k perfect: used through MVW Lemma 16.12 (via 13.14) and Theorem 15.2; MVW state Theorem 16.8 without the hypothesis although its proof uses 16.12 (part of MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E25).
i >= 0; for i = 0 both sides are Z.
proofSteps: Define Z_SF(i) (MVW 16.4) and the map Z_tr(P^i) -> z_equi(A^i, 0) with kernel Z_tr(P^{i-1}) (MVW 16.5, from 16.2 and 16.3).

Let F_i in z_equi(A^i, 0) be the sub-presheaf with transfers of cycles not meeting U x 0, and form the diagram of MVW Lemma 16.9, with rows 0 -> Z_tr(P^i - 0)/Z_tr(P^{i-1}) -> Z_tr(P^i)/Z_tr(P^{i-1}) -> coker_1 -> 0 and 0 -> F_i -> z_equi(A^i, 0) -> coker_2 -> 0 and injective vertical maps.
C_*(F_i) is chain contractible (MVW 16.10: the scaling (x, r, t) -> (x, rt), a flat pullback over X x (A^i - 0), with MVW 2.22), and C_*(Z_tr(P^i - 0)/Z_tr(P^{i-1})) is acyclic by MVW 15.1.

coker_1(S) -> coker_2(S) is an isomorphism for S Hensel local (MVW 16.11: a quasi-finite cycle over a Hensel local base splits into a part finite over the base and a part missing the closed fibre), hence C_*(coker_1) -> C_*(coker_2) is a Zariski quasi-isomorphism by MVW 13.14 (imported; k perfect): this is 16.12.

The five lemma gives C_*(z_equi(P^i, 0)/z_equi(P^{i-1}, 0)) quasi-isomorphic to C_*z_equi(A^i, 0) (MVW 16.8); combined with MC.4/projective-space-quotient this is Z(i)[2i] quasi-isomorphic to Z_SF(i)[2i] (MVW 16.7); take Zariski hypercohomology for the last assertion.
acceptance: For i = 1, Z_SF(1)[2] = C_*z_equi(A^1, 0) and the comparison recovers Z(1)[2] = C_*(Z_tr(P^1)/Z).
The identification with motivic cohomology is for smooth X and in the Zariski topology.
It is used both for M^c(A^i) = Z(i)[2i] and for motivic cohomology against higher Chow groups.

sources.excerpt: Assume that k is perfect. Then there is a quasi-isomorphism in the Zariski topology: Z(i) = Z_SF(i). In particular, H^{n,i}(X,Z) = H^n(X,Z_SF(i)) for all n and i.
sources.match: The theorem, literally.

sources.excerpt: We define the Suslin-Friedlander motivic complexes Z_SF(i) by: Z_SF(i) = C_*z_equi(A^i,0)[-2i]. ... THEOREM 16.8. There is a quasi-isomorphism in the Zariski topology: C_*(z_equi(P^i,0)/z_equi(P^{i-1},0)) = C_*z_equi(A^i,0).
sources.match: The definition and the key comparison whose proof (16.9-16.12) the steps follow.

nodes.title: The Suslin-Friedlander complexes and Bloch's cycle complexes
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field and i >= 0. For every smooth X, cycles in C_m z_equi(A^i, 0)(X) = z_equi(A^i, 0)(X x Delta^m) meet all faces of X x A^i x Delta^m properly, giving an embedding of complexes Z_SF(i)[2i](X) in z^i(X x A^i, *) into Bloch's cycle complex (MVW Lemma 19.4). The induced maps of homology presheaves are morphisms of presheaves with transfers (19.6) and isomorphisms on fields (19.7), and the embedding is a quasi-isomorphism of complexes of Zariski sheaves (Theorem 19.8). Consequently, for X smooth, H^{n,i}(X, Z) is isomorphic to H^{n-2i}(X, z^i(- x A^i, *)) (Corollary 19.9).
hypotheses: k perfect, through MC.4/suslin-friedlander-comparison.

Bloch's cycle complexes, their homotopy invariance (MVW 17.4), the structure of presheaves with transfers on their homology (MVW 17.21) and Suslin's comparison theorem for affine schemes (MVW 18.3) are imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.4.

MVW Proposition 11.2 (a morphism of homotopy invariant presheaves with transfers that is an isomorphism on all fields induces an isomorphism of associated Zariski sheaves) is imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a.
proofSteps: Lemma 19.4: a cycle in C_m z_equi(T, d - i)(X) is equidimensional over X x Delta^m, hence meets all faces properly; the face maps agree by MVW 1A.14.

Proposition 19.6: both homology presheaves carry transfers (16.3 and 17.21); compatibility of transfers reduces, by the affine vector bundle torsor argument of 17.15-17.17, to Y affine, where it is phi_W(Z) = pi_*((W x A^i x Delta^m) . f^*Z) = W^*(Z) by 17A.12 and 17A.13.
Example 19.7: on a field E the map is an isomorphism by Suslin's theorem 18.3 for A^i_E together with MVW 16.6.

Theorem 19.8: both homology presheaves are homotopy invariant presheaves with transfers (2.19 and 17.4); an isomorphism on fields is an isomorphism after Zariski sheafification (MVW 11.2), so the embedding is a Zariski quasi-isomorphism.
Corollary 19.9: combine with MC.4/suslin-friedlander-comparison: H^{n,i}(X, Z) = H^n(X, Z(i)), isomorphic to H^n(X, Z_SF(i)), isomorphic to H^{n-2i}(X, z^i(- x A^i, *)).
acceptance: On X = Spec E for a field E the composite is Suslin's isomorphism of motivic cohomology of E with CH^i(E, 2i - n).
The embedding lands in cycles meeting faces properly because equidimensional cycles meet every face properly; the converse inclusion fails (MVW Example 19.5).
Only Zariski-local statements are made here; the global comparison needs Zariski descent for Bloch's complexes (MC.4/motivic-cohomology-higher-chow).

sources.excerpt: Let T be smooth of dimension d. If 0 <= i <= d then for all X there is an embedding of simplicial abelian groups: C_.z_equi(T,d-i)(X) in z^i(X x T,.). In particular (for T = A^i), Z_SF(i)[2i](X) is a subcomplex of z^i(X x A^i,*).
sources.match: The embedding, literally.

sources.excerpt: The map Z_SF(i)[2i] = C_*z_equi(A^i,0) -> z^i(- x A^i,*) is a quasi-isomorphism of complexes of Zariski sheaves. COROLLARY 19.9. For any smooth scheme X, the inclusion of 19.4 induces an isomorphism: H^{n,i}(X,Z) -> H^{n-2i}(X,z^i(- x A^i,*)).
sources.match: The quasi-isomorphism and its consequence.

nodes.title: The localisation triangle for motives with compact support
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities. For a closed subscheme i: Z -> X of a scheme of finite type over k with open complement j: U -> X, there is a distinguished triangle M^c(Z) -> M^c(X) -> M^c(U) -> M^c(Z)[1] in DM^eff,-_Nis(k), the first map proper pushforward i_* and the second etale pullback j^*.
hypotheses: k perfect with resolution of singularities: the proof uses MVW Theorem 13.25 (perfect field with resolution) and Lemma 12.30; MVW Theorem 16.15 states only resolution (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E25).
X of finite type; Z closed and U = X - Z.
Platification (Raynaud-Gruson) and resolution are requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.4; Theorem 13.25 and the cdh topology from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a.
proofSteps: The sequence 0 -> z_equi(Z, 0) -> z_equi(X, 0) -> z_equi(U, 0) -> Q -> 0 of sheaves with transfers is exact; it suffices that C_*(Q) is acyclic.
By MVW Theorem 13.25 it suffices that Q_cdh = 0, and by Lemma 12.30 that every q in Q(S), S smooth, dies after a composite of blow-ups with smooth centres S' -> S.

Lift q to cycles W_a|U in U x S, quasi-finite and dominant over S, whose closures W_a in X x S are not quasi-finite; by platification there is a blow-up S' -> S over which the proper transforms are flat and dominant, and by resolution S' can be taken smooth with S' -> S a composite of blow-ups with smooth centres.
Then p^*(W_a) = j^*(W'_a) in z_equi(U, 0)(S') and p^*(q) = 0 in Q(S').
acceptance: For X = A^1 and Z the origin the triangle is Z -> Z(1)[2] -> M^c(G_m) ->; the first map lies in H^{2,1}(Spec k, Z) = 0, so M^c(G_m) = Z(1)[2] + Z[1].
Applying Hom gives the long exact sequences of MC.4/borel-moore-motivic-homology.
Without resolution of singularities the triangle is not available by this argument.

sources.excerpt: Assume that k admits resolution of singularities. If Z -> X is a closed subscheme with complement U -> X, there is a distinguished triangle: M^c(Z) -> M^c(X) -> M^c(U) -> M^c(Z)[1].
sources.match: The theorem, literally.

sources.excerpt: It is easy to see from the definitions that there is an exact sequence of sheaves with transfers: 0 -> z_equi(Z,0) -> z_equi(X,0) -> z_equi(U,0) -> Q -> 0. By 13.25 it suffices to show that Q_cdh = 0.
sources.match: The reduction the steps follow; 13.25 assumes k perfect.

nodes.title: The Kuenneth isomorphism for motives with compact support
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities. For schemes X and Y of finite type over k, M^c(X x Y) is isomorphic to M^c(X) tensor M^c(Y) in DM^eff,-_Nis(k); in particular M^c(X x A^i) is isomorphic to M^c(X)(i)[2i].
hypotheses: k perfect with resolution of singularities.

The comparison needs a natural map M^c(X) tensor M^c(Y) -> M^c(X x Y), the exterior product of equidimensional cycles; the source uses it without constructing it (it is part of the theory of Friedlander-Voevodsky's Bivariant cycle cohomology, not read; gap).
proofSteps: X and Y smooth and proper: M^c = M and M(X x Y) = M(X) tensor M(Y) (MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a).

X and Y proper: induct on dimension, using resolution and MC.4/blow-up-triangle-and-formula for both sides, compared through the natural map and the axioms of a tensor triangulated category (MVW 8A.1).
General X and Y: compactify and use MC.4/compact-support-localisation-triangle for the boundaries, with induction on dimension.
The last assertion from M^c(A^i) = Z(i)[2i] (MC.4/motives-with-compact-support).
acceptance: For X proper and smooth this is M(X x Y) = M(X) tensor M(Y) when Y is also proper and smooth.
M^c(G_m x G_m) = (Z(1)[2] + Z[1])^{tensor 2} has four summands.

sources.excerpt: For every X and Y, M^c(X x Y) = M^c(X) tensor^tr_{L,Nis} M^c(Y). In particular, M^c(X x A^i) = M^c(X)(i)[2i]. PROOF. If X and Y are smooth and proper, this is just the identity M(X x Y) = M(X) tensor^tr_{L,Nis} M(Y).
sources.match: The statement and the base case; the rest of the proof cites 13.26 and 16.15 with the axioms of 8A.1.

nodes.title: Motives with compact support are geometric
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities. For every scheme X of finite type over k, M^c(X) is an effective geometric motive.
hypotheses: k perfect with resolution of singularities.
An open embedding of X into a proper scheme (Nagata compactification) is requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.4.
proofSteps: X proper: M^c(X) = M(X), an effective geometric motive by MC.4/geometric-motives-generated-by-smooth-projective.

General X: embed X openly in a proper X-bar with closed complement Z; the triangle M^c(Z) -> M^c(X-bar) -> M^c(X) -> of MC.4/compact-support-localisation-triangle, with M^c(Z) geometric by induction on dimension, shows M^c(X) geometric, the subcategory being triangulated.
acceptance: M^c(A^i) = Z(i)[2i] is geometric.
M^c(G_m) = Z(1)[2] + Z[1] is geometric.
The argument needs resolution through the proper case.

sources.excerpt: For every scheme X in Sch/k, M^c(X) is in DM^eff_gm. PROOF. If X is proper, so that M^c(X) = M(X), this follows from (14.5.3), as pointed out in 14.1. The general case follows from this, using theorem 16.15.
sources.match: The statement and its proof, literally.

nodes.title: Bivariant cycle cohomology and the shifting theorem
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities and X a scheme of finite type. For r >= 0 and M in DM^eff,-_Nis(k) there are natural isomorphisms Hom(M(1)[2], C_*z_equi(X, r)) -> Hom(M, C_*z_equi(X, r + 1)) and Hom(M(r)[2r], M^c(X)) -> Hom(M, C_*z_equi(X, r)). For a flat map X -> Y of relative dimension r there is a morphism M^c(Y)(r)[2r] -> M^c(X).
hypotheses: k admits resolution of singularities (MVW's statement) and is perfect (as for MVW Theorem 14.20, which identifies the bivariant groups with Hom groups).
The first isomorphism is Friedlander-Voevodsky's theorem on bivariant cycle cohomology ([BivCy, 8.3]), cited without proof in the source; it is not proved in any source read here (gap).
proofSteps: Record the bivariant cycle cohomology A_{r,i}(Y, X), the cdh hypercohomology of C_*z_equi(X, r) on Y, and its identification with Hom(M(Y)[i], C_*z_equi(X, r)) via MVW 14.20 (Remark 16.21).
State Friedlander-Voevodsky's isomorphism A_{r,i}(Y(1)[2], X) = A_{r+1,i}(Y, X) (gap: [BivCy, 8.3] not obtained), and deduce the first isomorphism because the M(Y)[i] generate DM^eff,-_Nis.
The second isomorphism follows by induction on r, since M^c(X) = C_*z_equi(X, 0).
Corollary 16.23: flat pullback C_*z_equi(Y, 0) -> C_*z_equi(X, r) (MC.4/equidimensional-cycle-sheaves) and the second isomorphism with M = M^c(Y) give M^c(Y)(r)[2r] -> M^c(X).
acceptance: For r = 0 the second isomorphism is the identity of Hom(M, M^c(X)).
For the projection X x A^1 -> X the flat pullback is a map M^c(X)(1)[2] -> M^c(X x A^1), an isomorphism by MC.4/compact-support-kunneth.
The shifting theorem is what identifies Borel-Moore homology with higher Chow groups (MVW 19.18), which this layer does not plan.

sources.excerpt: Let X be in Sch/k, where k admits resolution of singularities. Then for any r >= 0 and any M in DM^{eff,-}_Nis, there are natural isomorphisms: Hom(M(1)[2],C_*z_equi(X,r)) -> Hom(M,C_*z_equi(X,r+1)); Hom(M(r)[2r],M^c(X)) -> Hom(M,C_*z_equi(X,r)).
sources.match: The theorem, literally.

sources.excerpt: In [BivCy, 8.3], they proved the following result: ... More precisely, they proved in [BivCy, 8.3] that there is a natural isomorphism A_{r,i}(Y(1)[2],X) = A_{r+1,i}(Y,X) for every X,Y in Sch/k.
sources.match: The source cites the result from Friedlander-Voevodsky and does not prove it.

sources.excerpt: Let X -> Y be a flat map of relative dimension r. Then we have a morphism in DM^{eff,-}_Nis: M^c(Y)(r)[2r] -> M^c(X).
sources.match: The flat pullback.

nodes.title: Friedlander-Voevodsky duality
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities and T a smooth scheme of dimension d over k. For schemes X and Y of finite type and every n there are canonical isomorphisms Hom(M(X x T)[n], M^c(Y)) -> Hom(M(X)(d)[2d + n], M^c(T x Y)) in DM^eff,-_Nis(k).
hypotheses: k perfect with resolution of singularities.
MVW cite the theorem from Friedlander-Voevodsky ([BivCy, 8.2]) and say that they cite it without proof; no source read here proves it (gap).
proofSteps: State the theorem as MVW do; its proof is Friedlander-Voevodsky, Bivariant cycle cohomology, Theorem 8.2, not read (gap).
Record the special cases used later: Y = A^d with M^c(A^d) = Z(d)[2d] and MC.4/compact-support-kunneth (the embedding of Chow motives); T = X smooth and Y = Spec k (the dual of M(X)).
acceptance: With T = Spec k (d = 0) both sides are Hom(M(X)[n], M^c(Y)).
With X = Y = Spec k and T = A^1: Hom(M(A^1)[n], Z) = Hom(Z(1)[2 + n], M^c(A^1)) = Hom(Z(1)[2 + n], Z(1)[2]), both Z for n = 0 and 0 otherwise.
It is the input of the duality M(X)^* = M^c(X)(-d)[-2d] and of the embedding of Chow motives.

sources.excerpt: The Duality Theorem below is also due to Friedlander and Voevodsky ([BivCy, 8.2]). We also cite it without proof. THEOREM 16.24. (Duality) Assume that k admits resolution of singularities. If T is a smooth scheme of dimension d over k then there are canonical isomorphisms
sources.match: The theorem and the source's statement that it is cited without proof.

sources.excerpt: Hom(M(X x T)[n],M^c(Y)) = Hom(M(X)(d)[2d+n],M^c(T x Y)).
sources.match: The isomorphism.

nodes.title: The dual of the motive of a smooth scheme
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities and X smooth of dimension d. The diagonal of X induces isomorphisms Delta_r: M^c(X)(r)[-2d] -> RHom(M(X), Z(d))(r) -> RHom(M(X), Z(d + r)) for r >= 0, where RHom(M(X), -) is the right adjoint of tensoring with M(X) (MVW Remark 14.12). Hence M^c(X) is isomorphic to RHom(M(X), Z(d))[2d], and RHom(M(X), Z(i)) is an effective geometric motive for i >= d.
hypotheses: k perfect with resolution of singularities (MVW Lecture 20).
X smooth of dimension d; MVW Corollary 20.4 is stated for X in Sch/k but its proof uses 20.3, which needs X smooth.
RHom and its adjunction are imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a (MVW 14.12).
proofSteps: For A = M(U)[n] with U smooth: Hom(A, M^c(X)(r)[-2d]) = Hom(A(d)[2d], M^c(X)(d + r)) by cancellation (M.5a), = Hom(A tensor M(X), Z(d + r)) by MC.4/friedlander-voevodsky-duality with T = X, = Hom(A, RHom(M(X), Z(d + r))) by adjunction.

The graph of the identity of X induces a natural map Delta_r; the class of A for which Hom(A, Delta_r) is bijective is triangulated, closed under direct sums and contains the generators M(U)[n], so it is all of DM^eff,-_Nis, and Delta_r is an isomorphism by Yoneda.
RHom(M(X), Z(d))(r) = RHom(M(X), Z(d + r)) by the same argument (MVW Exercise 20.5).
With MC.4/compact-support-geometric, RHom(M(X), Z(i)) is an effective geometric motive for i >= d.
acceptance: For X = Spec k, M^c(Spec k) = Z = RHom(Z, Z).
For X smooth projective, M(X) is isomorphic to RHom(M(X), Z(d))[2d].

sources.excerpt: If X is smooth of dimension d, the diagonal X -> X x X induces isomorphisms for r >= 0: Delta_r : M^c(X)(r)[-2d] = RHom(M(X),Z(d))(r) = RHom(M(X),Z(d+r)).
sources.match: The proposition, literally.

sources.excerpt: If X is smooth of dimension d, the dual M(X)^* is just an untwisting of M^c(X). To see this, we combine 20.3 with definition 20.6: M^c(X) = RHom(M(X),Z(d))[2d] = M(X)^*(d)[2d]. In particular, if X is projective then M(X) = M(X)^*(d)[2d].
sources.match: The consequence for the dual, which MC.4/geometric-motive-dual defines.

nodes.title: The dual of a geometric motive
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities. For M in DM_gm(k, Z) choose r with M(r) effective and set M^* = RHom(M(r), Z(i))(r - i) for i large; this is independent of r and i up to canonical isomorphism and lies in DM_gm. For X smooth of dimension d, M(X)^* = RHom(M(X), Z(d))(-d), isomorphic to M^c(X)(-d)[-2d]. M -> M^* is a contravariant triangulated functor on DM_gm with M(r)^* isomorphic to M^*(-r); M^* represents A -> Hom_gm(A tensor M, Z); and there is a natural evaluation epsilon_M: M^* tensor M -> Z adjoint to the identity of M^*.
hypotheses: k perfect with resolution of singularities; integral coefficients (MVW Lecture 20).
RHom is the internal Hom of MVW Remark 14.12, imported from MotivicEtaleKTheory:M.5a.
proofSteps: Independence of r and i: MVW Exercise 20.5 (RHom(M(X), L) = RHom(M(X)(1), L(1)), by the proof of 20.3) and MC.4/dual-of-motive-of-smooth-scheme; the object lies in DM_gm by 20.4.
Contravariant triangulated functor (MVW Lemma 20.7): on any finite diagram the dual agrees with the triangulated functor RHom(-, Z(i))(-i) for i large.

Representability (MVW Proposition 20.8): reduce to M effective by twisting; Hom_gm(A, M^*) = Hom(A(i), RHom(M, Z(i))) = Hom(A(i) tensor M, Z(i)) = Hom_gm(A tensor M, Z), by adjunction and cancellation.
epsilon_M is adjoint to the identity of M^* (MVW Corollary 20.9).
acceptance: The dual of the unit is the unit.
The dual is not RHom(-, Z): for the Lefschetz motive the two differ (MVW Remark 20.10).
For X smooth projective, M(X)^* = M(X)(-d)[-2d].

sources.excerpt: If X is in Sm/k and d = dimX, we define the dual to be: M(X)^* = RHom(M(X),Z(d))(-d). ... If M is any object of DM_gm, some twist M(r) is effective. We define the dual M^* to be RHom(M(r),Z(i))(r-i) for large i.
sources.match: The definition, literally.

sources.excerpt: The dual M^* of an object M in DM_gm represents the functor A -> Hom_gm(A tensor M,Z), in the sense that there is a natural isomorphism: Hom_gm(A,M^*) = Hom_gm(A tensor M,Z).
sources.match: The representability, literally.

nodes.title: Geometric motives are reflexive
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities. For M in DM_gm(k, Z) the map iota_M: M -> M^** adjoint to epsilon_M is a natural isomorphism.
hypotheses: k perfect with resolution of singularities.
proofSteps: Define iota_M through MVW Proposition 20.8 as the map adjoint to epsilon_M.
Both sides are triangulated functors of M; by MC.4/geometric-motives-generated-by-smooth-projective it suffices to treat M = M(X) with X smooth projective of dimension d.
For such X, M(X)^*(d) is M(X)[-2d] (MC.4/dual-of-motive-of-smooth-scheme), so (M(X)^*)^* = RHom(M(X)[-2d], Z(i))(d - i), isomorphic to M(X).

Check that this isomorphism is inverse to iota_{M(X)}; the source asserts this after 'a careful comparison' without writing it, and the diagram chase with the unit and counit of the adjunction must be written out.
acceptance: For M = Z, iota is the identity of Z.
Reflexivity fails for RHom(-, Z) in place of the dual, as the Lefschetz motive shows.

nodes.title: The dual of a tensor product
nodes.statement: Let k be a perfect field admitting resolution of singularities. For M and N in DM_gm(k, Z) the map M^* tensor N^* -> (M tensor N)^* induced by epsilon_M tensor epsilon_N is a natural isomorphism.
hypotheses: k perfect with resolution of singularities.
proofSteps: Construct the map from epsilon_M tensor epsilon_N through MVW Proposition 20.8.
Reduce to M = M(X) and N = M(Y) with X, Y smooth projective of dimensions d and e (MC.4/geometric-motives-generated-by-smooth-projective).

With L = Z(1)[2], M(X)^* tensor L^d = M(X) (MC.4/dual-of-motive-of-smooth-scheme), so M^* tensor N^* tensor L^{d+e} = M tensor N = (M tensor N)^* tensor L^{d+e}, and this isomorphism is the natural map.
acceptance: For M = N = Z both sides are Z.
For M = Z(a) and N = Z(b), both sides are Z(-a-b).
Together with the double dual isomorphism it gives bi-distributivity of the internal Hom.

nodes.title: Finite-dimensional comodules form an abelian category
nodes.statement: Let K be a field and C a coalgebra over K. The category of right C-comodules that are finite-dimensional over K (Tau Ceti's FGComoduleCat K C) is a K-linear abelian category, and the forgetful functor to finite-dimensional K-vector spaces is exact, faithful and reflects isomorphisms: the kernel and cokernel of a comodule map are computed on the underlying vector spaces and carry unique comodule structures making the canonical maps comodule maps.
hypotheses: K is a field, so that tensoring with C over K is exact.
The pinned Tau Ceti library has FGComoduleCat with its forgetful functors and monoidal, symmetric and rigid structures, but no preadditive or abelian structure; this lemma supplies it.
proofSteps: Show that comodule maps form K-vector spaces with bilinear composition, so that FGComoduleCat K C is K-linear.
For a comodule map f: M -> N, ker f is a subcomodule because the coaction maps it into ker(f tensor id_C) = ker f tensor C, by exactness of tensoring with C; coker f is a quotient comodule.

These are kernels and cokernels in the comodule category, finite-dimensional when M and N are; the canonical map from the coimage to the image is a comodule map that is bijective, hence an isomorphism, since a bijective comodule map has a comodule inverse.
Hence the category is abelian and the forgetful functor is exact, faithful and reflects isomorphisms.
acceptance: For C = K with the trivial comultiplication the category is finite-dimensional K-vector spaces.
Kernels are computed on underlying spaces; over a ring over which C is not flat this can fail, which is why the base is a field.
A bijective comodule map is an isomorphism of comodules.

nodes.title: The universal property of the diagram category
nodes.statement: Let R be a field, D a small diagram and T: D -> R-Mod a representation. For every R-linear abelian category A with a faithful exact R-linear functor f_A: A -> R-Mod and every representation F: D -> A with f_A o F = T, there is a faithful exact R-linear functor L: C(D, T) -> A with L o T~ isomorphic to F and f_A o L isomorphic to f_T, unique up to unique isomorphism (HMS Proposition B.8). In particular C(D, T) is functorial in D and T.
hypotheses: R is a field in the case used (HMS state it for R noetherian).

The source states the result and does not prove it ('Proof. [Le, N]. A detailed proof is given in [Br] or in [vW] Theorem 2.4'), and its introduction says the proof of universality is missing from its account; neither von Wangenheim's thesis nor Bruguieres' preprint was obtained (gap).
proofSteps: State the universal property.
Proof: not in the source read (gap); a source (von Wangenheim, Theorem 2.4) must be obtained before the node is built on.
Functoriality in (D, T) follows from uniqueness.
acceptance: Applied to A = C(D, T), f_A = f_T and F = T~ it gives L isomorphic to the identity.
Applied to the full subcategory generated by the T~(v) it gives generation (MC.5/diagram-category-generation).
It is the input of MC.5/diagram-localisation, MC.5/diagram-comparison and MC.6/fibre-functor-extension that the source does not prove.

nodes.title: The diagram category is generated by the vertices
nodes.statement: Let R be a field and T a representation of a small diagram D in R-Mod. (1) C(D, T) is its own smallest full abelian subcategory containing all T~(v); (2) every object of C(D, T) is a subquotient of a finite direct sum of objects T~(v); (3) if a: v -> v' is an edge with T(a) an isomorphism, then T~(a) is an isomorphism.
hypotheses: R is a field; the universal property is used for (1).
proofSteps: (1) The full subcategory C' generated by the T~(v) is abelian, the restriction of f_T is faithful and exact, and T~ factors through C'; the universal property gives C(D, T) -> C' inverse to the inclusion.
(2) The full subcategory of subquotients of finite direct sums of the T~(v) is closed under kernels, cokernels and finite sums, hence abelian, so it is C(D, T) by (1).
(3) f_T is faithful and exact between abelian categories, so it reflects isomorphisms.
acceptance: For a finite diagram with T(v) = Q for every vertex, every object is a subquotient of Q-sums of the T~(v).
Generation is by subquotients of finite direct sums, not by direct sums alone.
An edge sent to an isomorphism by T becomes an isomorphism in C(D, T).

sources.excerpt: (1) As an abelian category C(T) is generated by the T~(v) ... (2) Each object of C(T) is a subquotient of a finite direct sum of objects of the form T~(v). (3) If a : v -> v' is an edge in D such that T(a) is an isomorphism, then T~(a) is also an isomorphism.

nodes.title: Relative singular cohomology as a representation of the pair diagram
nodes.statement: Write X(C) for the complex points of a variety X over Q with the analytic topology. The representation H^* of the diagram D^eff of effective pairs in finite-dimensional Q-vector spaces sends (X, Y, i) to relative singular cohomology H^i(X(C), Y(C); Q), a functoriality edge f^*: (X', Y', i) -> (X, Y, i) to pullback along the map of pairs (X(C), Y(C)) -> (X'(C), Y'(C)), and a coboundary edge (Y, Z, i) -> (X, Y, i + 1) for X containing Y containing Z to the connecting map of the long exact sequence of the triple (X(C), Y(C), Z(C)); identity edges go to identities. Relative cohomology with rational coefficients is the Q-dual of relative singular homology with rational coefficients, so the long exact sequence of a triple is exact and its connecting map natural, being the transposes of the corresponding statements Tau Ceti proves for homology. Restricted to good pairs this is the representation H^* of HMS Section 1.
hypotheses: Varieties are reduced separated schemes of finite type over Q; Y and Z are closed.

The functor X -> X(C), the finite-dimensionality of H^*(X(C), Y(C); Q) and the relative Kuenneth isomorphism are requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2; relative singular homology with the long exact sequence of a triple and the naturality of its connecting map are in the pinned Tau Ceti library.

Cohomology is the dual of homology with Q coefficients (universal coefficients over a field); the connecting map in cohomology is the transpose of the homological one, with the sign convention fixed once.
proofSteps: Define H^i(X(C), Y(C); Q) as the dual of Tau Ceti's relative singular homology (TopPair.singularHomology) of the topological pair (X(C), Y(C)) with Q coefficients.
Functoriality edges go to the transposes of the pushforwards on homology of maps of pairs; identity edges to identities.
Coboundary edges go to the transposes of TauCeti.TopTriple.singularHomologyδ for the triple Z(C) in Y(C) in X(C).

Exactness of ... -> H^i(X, Y) -> H^i(X, Z) -> H^i(Y, Z) -> H^{i+1}(X, Y) -> ... and naturality for morphisms of triples, by dualising singularHomology_exact_inner, _total, _outer and singularHomologyδ_naturality (duality over a field is exact).
Restrict to good pairs, and extend to the localised diagram by Lemma B.21, using H^1(C^*, {1}; Q) = Q.
acceptance: (G_m, {1}, 1) goes to Q.
Exactness and functoriality of the long exact sequence of a triple are checked before the representation is used in the universal category, as the layer's acceptance asks.
(X, X, i) goes to 0 and (Spec Q, empty, 0) to Q.

sources.excerpt: We use the representation H^* : D_Nori -> Q-Mod which assigns to (X, Y, i) relative singular cohomology H^i(X(C), Y(C), Q).
sources.match: The representation on vertices; on edges it is the pullback and the connecting map, as the edges' names indicate.

In this case, it follows from the construction of R that there is a natural triangle R(X, Y) -> R(X, Z) -> R(Y, Z). We use the connecting morphism in cohomology to represent the edge

nodes.title: Nori's Basic Lemma
nodes.statement: Let k be a subfield of C, R a noetherian ring, X an affine scheme of finite type over k of dimension n and Z a closed subscheme of dimension at most n - 1. Then there is a closed subscheme Y containing Z with dim Y <= n - 1, H^i(X(C), Y(C); R) = 0 for i different from n and H^n(X(C), Y(C); R) a free R-module, so that (X, Y, n) is a good pair; moreover Y can be chosen with X - Y smooth. By induction on dimension every affine variety X has a very good filtration empty = F_{-1}X in F_0X in ... in F_nX = X, meaning that every (F_jX, F_{j-1}X, j) is very good (HMS Corollary D.11).
hypotheses: X affine of dimension n over a subfield k of C.
The source states the lemma without proof and attributes it to Nori, with a more general version by Beilinson ([B, Lemma 3.3]) and a similar argument by Vilonen; none of these was read (gap).
proofSteps: State the lemma as the source does; its proof is not in the source read (gap), and a source (Beilinson, On the derived category of perverse sheaves, Lemma 3.3, or Nori's notes) must be obtained before the node is built on.

Corollary D.11: put F_nX = X, choose a closed subvariety of dimension n - 1 containing the singular locus, apply the lemma to get F_{n-1}X with (F_nX, F_{n-1}X, n) good and F_nX - F_{n-1}X smooth, hence very good (the source misprints the smooth stratum: MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E33), and continue by induction.
Corollary D.12: very good filtrations of X form a filtered system, functorial in X, by the same induction.
acceptance: For n = 0 the lemma holds with Y empty.
For X = A^1 and Z empty, Y can be any nonempty finite set of r points: H^1(C, Y(C); R) = R^{r-1} and the other groups vanish.
The resulting pairs are very good, which is how very good pairs arise.

sources.excerpt: (Basic Lemma of Nori). Let X be an affine scheme of finite type over k in C of dimension n and Z in X be a closed subscheme of dimension <= n - 1. Then there is a closed subscheme Y containing Z such that (X, Y, n) is a good pair.
sources.match: The lemma; the three bullet conditions and 'Moreover X - Y can be chosen smooth' follow in the source.

sources.excerpt: A similar result holds in arbitrary characteristic by work of Beilinson [B, Lemma 3.3] and Kari Vilonen apparently used similar methods in his Master thesis [V].

nodes.title: The realisation functor on complexes of varieties
nodes.statement: Let R be a noetherian ring, A an R-linear abelian category with a faithful exact functor to R-Mod, and T a representation of the diagram of effective very good pairs in A. There is a natural contravariant triangulated functor R: C^b(Z[Var]) -> D^b(A), on bounded homological complexes of varieties with formal Z-linear combinations of morphisms, such that for every good pair (X, Y, i) the cohomology H^j(R(Cone(Y -> X))) vanishes for j different from i, equals T(X, Y, i) when the pair is very good, and whose composite with D^b(A) -> D^b(R-Mod) computes singular cohomology of X(C). For a rigidified affine cover of X with Cech complex C_*, R(X) -> R(C_*) is an isomorphism (HMS Corollary D.19).
hypotheses: The source's proof constructs R on objects and morphisms through rigidified affine covers (D.5-D.9), Cech complexes (D.10), very good filtrations from the Basic Lemma (D.11-D.16) and the cellular complexes of D.17, and asserts that different choices give isomorphic objects; it does not verify that R is triangulated or compute the cohomology of R(Cone(Y -> X)) (gap: MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E31).
The source's statement writes T(X, Y, i) for every good pair although T is defined only on very good pairs (part of E31).
The construction lands in D^+(A) in the source's proof; boundedness uses that covers are finite.
proofSteps: Rigidified affine covers of varieties and of bounded complexes of varieties form non-empty filtered functorial systems (D.5-D.9).
Take the Cech double complex of affine varieties attached to a cover (D.10).
Very good filtrations exist on affine varieties, on covers and on complexes, and form filtered functorial systems (D.11, D.12, D.14, D.16), by induction from MC.5/basic-lemma.

For an affine X with very good filtration F, let R~(F.X) be the complex ... -> T(F_jX, F_{j-1}X, j) -> T(F_{j+1}X, F_jX, j+1) -> ... whose differentials are the images of coboundary edges (D.17); for complexes take total complexes.

Define R(X_*) as R~ of the total Cech complex for a choice of cover and filtration, and R(f) through common refinements; prove that different choices give canonically isomorphic objects, that R is triangulated, and that for a good pair the cohomology of R(Cone(Y -> X)) is concentrated in degree i, by comparing with singular cohomology through the faithful exact fibre functor (steps not written in the source).
Corollary D.19 from the construction.
acceptance: For X affine with a very good filtration F, R(X) is represented by R~(F.X), whose realisation is the cellular cochain complex of the filtration.
R(Spec Q) is T(Spec Q, empty, 0) in degree 0.
Corollary D.19 is what computes H^2_Nori(P^1) from the standard cover in Lemma 1.12.

nodes.title: Generators of Nori motives from normal crossings pairs
nodes.statement: Every object of MM^eff_Nori is a subquotient of a finite direct sum of objects H^i_Nori(X, Y) for good pairs (X, Y, i) with X = W - W_inf and Y = W_0 - (W_0 intersect W_inf), where W is smooth projective over Q and W_0 union W_inf is a divisor with normal crossings. The source does not claim that the diagram of such pairs gives the same category: it may have too few relations (HMS Remark 1.9).
hypotheses: Resolution of singularities in characteristic zero, in the form of a proper surjection from such a W - W_inf that is an isomorphism over X - Y, is requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.4; normal crossings divisors from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.3.
Proper base change in the form of excision for such pairs is requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2.
proofSteps: By MC.5/diagram-category-generation and MC.5/diagram-comparison every object is a subquotient of a finite direct sum of H^i_Nori(X, Y) with (X, Y, i) very good.
Resolution gives W smooth projective, a normal crossings divisor W_0 union W_inf and a proper surjective pi: W - W_inf -> X with pi^{-1}(Y) = W_0 - W_inf and pi an isomorphism over X - Y.
Then H^i_Nori(W - W_inf, W_0 - (W_0 intersect W_inf)) -> H^i_Nori(X, Y) is an isomorphism, because it is one in singular cohomology (excision) and the fibre functor reflects isomorphisms.
acceptance: For X = A^1 and Y = {0, 1}, W = P^1, W_inf = {infinity} and W_0 = {0, 1}.
The pairs obtained are good but not very good in general (Remark 1.9).
The corollary gives generators, not a presentation.

sources.excerpt: Every object of MM^eff_Nori is subquotient of a direct sum of objects of the form H^i_Nori(X, Y) for a good pair (X, Y, i) where X = W - W_inf and Y = W_0 - (W_0 intersect W_inf) with W smooth projective, W_inf union W_0 a divisor with normal crossings.

nodes.title: Top cohomology of projective space and of projective varieties
nodes.statement: (1) For N >= n >= 0, H^{2n}_Nori(P^N) is isomorphic to 1(-n). (2) Let Z be a projective variety over Q of dimension n that is geometrically irreducible. Then H^{2n}_Nori(Z) is isomorphic to 1(-n). HMS Lemma 1.12(2) omits geometric irreducibility and is false without it (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E28).
hypotheses: (2) needs Z geometrically irreducible: for Z the union of two rational points of P^1, or Z = Spec Q(i), H^0(Z(C); Q) is two-dimensional.
The realisation functor, its Cech descent and the tensor structure are those of the nodes cited.
proofSteps: (1) Linear embeddings P^n in P^N induce isomorphisms on H^{2n} in singular cohomology, hence in MM_Nori, since the fibre functor reflects isomorphisms; so it suffices to treat H^{2N}(P^N).

For P^1, Corollary D.19 (MC.5/cellular-realisation-functor) for the cover by A^1 and P^1 - 0 gives R(P^1) isomorphic to Cone(R(A^1) + R(P^1 - 0) -> R(G_m))[-1], hence H^2_Nori(P^1) isomorphic to H^1_Nori(G_m) = 1(-1).
For P^N, the Cech complex of the standard affine cover relates H^{2N}_Nori(P^N) with H^N_Nori(G_m^N), which is 1(-1)^{tensor N} by the Kuenneth isomorphism in MM_Nori (MC.5/nori-tensor-category).

(2) Embed Z in P^N; restriction H^{2n}_Nori(P^N) -> H^{2n}_Nori(Z) is multiplication by deg Z on the one-dimensional H^{2n}(Z(C); Q) (Z geometrically irreducible), an isomorphism in singular cohomology and hence in MM_Nori. The source writes this arrow in the opposite direction (E28).
acceptance: H^2_Nori(P^1) is isomorphic to 1(-1).
For Z two rational points of P^1 (n = 0), H^0_Nori(Z) has rank two and is not 1(0).
For Z = Spec Q(i), H^0_Nori(Z) is the two-dimensional Artin motive of Q(i), not 1(0).

sources.excerpt: (1) H^{2n}_Nori(P^N) = 1(-n) for N >= n >= 0. (2) Let Z be a projective variety of dimension n. Then H^{2n}_Nori(Z) = 1(-n).
sources.match: The two statements as printed; (2) needs geometric irreducibility (E28).

sources.excerpt: (2) Let Z in P^N be a closed immersion with N large enough. Then H^{2n}_Nori(Z) -> H^{2n}_Nori(P^N) is an isomorphism in MM_Nori because it is in singular cohomology.
sources.match: The proof; the map is the restriction from P^N to Z.

nodes.title: The Gysin isomorphism for a smooth pair in Nori motives
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth variety over Q and Z a smooth closed subvariety of pure codimension n that is geometrically connected. Then H^{2n}_Z(X) is isomorphic to 1(-n) in MM_Nori. Without geometric connectedness the argument gives H^{2n}_Z(X) isomorphic to H^0_Nori(Z) tensor 1(-n); HMS Lemma 1.12(3) asks only that Z be irreducible, which is not enough (MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E28).
hypotheses: Z smooth, of pure codimension n, geometrically connected (for Z smooth this is geometric irreducibility).

The Thom (Gysin) isomorphism H^0(Z) -> H^{2n}_Z(X) in singular cohomology, and the Kuenneth formula with supports, are requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2; the deformation to the normal cone from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.4.
proofSteps: In singular cohomology H^0(Z(C); Q) -> H^{2n}_{Z(C)}(X(C); Q) is an isomorphism.

Deformation to the normal cone D(X, Z) -> A^1: Z x A^1 in D(X, Z) of codimension n restricts to Z in X over 1 and to the zero section Z in N_Z X over 0; with homotopy invariance the maps H^{2n}_Z(X) <- H^{2n}_{Z x A^1}(D(X, Z)) -> H^{2n}_Z(N_Z X) are isomorphisms in singular cohomology, hence in MM_Nori.
Restrict to a dense open U of Z over which N_Z X is trivial: H^{2n}_Z(N_Z X) -> H^{2n}_U(pi^{-1}(U)) is an isomorphism, both groups being H^0 of Z, respectively U.

For a trivial bundle, H^{2n}_{U x 0}(U x A^n) is H^0_Nori(U) tensor H^{2n}_0(A^n) by the Kuenneth formula with supports, and H^{2n}_0(A^n) is H^2_0(A^1)^{tensor n} with H^2_0(A^1) isomorphic to H^1_Nori(G_m) = 1(-1) by MC.5/cohomology-with-supports for 0 in A^1.
With Z geometrically connected, H^0_Nori(Z) = 1.

nodes.title: The duality morphism for pairs from a normal crossings divisor
nodes.statement: Let W be a smooth projective variety over Q of dimension i that is geometrically connected, and W_0, W_inf divisors with W_0 union W_inf a normal crossings divisor. Put X = W - W_inf, Y = W_0 - (W_0 intersect W_inf), X' = W - W_0 and Y' = W_inf - (W_0 intersect W_inf), and assume (X, Y) is very good. Then there is a morphism q: 1 -> H^i_Nori(X, Y) tensor H^i_Nori(X', Y')(i) in MM_Nori whose image under the fibre functor is dual to a perfect pairing.
hypotheses: W geometrically connected is used through MC.5/nori-gysin-isomorphism for the diagonal; for general W replace 1(-i) by H^0_Nori(W)(-i) and compose with the unit 1 -> H^0_Nori(W).

Poincare-Lefschetz duality between the two pairs in singular cohomology (the duality of j_* and j_! on W) is requested from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.2; normal crossings divisors from SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.3.
proofSteps: In singular cohomology the two pairs are Poincare dual, so both are good pairs.
Kuenneth (MC.5/nori-tensor-category): H^i_Nori(X, Y) tensor H^i_Nori(X', Y') is H^{2i}_Nori(X x X', X x Y' union Y x X').

With Delta the diagonal of W - (W_0 union W_inf), X x Y' union X' x Y lies in X x X' - Delta, so cohomology with supports (MC.5/cohomology-with-supports) gives H^{2i}_Delta(X x X') -> H^{2i}_Nori(X x X', X x Y' union Y x X'), and functoriality gives H^{2i}_{Delta-bar}(W x W) -> H^{2i}_Delta(X x X') for the diagonal Delta-bar of W.
H^{2i}_{Delta-bar}(W x W) is 1(-i) by MC.5/nori-gysin-isomorphism.
Twist the composite by (i) to get q; its dual under the fibre functor is the Poincare duality pairing, hence perfect.
acceptance: For W = P^1, W_0 = {0}, W_inf = {infinity} and i = 1, q pairs H^1(A^1, {0}) = 0 with itself trivially.
For W = P^1, W_0 = {0, 1}, W_inf = {infinity}: H^1(A^1, {0, 1}) = Q is paired with H^1(P^1 - {0, 1}, {infinity}) = Q.
The pairing realises Poincare duality for the relative cohomology of the two pairs.

nodes.title: Nori's rigidity criterion
nodes.statement: Let R be a field or a Dedekind domain, C an R-linear abelian tensor category (associative, commutative, unital) and T: C -> R-Mod a faithful tensor functor, so that T(1) = R. Suppose a set of objects V_i generates C as an abelian tensor category and for each V_i there are an object W_i and a morphism q_i: V_i tensor W_i -> 1, or q_i: 1 -> V_i tensor W_i, with T(q_i), respectively its dual, a perfect pairing of free R-modules. Then C is rigid: every V has a dual V^dual with Hom(V tensor A, B) = Hom(A, V^dual tensor B) and Hom(V^dual tensor A, B) = Hom(A, V tensor B); equivalently the bialgebra of the Tannaka dual is a Hopf algebra (HMS Proposition C.4 and Remark C.5).
hypotheses: C is commutative: the commutativity constraint is used to factor through a symmetric algebra.

The 'standard Tannakian formalism' step (a full abelian tensor subcategory generated by one object is comodules over a bialgebra of finite type) is cited from Deligne-Milne, not read; for a diagram category over a field it follows from MC.5/diagram-category applied to the restricted representation.
proofSteps: Replace V_i by V_i + W_i with the symmetric pairing q'_i, and for finite J take V_J the sum of the V_j with the orthogonal sum q_J; C is the union of the subcategories generated by the V_J.
By the Tannakian formalism each of these is comodules over a bialgebra A_J and C is comodules over the colimit A; it suffices that each A_J is a Hopf algebra.

Lemma C.3: A_J is a quotient of the sum of the End(T(V)^{tensor n})^dual, which factors through the symmetric algebra of End(T(V))^dual by the commutativity constraint; compatibility with q gives the equations X^t a X = a on matrix coefficients, so Spec A_J is a closed submonoid of the isometry group G(q).

Lemma C.6: a closed submonoid M with 1 in M(R) of an algebraic group G of finite type over a noetherian R is a group: for g in M(R) the chain M, gM, g^2M, ... of closed subschemes stabilises, so gM = M.
Hence each A_J and A are Hopf algebras; for a comodule category over a field, rigidity then follows from Tau Ceti's instRigidCategory.
acceptance: For C finite-dimensional vector spaces and T the identity, the criterion holds with V = K and q the multiplication.
For the monoid scheme of all endomorphisms (no pairing) the criterion does not apply and the Tannaka dual is only a monoid.
The criterion is applied to Nori motives in the dual form, with q: 1 -> V tensor W.

nodes.title: The left and right groups of a nonempty heap
nodes.statement: Let X be a nonempty heap. On X × X put μ_l((a, b), (c, d)) = ((a, b, c), d). Then μ_l is associative with left neutral elements (x, x); the relation (a, b) ∼_l μ_l((a, b), (x, x)), x in X, is an equivalence relation, μ_l descends to G_l = (X × X)/∼_l, and G_l is a group with inverse [(a, b)]⁻¹ = [(b, a)], acting on X on the left by [(a, b)]·x = (a, b, x); this action is simply transitive and the heap operation factors through it. For e in X the map x ↦ [(x, e)] is a group isomorphism from the group G_e of Lemma A.3 to G_l, with inverse [(a, b)] ↦ (a, b, e). Symmetrically μ_r((a, b), (c, d)) = (a, (b, c, d)) defines a group G_r acting simply transitively on the right.
hypotheses: X is a nonempty heap; for the empty heap the quotient is empty and is not a group (finding MotivesAndAlgebraicCycles/E42).
The construction chooses no point; a point e is used only to compare G_l with G_e.
proofSteps: Prove associativity of μ_l and that each (x, x) is a left neutral element, from axioms (2) and (1).
Prove that ∼_l is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, by the chains of equalities in the source.
Show that μ_l is well defined on classes, that [(x, x)] is a two-sided neutral element and [(b, a)] an inverse, so G_l is a group; nonemptiness of X provides the neutral element.
Define the action [(a, b)]·x = (a, b, x) and check its compatibility with μ_l and with ∼_l from axiom (2).
For e in X show that x ↦ [(x, e)] is a homomorphism from G_e with inverse [(a, b)] ↦ (a, b, e); simple transitivity follows because G_e acts on itself simply transitively.
Repeat with μ_r and the relation with the opposite order for G_r; the source leaves this case to the reader, and it is the mirror image of the left case.
acceptance: For the heap of a group G, the left group is canonically isomorphic to G acting by left translation, and the right group to G acting by right translation.
The two groups are defined without choosing a point and are identified with G_e only after a point e is chosen.
For the empty heap the construction gives no group; the hypothesis that X be nonempty is required.

nodes.title: Torsors in the category of affine schemes
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring. An affine heap over R (a torsor in the category of affine R-schemes in the sense of Definition A.5) is an affine R-scheme X = Spec A with a morphism X × X × X → X of R-schemes, products taken over R, which on S-valued points is a heap for every R-algebra S; equivalently the two heap axioms hold as identities of morphisms of schemes. Dually it is an R-algebra homomorphism A → A ⊗_R A ⊗_R A whose induced operation on the S-points Hom(A, S) is a heap operation for every R-algebra S. A morphism of affine heaps is an algebra homomorphism compatible with these maps.
hypotheses: X is affine over the base ring R and products are fibre products over R.
No section of X over R is assumed; X may have no R-point.
proofSteps: Define an affine heap as a morphism of affine R-schemes X × X × X → X together with the two heap axioms as equalities of morphisms.
Show, by the Yoneda lemma, that this is equivalent to asking that the operation on S-valued points is a heap for every R-algebra S.
Dualise to an R-algebra homomorphism A → A ⊗ A ⊗ A.
Record that the affine group scheme of a commutative Hopf algebra is an affine heap, with operation g h⁻¹ k on points.
acceptance: The affine group scheme of a commutative Hopf algebra is an affine heap with operation g h⁻¹ k on points.
An affine heap need not have an R-point; its group structures appear only after a point is chosen or through Proposition A.6.
The heap axioms are identities of morphisms of schemes, not only of R-points.

nodes.title: A nonempty affine torsor carries affine group schemes on both sides
nodes.statement: Let X be a nonempty affine heap over a field k. Then there are affine group schemes G_l and G_r over k acting on X on the left and on the right such that X is a G_l-torsor and a G_r-torsor; G_l is the quotient of X × X by the equivalence relation of Proposition A.4, formed as an affine scheme, and G_r likewise.
hypotheses: X is a nonempty affine heap over a field; for the empty heap the statement fails (finding E42).
The quotient of X × X by the relation R = X × X × X, with p₀(a, b, x) = (a, b) and p₁(a, b, x) = ((a, b, x), x), is taken from SGA 3, Exposé VII, Theorem 1.4, which was not obtained (gap).
proofSteps: Form R = X × X × X with the maps p₀ and p₁; p₀ is flat, being a base change of X over the field.

Show that (p₀, p₁) : R → (X × X) × (X × X) is a closed immersion, a graph-type morphism into a separated scheme, and that on T-points its image is an equivalence relation for every T, by Proposition A.4 applied to T-points.
Apply the quotient theorem of SGA 3 (gap) to obtain the affine quotient G_l = (X × X)/R, and descend μ_l and the action to morphisms of schemes.
Check the group scheme axioms and that (g, x) ↦ (g x, x) is an isomorphism G_l × X → X × X, from Proposition A.4 on T-points; G_r is the mirror image.
acceptance: For the affine heap of an affine group scheme G, the groups G_l and G_r are G acting by left and right translation.
The theorem is not on the path to the period torsor: there the two groups are the tensor automorphism groups of the two fibre functors, acting by composition, and no quotient is formed.
The hypothesis that X be nonempty is needed.

nodes.title: A commutative bialgebra with a rigid comodule category is a Hopf algebra
nodes.statement: Let B be a commutative bialgebra over a field k such that the tensor category of finite dimensional B-comodules is rigid. Then, for every commutative k-algebra R, every tensor endomorphism of the forgetful functor extended to R is an automorphism; hence the affine monoid scheme Spec B, which represents these tensor endomorphisms, is a group scheme, and B has a unique antipode making it a commutative Hopf algebra.
hypotheses: B is a commutative bialgebra over a field k, and its finite dimensional comodules, with the tensor product of the bialgebra and the forgetful functor, form a tensor category.
That category is rigid.
proofSteps: Identify the tensor endomorphisms of the forgetful functor extended to R with the algebra maps B → R, so that End⊗ is represented by the affine monoid scheme Spec B; this part of Deligne and Milne's proof of their Theorem 2.11 uses no rigidity.

Apply Deligne and Milne's Proposition 1.13, that a morphism between tensor functors from a rigid category to a rigid category is an isomorphism, to the forgetful functor extended to R, whose target category of finitely generated projective R-modules is rigid.
Conclude that every R-point of the monoid scheme is invertible, naturally in R; by the Yoneda lemma the inversion comes from a unique algebra map B → B, which is the antipode.
Record the converse, which the pinned library proves: the finite dimensional comodules over a commutative Hopf algebra over a field form a rigid category.
acceptance: With the pinned converse, rigidity of the comodule category and existence of an antipode are equivalent for commutative bialgebras over a field.
The bialgebra k[t] with t group-like has a non-rigid comodule category, the one-dimensional comodule with coaction 1 ↦ 1 ⊗ t having no dual, and k[t] has no antipode.
The lemma is what makes Nori's category a category of representations of a group and not only of a monoid.

nodes.title: The scheme of tensor isomorphisms between two fibre functors on a diagram category
nodes.statement: In the setting of Section 3, with T_1 and T_2 unital graded multiplicative representations of the same diagram over Q, a multiplicative comparison isomorphism over a field K ⊃ Q and C(T_1) neutral Tannakian, let T_2 also denote its extension to a tensor fibre functor on C(T_1) (MC.6/fibre-functor-extension). The functor on commutative Q-algebras R ↦ Iso⊗(T_1 ⊗ R, T_2 ⊗ R) is represented by the affine scheme X_{1,2} = Spec A_{1,2}, and likewise X_{2,1} = Spec A_{2,1}. Composition of tensor isomorphisms gives natural morphisms X_{1,2} × X_{2,1} → G_1, X_{2,1} × X_{1,2} → G_2, G_1 × X_{1,2} → X_{1,2} and X_{1,2} × G_2 → X_{1,2}, with G_i the tensor automorphism group of T_i.
hypotheses: T_1 and T_2 are unital graded multiplicative representations over Q and the comparison isomorphism is compatible with the multiplicative structure (finding E36).
C(T_1) is neutral Tannakian, and G_1, G_2 are as in MC.6/tensor-automorphism-group.
proofSteps: Describe the R-points of Spec A_{1,2}: algebra maps A_{1,2} → R are compatible families, over finite subdiagrams F, of R-linear maps T_1|F ⊗ R → T_2|F ⊗ R commuting with the edges and respecting the product structure, by the duality defining A_{1,2}.

Identify such families with tensor morphisms f_{T_1} ⊗ R → T_2 ⊗ R on C(T_1), using that C(T_1) is generated by the objects attached to vertices (Proposition B.9) and its description by finite comodules.

Show that every tensor morphism is an isomorphism, by rigidity and Deligne and Milne's Proposition 1.13 (the second step of MC.6/rigid-bialgebra-is-hopf), so that the functor of tensor isomorphisms is represented by Spec A_{1,2}.

Construct the composition morphisms and check that they are morphisms of affine schemes, dually by the coactions of MC.6/comparison-algebra and the maps A_1 → A_{1,2} ⊗ A_{2,1} and A_2 → A_{2,1} ⊗ A_{1,2}.
acceptance: For T_1 = T_2 the scheme is the group G_1 and the composition morphisms are its multiplication and its actions on itself.
The scheme has a complex point, the comparison isomorphism (MC.6/period-point); no rational point is asserted.
Faithful flatness over Q and the torsor property are the general statement MC.6/tensor-iso-torsor.

nodes.title: Tensor morphisms between fibre functors form a torsor
nodes.statement: Let C be a neutral Tannakian category over a field k with fibre functor ω and G = Aut⊗(ω), and let η be a fibre functor on C with values in a commutative k-algebra R. Then the functor Hom⊗(ω, η) on R-algebras is represented by an affine scheme faithfully flat over Spec R, every tensor morphism from ω to η is an isomorphism, and Hom⊗(ω, η) is a G-torsor over R. In this packet C is the category of finite dimensional comodules over a commutative Hopf algebra, which by MC.6/tensor-automorphism-group covers every neutral Tannakian category it uses.
hypotheses: C is neutral Tannakian over the field k with fibre functor ω; η is exact, faithful, k-linear and tensor, with values in finitely generated projective R-modules.
Deligne and Milne's Remark 3.3(b) allows C to be replaced by the finite dimensional representations of G with its forgetful functor.
proofSteps: For each object X define the ring P_X of Deligne and Milne's proof and represent Hom⊗(ω, η) by η applied to the ind-algebra (P_X^∨)_X, whose image under ω is the coordinate ring of G.
Show that η(P_X^∨) is a projective R-module for each X, so that the colimit is flat over R.
Use the surjection P_X → 1 and the exact sequence 0 → 1 → P_X^∨ → P_X^∨/1 → 0 to see that the colimit is faithfully flat over R.
Every tensor morphism is an isomorphism by Proposition 1.13, and G acts on Hom⊗(ω, η) by composition; faithful flatness makes it a G-torsor.
acceptance: For η = ω the torsor is G itself, trivial.

For C(T_1) with η the extension of T_2 and R = Q, the theorem makes X_{1,2} = Spec A_{1,2} faithfully flat over Q and a G_1-torsor; applied with the roles of T_1 and T_2 exchanged it makes it a G_2-torsor.
The theorem is the general form of the tensor isomorphism torsors the layer exports; the unipotent path torsors of AnabelianGeometryAndNonabelianChabauty:NC.2 are special cases.

sources.locator: Theorem 3.2(a) with its proof, and Remark 3.3 (pages 30 to 31), in the corrected version of 2012
sources.excerpt: THEOREM 3.2. Let C be a neutral Tannakian category over k: (a) For any ﬁbre functor η on C with values in R, Hom⊗(ω,η) is representable by an afﬁne scheme faithfully ﬂat over Spec R; it is therefore a G-torsor.
sources.match: The node is part (a) of that theorem; part (b), the equivalence between fibre functors and torsors, is not needed here.
